ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Prologue: Kael's Tale
p: I've been told I have a flair for the dramatic.
My queen—my beloved Glacia—says it's because I spent too many centuries as a force of nature rather than a man, and forces of nature don't do anything by halves.
She's probably right. She usually is.

But tonight, on this anniversary of our freedom, standing before you all in the great hall of Frostspire with snowflakes drifting lazily through the enchanted ceiling and my people gathered close with cups of mulled wine and eager faces, I think a little drama is warranted.
After all, you've come to hear a story. Not just any story
—the story.
The one you think you already know. I can see it in your eyes, especially you children in the front row, practically vibrating with excitement.
You know about the Snow Queen, don't you? The beautiful, terrible ice witch who stole a boy named Kai and imprisoned him in her frozen palace.
You know about brave little Gerda who journeyed across the world to save him, whose warm tears melted the ice in his heart and broke the Snow Queen's wicked spell.
It's a good story. Simple. Clean. A villain defeated, a hero triumphant, love conquering all.
It's also almost entirely wrong.
That gets your attention, doesn't it?

I see the adults shifting in their seats, exchanging glances. Some of you look skeptical. Others intrigued. A few of you—those who've lived in Frostspire long enough to know us—are already smiling, because you've suspected the truth all along.
The real story is so much stranger, so much more complicated, and so much more beautiful than the tale the world has told itself for the past century.

It involves not one curse but two, not one magical artifact but a mirror forged in hell itself, not one immortal being but six—four sister goddesses of the seasons, a sorceress, and one very old, very foolish force of winter who didn't understand what love was until it was almost too late.

That would be me, in case you're wondering. My name is Kael. I am the Ice King of Frostspire, husband to Queen Glacia, and once upon a time I was something else entirely. Something ancient and wild and not quite human.
Old Man Winter, they called me. A primordial force given form and consciousness, tasked with bringing the cold and snow to the world each year. I was also, for a very long time, a polar bear.
That part of the story, at least, they got right. But Gerda wasn't the hero. Glacia wasn't the villain. And the love story everyone remembers? It wasn't even the right one.
This is the right one. Mine and Glacia's. A tale of how winter learned to love, and how love learned to forgive itself.

I glance up at the dais where my queen sits, serene and radiant in her gown of ice and starlight, and she meets my eyes with the smallest smile—the kind only I can read after all our years together. She's given me permission to tell this tale, though it costs her something to have her pain laid bare. But she agrees it's time.
Time for the truth.

Time for you to understand that the Snow Queen never stole anyone. That she was a victim long before she was ever called a villain. That the mirror shard in young Kai's eye was only one piece of a much larger, much more terrible puzzle—and that the real question was never how to save a boy from the Snow Queen, but how to save the Snow Queen herself.

How to save someone who's forgotten how to feel. How to love someone who's been corrupted by demonic magic into something cold and cruel. How to break a curse when breaking it might destroy the very person you're trying to save.
These are not simple questions. The answers required sacrifice.
Blood. Death. Transformation.

They required a love story for the ages. So settle in, my friends. Pour another cup of wine. Pull the little ones onto your laps and stoke the fires high, because this is a tale of winter, and winter is never brief.
This is a story that spans centuries, that crosses realms, that involves goddesses and demons and magic both beautiful and terrible. This is the story of how the Snow Queen found her heart.
And how I found mine.

Let me tell you how it really happened, starting not with Gerda or Kai or even with me, but with five sisters and a mirror that should never have been made. Let me tell you about the day winter itself shattered, and how we spent the next hundred years trying to piece it back together.
Let me tell you the truth of winter.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 1: The Reflection
p: This is how it all began...

The sisters were old when the world was young. Not goddesses, exactly—they would have bristled at the word—but something close enough that mortals couldn't tell the difference and good enough for our purposes.

Elemental forces given form and consciousness, each one bound to an aspect of the turning year, each one powerful enough to reshape the world with a thought. There was Talia, where she walked, life erupted from the earth. She was all soft curves and gentle hands, with flowers perpetually tangled in her hair and dirt under her fingernails from coaxing reluctant seeds to grow. She mothered everything—plants, animals, lost travelers, her sisters. Especially her sisters. She couldn't help herself. It was her nature to nurture, to fuss, to encourage growth even when growth wasn't wanted. Then was Alessia the Queen of Summer, regal and resplendent, crowned in golden light. She presided over abundance, over the peak of life's power, over long days and warm nights and fields heavy with grain. She was generous but demanding, warm but fierce. She knew her worth and expected others to recognize it too. Of all the sisters, she was the one most comfortable with her power, the one who never questioned whether she deserved the realm she'd been given.

Autumn was Cora, and she understood what her sisters did not: that all things must end so that new things can begin. She walked through forests ablaze with color, gathering the harvest, preparing the world for sleep. She was wise in the way that only those who've watched countless cycles of death and rebirth can be wise. She didn't fear endings. She saw them as transformations, as necessary transitions. And because of this, she understood Glacia better than anyone.

Marina was the youngest, though "young" is a relative term when you're discussing beings who remember the first frost and the first thaw. She was the embodiment of Water itself—rivers and lakes and rain and mist—not yet bound to a single realm, not yet the Lady of the Lake she would become. She flowed between her sisters' domains, connecting them, visiting them, never staying long enough to put down roots. She was mercurial, changeable, sometimes shallow and sometimes impossibly deep.

And then there was Glacia. Winter. The eldest, though she never claimed the authority that should have come with age. The most powerful, though she wielded that power with reluctance. The most necessary, though she could never quite believe it.

Glacia told me once, in a moment of rare vulnerability, that she remembered the first time she understood what she really was. She'd been walking through a forest in early autumn—Cora's time, really, but the seasons weren't so rigidly defined back then—and everywhere she stepped, frost spread like a disease. Flowers blackened. Leaves fell. A rabbit, too slow to flee, had frozen solid mid-hop. She'd wept over that rabbit for three days.

"I thought I was broken," she told me, her voice barely a whisper. "I thought something had gone wrong when I was made. That I was supposed to be like Talia, bringing life, but instead I only brought death."

The tragedy of Glacia was that she never saw herself clearly. She saw only what she took away, never what she gave. She saw the flowers dying but not the earth resting. She saw the frost but not the beauty of ice crystals catching the light. She saw the silence of winter but not its peace.

Her sisters tried to help, in their way. But they were wrapped up in their own realms, their own responsibilities, their own understanding of their purpose. They loved each other—of course they did, with the fierce loyalty of those who've known each other since before memory—but they were also estranged in the way that immortal families often are. Too much time, too much space, too many centuries of small hurts and misunderstandings that never quite healed.

Talia tried to comfort Glacia by showing her how spring always followed winter, how the death Glacia brought made room for new life. But Glacia only heard that she was something to be overcome, something to be endured until the real beauty could return.
Alessia, in her direct way, told Glacia to take pride in her power, to stop apologizing for what she was. "You're Winter," she'd said, golden and glorious and utterly certain. "Act like it."

But Glacia didn't want to be Winter. She wanted to be anything else. Only Cora seemed to understand, because Cora also dealt in endings. They would walk together sometimes, Autumn and Winter, through the boundary places where their realms touched. They didn't always talk. Sometimes they just existed together in comfortable silence, two sisters who understood that not everything needed to be fixed or explained or made better.

"You're not death," Cora told her once. "You're rest. You're the pause between breaths. You are a necessity." But Glacia couldn't hear it. Or maybe she heard it but couldn't believe it. The sisters saw each other less and less as the centuries passed. Talia was busy with her endless gardens, coaxing life from every corner of her realm. Alessia held court in her golden palace, presiding over festivals and celebrations. Cora walked her forests, gathering wisdom like fallen leaves. Marina flowed between them all, carrying messages, but even she came less frequently to Glacia's frozen halls. And Glacia... Glacia retreated into her winter realm and tried to make herself smaller, tried to make her season shorter, tried to be less of what she was. It was killing her, though she didn't die the way mortals do. It was dimming her light, freezing her heart in ways that had nothing to do with ice and everything to do with loneliness and self-loathing.

That's when the demon made his move. His name was Malakar: an ancient thing from the spaces beneath the world, from the cracks between realms where darkness pools and festers. He was old and patient and cruel, and he understood desire the way a jeweler understands gems.

He forged a mirror in the deepest pits of the underworld, in fires that burned cold instead of hot. He made it from ice that would never melt and silver that would never tarnish, and he poured into it every twisted, corrupting enchantment he knew.
It was beautiful—achingly, impossibly beautiful—with a frame of silver thorns and a surface that reflected not what was, but what the viewer most desperately wanted to see.
That was the genius of it, the terrible cleverness. The mirror didn't lie, exactly. It showed truth—but truth filtered through desire, through need, through the aching gaps in a person's soul.

It showed you what you wanted, and in showing you, it made you want it more. It amplified longing until it became obsession. It took natural desire and twisted it into something hungry and desperate and ultimately corrupting.

The demon left it where Glacia would find it. She told me later that she'd been walking through a part of her realm she rarely visited—a deep valley where the ice was ancient and blue-black, where even she felt the cold.

She'd gone there because she wanted to be alone, because Talia had sent another cheerful message about spring preparations and Glacia couldn't bear the reminder that her time was ending again, that she would once more give way to her sister's warmth and growth and life.

The mirror was lying on the ice, half-buried in snow, as if it had been there forever. As if it had been waiting. Glacia said she knew immediately that it was wrong. She could feel the corruption radiating from it like heat from a fire. But she was drawn to it anyway, the way you're drawn to look at something terrible, something you know you shouldn't see. She picked it up. The frame was cold even to her touch.

The silver thorns bit into her palms, drawing blood that froze before it could fall. She looked into the mirror. And she saw winter as she'd always dreamed it could be. Not the harsh, killing cold that she knew herself to be. Not the barren wasteland that followed in her wake. Not the death and silence and emptiness that made her sisters turn away.

She saw peace. She saw a world blanketed in pristine snow, every surface softened and gentled. She saw ice crystals catching the light like diamonds, turning the world into something magical. She saw the quiet beauty of a frozen lake, the delicate architecture of frost on a window, the way snow muffled sound and created a sense of sacred stillness. She saw winter not as death but as rest. Not as ending but as pause. Not as something to be endured but as something to be cherished. She saw herself not as a monster but as a blessing.

The mirror showed her what she'd never been able to see on her own: that winter was beautiful. That it was necessary. That it was worthy of love. And in showing her this, it planted a seed of desire so deep and so powerful that it would reshape the world.

What if winter didn't have to end? The thought came to her fully formed, as if it had always been there, just waiting for permission to surface. What if she didn't have to give way to Talia's spring? What if the world could stay in this state of peaceful, beautiful rest? What if she could give the world the gift of eternal winter

—not harsh and killing, but gentle and lovely, like what she saw in the mirror? Wouldn't that be better? Wouldn't that be kinder? No more cycles of growth and death, no more struggle and striving. Just peace. Just rest. Just the quiet beauty of snow falling forever. She clutched the mirror to her chest, and for the first time in centuries, Glacia felt something like hope. She would take the mirror to the heavens. She would show the gods what she'd seen. She would ask them—no, she would convince them—to grant her this one thing. Eternal winter. Beautiful, peaceful, restful winter. The world would thank her. Her sisters would finally understand. She would finally be able to give something instead of only taking away.

She didn't see the corruption already taking root in her heart. She didn't feel the demon's magic wrapping around her thoughts like frost on glass. She didn't understand that the mirror was showing her not truth but a beautiful lie, and that the difference between the two was the difference between love and obsession. She only knew that she'd finally found the answer. Finally understood her purpose. Finally saw a way to be worthy of the power she'd been given.

Glacia spread her wings—great wings, pristine, and white as snow that could carry her between realms—and clutched the mirror tight. She didn't tell her sisters where she was going. She didn't ask for their counsel or their blessing. She was afraid they would try to stop her, try to talk her out of it, try to convince her that the cycles were necessary and good. But she knew better now. The mirror had shown her.
She launched herself into the sky, flying higher and higher, past the clouds, past the stars, toward the realm of the gods themselves.

The mirror's surface gleamed in her arms, reflecting her face back at her, and in that reflection she saw not the uncertain, self-loathing creature she'd always been, but a goddess with purpose. A savior. A bringer of peace. She flew toward the heavens with hope in her heart and a demon's mirror in her hands, and she had no idea that she was carrying the instrument of her own destruction.
Below her, in the mortal world, the first unnatural cold began to spread. In her realm, the ice grew thicker, darker, colder. And in the spaces between realms, something ancient and patient smiled.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 2: The Shattering
p: Glacia flew higher than any of the sisters had ever dared.

Her wings—gods, her wings were magnificent. Each feather was formed of crystallized snow that never melted, white as fresh powder, edged with frost that caught the light and threw it back in prismatic colors. They spanned wider than a house when fully extended, powerful enough to carry her between the mortal realm and the divine, graceful enough to navigate the currents of magic that flowed between worlds. She'd always been self-conscious about them. Talia's wings were delicate things of cherry blossoms and new leaves. Alessia's were golden and warm, like sunlight given form. Cora's shifted with her moods—sometimes autumn leaves, sometimes the dark wings of migrating birds.
But Glacia's wings were winter itself, and she'd always thought them harsh. Unlovely. Too cold, too sharp, too much like everything else about her that she wished she could change.
She didn't know, as she climbed toward heaven, that she would never fly with them again.

The mirror pulsed against her chest, warm in a way that should have warned her. Nothing about winter should be warm. But she was so full of hope, so certain of her purpose, that she mistook the heat for validation. The mirror showed her reflection as she flew—beautiful, determined, worthy—and she believed it. Higher. Higher still. The air grew thin, the stars closer. She could see the boundaries now, the places where the mortal realm ended and the divine began. Shimmering barriers of pure magic, the walls between what was and what should never be touched.
She didn't hesitate. She flew straight toward them. That's when everything started to go wrong.

The air changed first. It had been cold—her element, her comfort—but now it became something else. Hostile. Burning cold, the kind that sears rather than numbs. The magic that flowed around her, that had always welcomed her as one of the seasonal goddesses, suddenly recoiled. She felt it pull away from her like a living thing, felt the divine realm itself recognize the corruption she carried.

The mirror began to vibrate in her hands. She looked down at it, confused, and saw that the surface was no longer smooth. It rippled like water, like something was moving beneath the glass. The reflection it showed her was changing—her face flickering between the hopeful goddess and something else. Something with eyes too cold, features too sharp, a smile too cruel. "No," she whispered. "No, you're supposed to show the truth—"

The mirror showed her the truth. It showed her what she was becoming. What she'd already begun to become the moment she'd picked it up from the ice. The demon's corruption had been seeping into her all along, so slowly she hadn't noticed, whispering its poison in a voice that sounded like her own thoughts.

She tried to turn back. Tried to dive, to flee, to get away from the divine boundary before— Too late. The barrier recognized what she carried. Recognized the demonic magic wrapped around her like chains, embedded in the mirror she clutched to her chest. And the divine realm did what it was designed to do: it rejected the corruption.
Violently.

The clash of magics was like nothing that should exist in any world. Divine light, pure and absolute, met demonic darkness, ancient and hungry. The mirror was caught between them, a vessel too fragile to contain the forces that suddenly warred within its glass. Glacia felt it building, felt the pressure mounting, felt the mirror growing hot enough to burn even her winter-cold hands. She tried to throw it away. Her fingers wouldn't open. The mirror had her now, held her fast, and she realized with dawning horror that it had always been holding her. Since the moment she'd found it. Since the moment she'd looked into it and seen what she wanted to see.
The mirror exploded.

I've seen a lot of terrible things in my long existence. I've watched civilizations fall, seen plagues sweep across continents, witnessed the cruelty that mortals and immortals alike can inflict on each other. But I don't think I've ever heard of anything quite as catastrophic as the shattering of that mirror.
It didn't just break. It detonated. Shards of corrupted glass erupted outward in all directions, each piece carrying a fragment of the demon's curse, each one seeking a home in the world below.
They scattered like falling stars, like a plague of frozen rain, spreading across the mortal realm in a pattern too perfect to be random. The demon had planned this. Had always planned this.

One mirror, one goddess corrupted, was never the goal. The goal was to spread the corruption everywhere. Glacia screamed. The force of the explosion threw her backward, but worse—so much worse—the shards tore through her as they scattered. Her wings, those beautiful wings of crystallized snow, were shredded. Feathers ripped away, the delicate structure that had carried her between realms torn to ribbons.

Some shards passed through cleanly, leaving holes that wept golden blood. Others embedded themselves in the membrane, in the bone, in the muscle. But the largest shard, the piece that had been at the mirror's heart, the fragment that contained the deepest concentration of demonic magic—that shard drove straight into her chest.

She felt it pierce her skin, felt it slide between her ribs, and burrow deep into her flesh like a living thing seeking her heart. It stopped just short, embedded so close to that vital organ that she could feel it pulse with every beat.

Cold. So cold. Colder than winter had ever been, colder than death, colder than the spaces between the stars. The pain was absolute. She'd never felt pain before, not really. The seasonal goddesses were beyond such mortal concerns. But this—this was agony that rewrote what she understood about suffering.
The shard burned with cold fire, sent tendrils of corruption spreading through her veins like ice crystals forming in water. She could feel it reaching, spreading, claiming her from the inside out.
And then she fell.

Her wings were ruined, useless, trailing behind her in tatters. She plummeted from the heights she'd climbed, tumbling through the air with no control, no way to stop or slow her descent. The world spun around her
—sky, earth, sky, earth—and all she could feel was the shard in her chest and the terrible cold spreading through her body.

She crashed into the mortal realm at the foothills of her mountain domain, near a small village whose name I never learned. The impact carved a crater in the frozen ground, sent shockwaves rippling outward that shattered windows and knocked mortals from their feet. Trees snapped. The earth itself groaned. And in the center of the devastation, Glacia lay broken. ✽✽✽

In her autumn realm, Cora gasped and clutched her chest. The bond she shared with Glacia, that thread of understanding between the two who knew what it meant to be endings and silence, went taut and then screamed with agony that wasn't her own.
"Glacia," she whispered, and the roses around her withered and turned to ash, crumbling to nothing as if winter had come and gone in an instant, as if they'd skipped straight past death to dust.

Cora fell to her knees, pressing both hands to her heart, trying to follow that thread back to its source. She was the goddess of thresholds, of transformations, of the space between life and death. She knew the shape of endings. And what she felt through that bond was wrong—not death, which she would have understood, but corruption. Twisting. Something that shouldn't exist trying to unmake what was.

She reached out with her magic, trying to send warmth, trying to send help, trying to send anything that might ease what she felt screaming through their connection. But it was like trying to grasp smoke, like trying to hold water in her hands. The distance was too great, and whatever had happened to Glacia was too catastrophic, too alien. Her magic slid away, unable to find purchase, unable to help.
"No, no, no—" Cora's voice broke.

Around her, the entire garden was dying, the careful balance of her realm responding to her distress. Leaves fell from trees in a sudden rush, carpeting the ground in brown and gold. The air grew cold. She could feel it in her bones, in her divine essence—her sister was broken, and she was too far away to do anything but feel it happen.
She tried to stand, tried to gather herself to go to Glacia, but her legs wouldn't hold her. The horror of what she sensed was too much.
"Someone help her," she whispered to the dying garden, to the autumn wind, to anyone who might hear. "Please, someone help her."
But there was no answer. Only the sound of leaves falling and the terrible, aching silence where her sister's essence should have been.

In the spring realm, Talia felt it too, though less clearly. She was dancing with her nymphs when the music suddenly soured, when the flowers around her drooped and the air grew cold. She stopped mid-step, her bare feet suddenly chilled against grass that had been warm moments before. Something was wrong. Something was very, very wrong. She could feel it like a discordant note in a perfect song, like a crack in the foundation of the world.

"Sisters?" she called out, her voice uncertain. The nymphs had stopped dancing, were looking at her with worried eyes. "Do you feel that? Something's—" But even as she spoke, the feeling was already slipping away from her, becoming vague and undefined. What had she been saying? There was something... something important. Something about winter? About Glacia? The thought flickered and faded like a dream upon waking.

Around her, spring itself was trying to tell her what her scattered mind couldn't hold. Flowers were closing their petals in the middle of the day, buds that had been ready to bloom were sealing themselves tight. Birds stopped singing. The wind, usually so playful and warm in her realm, turned sharp and cold. Even the nymphs were shivering, drawing closer to each other for warmth.

Talia pressed her hands to her temples, trying to hold onto the feeling, the knowledge that something catastrophic had just happened. She needed to go—where? To Glacia. Yes, to Glacia. Something was wrong with Glacia. She took a step, then another, her motherly instincts screaming at her to go, to help, to fix whatever was broken. But then one of the nymphs touched her arm.
"My lady? Are you well? You look pale."
Talia blinked, looking down at the nymph. "I... yes. I think so. I was just..."

What had she been doing? There was something she needed to remember, something urgent, but it was like trying to hold water in a sieve. The harder she grasped for it, the faster it slipped away. She looked around at her realm, at the closed flowers and the shivering nymphs, at the wrongness that hung in the air like frost.
"Something happened," she said softly, and even as she spoke, tears were sliding down her cheeks though she couldn't quite remember why. "Something terrible. I should—I need to—"

But the thought wouldn't complete itself. Wouldn't stay. And so Talia stood in her spring garden, weeping for a sister she couldn't quite remember needing her, while around her the flowers stayed closed and the world grew colder and the moment for intervention slipped away like snow melting in the sun.
By the time she remembered clearly enough to act, it would be far, far too late.

Glacia didn't know how long she lay in the crater. Time had become strange, elastic, meaningless. She was aware of pain—so much pain—and of the cold spreading through her body from the shard embedded in her chest.
Her wings were destroyed, she knew that much. She could feel the absence of them, the wrongness of the tattered remains that lay beneath her.

She tried to move and immediately regretted it. Everything hurt. Her body was broken in ways that should have killed her, would have killed her if she were mortal. But she was a goddess, and goddesses didn't die easily. They just suffered.
Slowly, agonizingly, she pushed herself up to sitting. Her hands were cut, bleeding ichor. Her white dress

—the simple, beautiful gown she'd worn because she was going to meet the gods, because she wanted to look worthy—was torn and stained. Her hair, always so perfectly white and soft as fresh snow, was matted and tangled.

She looked down at her chest and saw the shard. It protruded from her flesh just left of center, a jagged piece of mirror glass that pulsed with dark light as it sank deeper into her flesh. She could briefly see her reflection in it, distorted and wrong. Her face looked back at her, but it wasn't the face she remembered. The features were sharper now, harder. Her eyes were colder, paler, like ice over deep water. Her lips had lost their softness. She looked like winter. Not the gentle winter of soft snowfall and cozy hearths, but the winter that killed. The winter that took and never gave back. "What have I done?" she whispered.

The shard pulsed in response, and she felt the corruption spread a little further. It was in her blood now, in her bones, in her very essence. And with it came a terrible clarity. She could feel the other shards, scattered across the world. Could sense them like distant stars, each one calling to the piece embedded in her chest. And she knew, with horrible certainty, that she needed to gather them.
All of them.
The compulsion was overwhelming, undeniable, a hunger that made her previous self-doubt seem like nothing. She had to find the shards. Had to collect them. Had to— "Miss? Miss, are you hurt?"

Glacia's head snapped up. A young man stood at the edge of the crater, looking down at her with concern. He was mortal, perhaps twenty years old, with kind eyes and work-roughened hands. A villager, probably drawn by the sound of her impact. He started to climb down toward her, his face full of worry.
"Don't move," he said. "You're injured. Let me help you
And that's when Glacia saw it. The shard. It was so small, barely visible, embedded in his left eye. Just a tiny fragment of mirror glass, small enough that he probably didn't even know it was there.

Maybe he'd felt something, a brief sting when the shards fell like rain, but had dismissed it as dust or grit. But Glacia could see it. Could feel it. Mirror calling to mirror, shard calling to shard. The piece in her chest burned with sudden, fierce need. Take it, the corruption whispered. Retrieve what was lost. Gather the pieces. Make yourself whole.
"No," Glacia breathed.
The young man reached her, knelt beside her. "It's alright," he said gently. "You're safe now. Let me help you back to the village. We have a healer—"
'Take it. TAKE IT.'

Glacia tried to resist. Tried to hold onto herself, onto the goddess she'd been just hours ago. She didn't want to hurt him. He was kind. He was trying to help. He didn't deserve— The shard in her chest pulsed, and pain lanced through her body. The compulsion became overwhelming, undeniable. Her hand moved of its own accord, reaching up to cup the young man's face. "Miss?" he said, confused but not yet afraid. "I'm sorry," Glacia whispered, and she meant it. In that moment, with the last shred of her true self, she meant it with everything she had. "I'm so sorry."
She kissed him.

It was called the Winter's Kiss, though she didn't know that yet. Didn't know that this would become her curse, her method, the terrible thing she would do again and again in the years to come. All she knew was that her lips touched his, and frost spread from the point of contact.
It happened fast. Too fast for him to scream, though not fast enough to spare him the knowledge of what was happening.

The ice spread across his skin, into his mouth, down his throat. It crystallized the moisture in his eyes, froze the blood in his veins, turned his flesh hard and cold and dead. His eyes went wide. Not with pain—the cold was too complete for that—but with betrayal. With confusion. With the terrible understanding that the beautiful woman he'd tried to help was killing him. Glacia felt his life end. Felt the warmth leave his body, felt him become a statue of ice, frozen in the moment of his death. And as he died, as the last spark of life left him, a single frozen tear formed in his left eye. The shard came free with it. The tiny piece of mirror glass, embedded in his eye, was pushed out by the ice. It fell into Glacia's palm, cold and sharp and wrong. The young man stood before her, frozen solid, his eyes still wide with that terrible betrayal. A monument to her first murder. To the moment the Snow Queen was truly born. Glacia stared at him. At what she'd done. Horror crashed over her in waves. She'd killed him. She'd murdered a kind young man who'd only wanted to help her. She'd taken his life to retrieve a shard of glass, and she'd done it without being able to stop herself.
"No," she whispered. "No, no, no—"

But even as the horror filled her, even as guilt and shame threatened to drown her, she felt something else. The corruption in her chest was spreading, numbing, smoothing away the sharp edges of her emotions. The guilt was still there, but it was becoming distant. Muted. Like something happening to someone else.

The shard in her palm pulsed, and she felt the others more clearly now. Hundreds of them. Scattered across the world, embedded in mortals who had no idea what they carried. And she needed them. Needed to gather them all, needed to retrieve every piece, needed to— She looked down at the shard in her hand. Then at the frozen young man. Then at her reflection in the ice that coated his body. The face that looked back at her was beautiful. Cold and hard and sharp, but beautiful. Regal. Powerful. The face of a queen, not a frightened goddess who'd made a terrible mistake. The face of winter itself. Glacia closed her hand around the shard and stood. Her body still hurt, but the pain was becoming distant too. Everything was becoming distant. The corruption was settling into her bones, into her heart, changing her from the inside out.
She looked at the frozen young man one last time. Tried to hold onto the guilt, the horror, the humanity that said what she'd done was wrong. But it was slipping away, like snow melting in spring.

"I'm sorry," she said again, but her voice was colder now. Harder. She turned away from him, from the crater, from the village. Her wings were ruined, but she could still walk. And she could feel the other shards calling to her, pulling her forward.

The Snow Queen had been born in that moment of terrible violence. Born from a goddess's good intentions and a demon's corruption. Born from a kiss that killed and a compulsion that couldn't be denied. And she had so many more shards to collect.

Glacia walked into the frozen night, leaving the young man's body behind her like a monument to everything she'd lost. The corruption spread through her with every step, numbing her emotions, hardening her heart, transforming her into something cold and terrible and powerful.

Somewhere in the distance, her sisters were searching for her. But she didn't want to be found. Not like this. Not as this. The Snow Queen walked alone into winter, and the world grew colder in her wake.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 3: Old Man Winter
p: I should tell you what I was before the mirror shard found me. Before everything changed. Before I became the beast in the story everyone thinks they know. I was once called Old Man Winter. Not a title I chose, mind you—it's what mortals called me when they bothered to give me a name at all. Some cultures had other names: Morozko, Jack Frost's father, the Walker of Snows. But Old Man Winter was the one that stuck, probably because it was the most accurate.

I was old. Ancient beyond mortal reckoning, though I didn't appear so. I took the form of a man in his prime when I chose to be seen at all—tall and imposing, with hair the color of moonlit snow that fell past my shoulders. My eyes were the pale blue of glacial ice, sharp enough to cut, and my skin had the luminous quality of fresh snow under starlight.
Mortals who glimpsed me often said I was beautiful like a winter storm: magnificent, dangerous, impossible to ignore. I suppose I was vain about it. I'd had millennia to perfect the image.

But the appearance was just window dressing for what I really was: a primordial force. One of the fundamental powers that kept the world turning. I was winter's hand in the mortal realm—the blizzard that buried mountains, the frost that split stone, the ice that locked rivers in crystalline sleep.
Where I walked, breath froze in lungs. Where I gestured, storms were born. I painted continents white and made the very air sharp enough to cut. But I wasn't winter itself. That was Glacia's domain.

The Horai—the seasonal sisters—were the essence of their seasons, the living embodiment of cosmic principles. Glacia was winter as a concept, as a state of being. She held dormancy and rest, the quiet death that preceded rebirth, the spiritual truth of the cold months. Where I brought the weather, she held the realm itself. We were complementary forces, two halves of a cosmic whole. She was winter's soul; I was winter's body. The same was true for her sisters. Talia held spring's essence while others brought the thaw and the first blooms. Alessia was summer's warmth and abundance while her counterparts delivered the heat and growth. Cora embodied autumn's transition and harvest while the world around her changed colors and prepared for sleep.

I'd worked with all four sisters since the world was young, coordinating the endless dance of seasons. We'd meet at the turning points—the equinoxes and solstices—to ensure smooth transitions, to maintain the balance.

It was a partnership as old as the world itself, and it had always worked beautifully. Until recently. Glacia had been withdrawing. Pulling away from our coordination, missing our meetings, retreating into her crystalline realm. It had started gradually—perhaps six mortal months prior, though time moved strangely for beings like us.

At first, I'd thought she simply needed solitude. Even ancient forces require periods of stillness. But as the months passed, her absence became a void I could feel in the seasonal order itself, like a missing note in a cosmic symphony.
The sisters had mentioned she was struggling with something, though they'd been vague about what. "Give her time," Talia had said, her spring-green eyes troubled. "She'll come around."

But she hadn't. And I'd found myself shouldering more and more of winter's work alone, maintaining the balance without her essence to guide me. It was like trying to paint with only half the colors, like dancing a duet with an absent partner. I'd been meaning to seek her out in her palace of eternal ice. But something had been... distracting me. Binding my attention. Consuming my time in ways I didn't fully understand. Without proper coordination with Glacia, the seasonal order would fracture. There would be no spring thaw, no summer growth, no autumn harvest. Everything would stagnate, rot, collapse. The balance was essential. I was essential. I was eternal.
Or so I thought.

My duties took me everywhere—across continents and oceans, to mountains and valleys, forests and tundras. I would arrive with the first frost, reshape the world in ice and snow, and then move on when my work was done. It was a solitary existence, but I'd never minded. Solitude was part of my nature, as fundamental as the cold itself.

And then, about a year before the shattering, I encountered Gerda. She found me in the northern reaches, where the auroras danced and the snow never fully melted even in summer. I was crafting a glacier—coaxing ice from the bedrock, shaping it into rivers of frozen time that would flow for millennia. The work required my full attention, my full power, the kind of deep magic that resonated with the bones of the earth itself.

That's when I felt her. A pulse of magic so powerful it made the air itself recoil. Not mortal magic—or at least, not entirely. Something older. Something that tasted of blood and binding and ancient, hungry things. I turned, and there she was. She stood at the edge of my working, utterly unafraid of the cold that would have killed any mortal in seconds. Dark hair whipped around her face in the wind I'd summoned, and her eyes—gods, her eyes were fathomless, holding depths that even I couldn't fully read.
She wore furs and leather that writhed with their own life, and the magic that radiated from her was intoxicating and wrong in equal measure.
"Old Man Winter," she said, and her voice carried over the howling wind as if the storm itself dared not drown her out. "I've been hunting you."

Not "looking for." Hunting. I should have paid attention to that word. Should have recognized the predator's gleam in her eyes. But I was arrogant, and I was curious, and she was magnificent in the way a forest fire is magnificent—beautiful and terrible and utterly consuming.

"Have you?" I let the glacier-working fade, turning my full attention to her. The temperature dropped another twenty degrees. Frost formed in intricate patterns across every surface. "And what does a mortal want with winter's hand?"
She smiled, and it was like watching a wolf bare its teeth.
"To understand it. To touch it. To possess it." The last word should have been a warning. Instead, it was a challenge.

"Many have tried," I said, and let my power unfurl around me—the temperature plummeting, the wind rising to a shriek, snow beginning to fall upward in defiance of natural law. "None have succeeded." "I'm not like the others."

She stepped forward, into the heart of my power, and didn't even flinch. Her own magic rose to meet mine—red and gold and colors that shouldn't exist in a mortal's repertoire. Where our powers touched, the air crackled and sparked.
"I don't want to control winter, Old Man. I want to bind myself to it. To you."

And gods help me, I was intrigued. What followed was not a relationship in any mortal sense. It was a collision. A conflagration. Two vast powers circling each other, testing boundaries, pushing limits.

Gerda was formidable in ways I'd never encountered. She could weather my storms, walk through my blizzards, touch my ice without flinching. Her magic was ancient and dark and powerful enough to make even me take notice.

When we came together, it was like two weather systems colliding—violent, intense, reality-bending. The sex was apocalyptic. We'd couple in the heart of blizzards, our powers intertwining and feeding off each other until the very air around us screamed. I'd summon storms and she'd ride them, her magic weaving through mine in patterns that were almost binding, almost possessive. Afterward, the landscape would be transformed—new mountains of ice, valleys scoured clean, the very shape of the land altered by our joining.
It was intoxicating. Addictive. For the first time in my endless existence, I'd found something—someone—who could match my power, who could stand in the full force of what I was and not be destroyed.

I should have wondered why. Should have questioned what she really was, what she really wanted. But I was too caught up in the collision to see the trap closing around me. The first time I tried to leave to attend to my duties, she stopped me. Not with words. With magic. I'd been preparing to depart from her tower—a structure of black stone that jutted from the mountainside like a talon—when I felt it. Threads of her power, woven through mine while I'd been distracted. Not quite binding, not quite controlling, but... tethering. Anchoring.
"You're leaving," she said. It wasn't a question. "The southern valleys need their first frost." I pulled against the threads, testing them. They held. "If I don't bring winter—"
"Let someone else bring it." She moved closer, and her magic pressed against mine, invasive and possessive. "Stay."
"There is no one else. I am winter's hand. This is what I am."
"And what am I?" Her eyes flashed with something dangerous, something that made the air in the room feel suddenly thin. "A distraction? A momentary amusement?"
"You know that's not—"
"Then stay." The threads tightened. Not painful, not yet, but the intent was clear. "Prove that I matter more than your endless duties. That I'm worth more than frost and snow."

I could have broken free. Should have. I was a primordial force—her magic, however formidable, shouldn't have been able to hold me. But breaking free would have meant shattering the threads entirely. Severing whatever this was between us. And despite the warning bells ringing in the back of my mind, I wasn't ready to do that.
So I stayed. For three days, then four, while the southern valleys waited for winter that didn't come. While the seasonal order strained and groaned under the disruption.

When I finally did leave, tearing free of her threads with more force than I'd intended, I could feel her fury following me like a cold wind. It got worse after that. Every departure became a battle. Not of words—we were beyond words. Of wills. Of power. She'd weave her magic through mine, trying to bind me, to hold me, to keep me tethered to her tower and her bed. And I'd have to tear free each time, the effort growing harder, the threads growing stronger.
"You belong to me," she'd say, her magic wrapping around me like chains. "Winter belongs to me." "I belong to no one. I am a force of nature, not a possession."
"Everything can be possessed. Everything can be owned. Even you."

When I was with her, she demanded all of me. Every moment, every thought, every ounce of power. If I tried to work—to maintain the seasonal balance, to coordinate with the distant Horai, to simply exist in the vast, elemental way I'd existed for millennia—she took it as rejection.
"You're pulling away," she'd say, and her magic would flare, pressing against mine, trying to force connection. "I can feel you retreating."
"I'm not retreating. I'm simply being what I am." "What you are is mine."

The worst part was that I couldn't quite bring myself to end it. There were still moments when the collision of our powers felt transcendent rather than suffocating. Moments when she'd soften, when her magic would caress rather than bind, when she'd whisper things that sounded almost like vulnerability. And beneath it all, I was lonely. Had been lonely for longer than I cared to admit.

The Horai were colleagues, not companions. My existence was vast and cold and solitary. Gerda had offered something different—connection, passion, intensity. I just hadn't realized the price would be my freedom.

The day of the shattering, I'd been gone for two weeks. Two weeks of bringing winter to the eastern steppes, of painting the world in frost and ice, of doing what I was meant to do. Two weeks of feeling Gerda's fury like a distant storm on the horizon, growing darker with each passing day. When I returned to her tower, I could feel her magic before I even entered—roiling, furious, barely contained. She was waiting in the upper chamber, and the air around her crackled with power.
"Two weeks," she said, and her voice was deadly calm. Worse than rage. "Two weeks, Kael."
"I had duties—" "Duties." She laughed, and the sound made the windows rattle.
"Always duties. Always the world needing you more than I do."
"It's not about need. It's about what I am. What I've always been."
"And what am I?" Her magic exploded outward, slamming into mine with enough force to crack the stone floor. "What am I to you?"
I could have lied. Should have, perhaps. But I was tired of the binding, tired of the constant battle, tired of feeling like I was being slowly consumed.
"I don't know," I said.
The truth hung between us like a blade. Her face went very still. Very cold. When she spoke again, her voice was barely above a whisper, but it carried the weight of mountains.
"I have given you everything. Opened myself to you. Bound myself to you. And you don't even know what I am to you?"
"Gerda—"

"No." Her magic flared, red and gold and black, colors that definitely shouldn't exist in mortal sorcery. "No more excuses. No more duties. You will stay, Kael. You will be mine. I will bind you so thoroughly that you'll never leave again."

The threads of her power lashed out, trying to wrap around me, to sink into my essence itself. Not tethering this time. Binding. True binding, the kind that would make me hers in ways that couldn't be undone. I reacted on instinct, summoning my full power. The temperature in the room plummeted. Ice exploded across every surface. A blizzard manifested inside the tower itself, howling and furious.
"I am not yours to bind!" My voice carried the weight of glaciers, the cold of the void between stars. "I am winter's hand, a primordial force, and I will not be caged!"

Our powers collided with a sound like reality breaking. And then the sky tore open. It started with a sound that shouldn't exist—a ripping, tearing noise that came from everywhere and nowhere, from the fabric of existence itself. The tower shook. The windows exploded. The air shrieked. I threw up a shield of ice instinctively, protecting us both from the debris. "What—"

But Gerda was already at the shattered window, staring out at something that made even her face go pale. I joined her, and felt my ancient heart stutter. The sky was wrong. Fundamentally, cosmically wrong. Reality itself had been slashed open, torn like cloth, and through the wounds I could see colors that hurt to perceive—purples that burned, greens that screamed, blacks that devoured light and meaning and hope. And the storm. Gods and demons and all things between, the storm. This wasn't weather. This was the death of natural law. Wind howled with voices that spoke in languages older than time. Snow fell in directions that didn't exist. Lightning cracked in patterns that formed symbols I almost recognized—ancient, terrible, wrong. The magic saturating the air tasted of corruption and chaos and the ending of all things. My first thought was of the Horai. Of the seasonal order. This felt like what would happen if the fundamental balance shattered—if one of the sisters had fallen, if the boundaries between the seasonal realms had collapsed entirely.

I reached out with my senses, searching for Glacia's presence. If this was winter magic gone catastrophically wrong, she would know. She would feel it. Our connection was ancient, woven into the fabric of the seasons themselves.
But there was nothing. Not just absence. A void. A hole in the cosmic order where winter's essence should be, like a missing tooth in the mouth of reality. Terror
—true, primal terror—seized me for the first time in millennia.
"Glacia," I whispered, and my voice shook. "She's gone. She's—"
"What is this?" Gerda's hand gripped my arm, her fingers digging in with desperate strength.
"This magic—it's older than anything I've ever felt. Older than—"

"Than the world," I finished, still searching desperately for any trace of the Horai. Talia, Alessia, Cora—anyone. But the storm's chaos was too overwhelming, too allconsuming. "This is what happens when the order breaks. When the foundations crack."
"Can you stop it?"

"I don't know!" I was already reaching out with my power, trying to impose order on the chaos, trying to calm the impossible storm. But it was like trying to freeze the sun—my magic simply slid off the wrongness, unable to find purchase.

"This is beyond me. Beyond any single force. If the Horai are gone, if the seasonal order has collapsed—" The tower shook again, harder. Cracks spider-webbed across the walls. The floor tilted at a sickening angle. "We need to—" Gerda started.

That's when it happened. Something struck my eye. The pain was immediate and absolute—like a shard of frozen starlight had been driven directly into my skull, into my brain, into my very essence. I cried out, stumbling backward, my hands flying to my face. "Kael!" Gerda was beside me instantly, her earlier fury forgotten. "What is it?"

"My eye," I gasped. The pain was already transforming into something else—a burning, itching feeling, like something foreign had lodged itself where it absolutely should not be. "Something struck my eye."
She pulled my hands away, tilting my face toward what little light remained. Her expression shifted from concern to confusion.
"There's nothing there," she said. "No wound, no debris. Your eye looks—"
"It's not fine!" I blinked rapidly, desperately, trying to dislodge whatever had embedded itself in my vision. "There's something in it. I can feel it."
And I could. Not just physical irritation, but something deeper. Something that felt like it was burrowing into my being, like a splinter working its way toward my heart.
"Kael." Gerda's voice was strange now, distant. "The storm."

I turned, still rubbing at my eye. The storm was ending. Not gradually, not naturally, but all at once—like someone had simply erased it from existence. The tears in reality sealed themselves. The impossible colors faded. The wind died to nothing. In the space between one heartbeat and the next, it was over. We stood in the wreckage of the tower's upper room, surrounded by broken stone and shattered glass, and stared at the nownormal sky in stunned silence. "What," Gerda said slowly, "was that?"
"I don't know."

My eye still burned with that persistent wrongness. I tried blinking again, but whatever was lodged there wasn't coming out. And beneath the physical discomfort, a deeper terror gnawed at me: Where was Glacia? Where were the Horai? What had just happened to the seasonal order?
"But I've never felt magic like that. Never seen reality itself tear open."
"It felt old," she whispered. "Ancient. Like something from before the world was made."

I nodded, still rubbing at my eye. The pain had faded almost completely now, leaving only that maddening sensation of something foreign embedded where it didn't belong. Like a grain of sand, except I couldn't seem to blink it away. And beneath that, something else. A wrongness that went deeper than physical discomfort. A sense that something fundamental had shifted, changed, broken. Not just in the world. In me. "Are you sure you're all right?" Gerda's hand touched my face, surprisingly gentle given our earlier battle. "Your eye—"
"It's fine. Just irritated." I lowered my hand, forcing myself to stop rubbing. "It'll pass."

But even as I said it, I knew it was a lie. Something had changed. I just didn't know what yet. Gerda was watching me with an expression I couldn't quite read. The fury from before had been replaced by something else—concern, yes, but also a calculating look that made me uneasy.
"We should check the damage," I said, needing to do something, anything, to break the strange tension. "Make sure the tower is stable."

She nodded slowly, but her eyes never left my face. We spent the next hour assessing the destruction. The upper floors were badly damaged, but the structure itself was sound. Whatever that storm had been, physical destruction hadn't been its primary purpose. It had been delivering something. Distributing something. Planting something. The thought came unbidden, and I couldn't shake it. Couldn't shake the feeling that whatever was in my eye, hadn't been an accident.

The argument from before felt distant now, unimportant in the face of what we'd just witnessed. "You should rest," Gerda said. She looked drained in a way I'd never seen her, her formidable power dimmed. "We both should."

I nodded, but I knew I wouldn't sleep. Something was wrong. Something had changed. And somewhere in the cosmic order, there was a void where Glacia should be. That night, lying in Gerda's bed while she slept fitfully beside me, I stared at the ceiling and tried to ignore the persistent itch in my eye. Tried to ignore the strange, cold feeling that had settled in my chest—colder than anything I'd ever created.

Tried to ignore the small, insistent voice in the back of my mind that whispered something was very, very wrong. I reached out one more time with my senses, searching for Glacia across the vast distances that separated us. Searching for any trace of winter's essence, winter's soul.
Nothing.

ch.t: Chapter 4: The Poison and The Curse
p: The mirror shard wasn't just lodged in my eye; it was lodged in my perception.
It took time—a few weeks, perhaps, in mortal measure
—for the corruption to fully take hold. It didn't burn, it didn't ache; it simply shifted my vision. Slowly, subtly, everything became gray. Not physically, not at first, but morally.

Where I had once seen the necessity of the seasonal cycle—Talia's hopeful, messy growth, Alessia's demanding, glorious light, Cora's patient, profound endings—I now saw only weakness. I saw Talia's spring as chaos, Alessia's summer as exhausting excess, and Cora's autumn as decay.

My primordial nature, which had always balanced the whole, was now hyper-focused on one truth: Winter is the only clean slate. Silence is the only perfection. The greatest casualty of this new, corrupted sight was Gerda. The moment the shard found its place, the intoxicating passion I felt for her vanished. The truth was, my feelings for her had always been conditional
—a dangerous mix of novelty, fascination, and the desperate need to feel something other than solitude. The shard stripped away the novelty and left only the possession.
I saw her not as a magnificent, formidable sorceress, but as a tedious, grasping creature trying to cage a force she didn't deserve.

"You're cold," she said one evening, sliding into the immense bed beside me, her own magic seeking the familiar blend with mine. She was looking for the passionate collision, the apocalyptic joining that used to transform the landscapes.
"I am cold," I replied, without turning my head. "It is my nature."

"No. This is different. You're distant. Like the moon." She reached out, her fingers running across my snow-white hair. "You haven't touched me since the storm." "The storm was tiresome. Our time is better spent rebuilding." I said it with clinical detachment. The shard in my eye presented her as a problem to be managed, a distraction from the work of restoring order.

The very idea of the collision that had once drawn me in now seemed beneath my dignity. Her confusion soon turned to heartbreak, and then, inevitably, to fury. The arguments escalated not because I resisted her, but because I simply stopped caring about her. Her possessiveness, which had once felt like a fascinating challenge, now seemed petty and pathetic.
" What happened that night?" she screamed one night, throwing a vase of withered mountain lilies against the stone wall.
"Nothing happened," I said, looking right through her, my glacial eyes utterly empty of emotion. "You are overreacting. Perhaps you lack the fortitude for the truly ancient things."
"I lack fortitude? I faced that chaotic horror beside you, Kael! I saw the fear in your eyes when you realized Glacia was gone! Don't you dare insult me with your cold detachment."

The mention of Glacia—the beautiful, self-loathing sister whose absence had briefly terrified me—only irritated me now. Glacia was a flaw, a weakness in the cosmic armor, and the only correct reaction was indifference.

"I have no time for your tantrums, Gerda," I stated, rising from my seat. "The world needs Winter. I need to leave." "No!" Her power exploded, threads of red and gold magic lashing out, but they no longer sought to entangle me in passion. They sought to bind me with iron will. "You will not leave until you look at me and tell me what you see! Tell me that I matter more than the frost!"

She was desperate now, grasping for the man she remembered, fighting the phantom of the old relationship. But the shard in my eye filtered her actions, making her movements appear clumsy, her desperation pitiful. I saw only a cage, and I knew how to deal with a cage.
I finally turned my full attention to her, letting my own cold power—now enhanced by the demonic shard
—flow outward.
"I see a flawed creature attempting to possess a primordial power," I said, my voice cutting through the air like a sheet of ice. "I see a distraction. I see an end that should have come sooner."

I took a step toward her, forcing her to shrink back. "You were momentary amusement, Gerda. Nothing more. Now, release the binding and stand aside." The words, cold and cruel, were not entirely mine, but the shard gave them voice. They were the perfect distillation of the Snow Queen's corruption—indifference, cruelty, and the absolute refusal to accept anything less than perfection.
Gerda looked utterly destroyed. Her power, which had been burning with fierce rage, sputtered and died, leaving her exposed and shaking.
"Momentary amusement," she repeated, the sound thin and broken.
She finally understood that I was gone. Whatever had been lodged in my eye had not simply wounded me; it had stolen the man she knew, leaving behind an indifferent god.

"Only 'true love and devotion' can break this." The voice was not mine. It was hers, but ancient, powerful, resonant—the voice of a high sorceress whose heart had just been shattered by a demon-poisoned primordial force. All the rage, the possessiveness, the heartbreak, the humiliation—she poured it all into a single, terrifying magical declaration.
"You wished to be only Winter's Hand? Then Winter's Hand you shall be."
I tried to move, tried to fight her, but her magic—the ancient, binding magic that had always felt suffocating

—now felt absolute. It wrapped around my limbs, my body, my very essence. It was an unbreakable prison forged of pure, agonizing emotional rejection. "You wished to be free of my touch? You are free. You will roam the winter wastes, forgotten and unseen," she declared, her eyes now gleaming with terrifying, righteous power.

"You will not return to this form, you will not reclaim your strength, and you will not regain your memory, until you prove what you swore you already possessed." I felt the transformation begin. It was not gentle. It felt like my very essence—the cosmic code that defined me as Old Man Winter—was being violently rewritten. My limbs cracked and strained. My skin thickened and turned to massive white fur. My mind clouded, the complexity of millennia collapsing into simple, primal instinct.

The shard in my eye burned, but it, too, was consumed by the transformation, sinking deep into my nowfurred brow. "Go," she commanded, tears finally mixing with the terrible light in her eyes. "Go, and be the beast you have become in your heart. Only true love and devotion can break the curse and return you to Kael, the Ice King." With a final, shattering surge of power, Gerda cast me out. I stumbled out of the ruined tower—no longer Kael, no longer Old Man Winter. Just a magnificent, wounded Polar Bear, blinded by instinct, confused by the sudden loss of memory, and driven by an overwhelming need to flee the woman whose heart I had just broken. I fled into a storm I had not created, leaving behind the shattered sorceress and the final, devastating piece of the story everyone thinks they know: the hero, driven by demonic corruption, transforming into the very monster he needed to become to one day prove his love. Gerda, seeing the result of her despair, slumped against the cold stone, immediately consumed by regret. The curse was set. Unbreakable. Unchangeable. The curse required the impossible. And the two most powerful beings in all of Winter—Glacia, corrupted by the mirror, and Kael, cursed by his love—were now broken, cast out, and wandering the world alone.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 5: The Snow Queen's Quest
p: By the time I found her palace, Glacia had been hunting shards for over a century. This is what those years had made of her. I learned the details later—pieced together from what she told me in her rare moments of clarity, from what I witnessed myself, and from what the mirror itself revealed when it was finally whole. But I need you to understand what she had become before I tell you how we met. I need you to see the Snow Queen as the world saw her: magnificent, terrible, dangerous, and utterly alone.

For over a hundred years, she had walked the earth with a single purpose. The shard in her chest called to its scattered siblings, and she answered that call with the mechanical precision of a clock striking the hour. She felt the pull of each piece—a distant ache, a directional hunger—and she followed it without question, without hesitation, without mercy.

She had killed hundreds. Most didn't survive the Winter's Kiss. Their bodies weren't strong enough to withstand the cold required to extract the shards from their eyes. They froze from the inside out, their last moments filled with confusion and terror as the beautiful woman with colorless eyes pressed her lips to theirs and stole their warmth, their breath, their lives. She felt nothing about it. The shard in her chest had seen to that.

The palace rose from the frozen wasteland like a crown of ice thrust up from the earth itself. It shouldn't have been possible—the architecture defied natural law, spires twisting in geometries that hurt to look at too long, bridges of crystalline ice spanning impossible distances without support, towers that seemed to exist in multiple places at once depending on the angle of observation.

Starlight filtered through walls of ice so pure they were nearly transparent, refracting into patterns that shifted and changed like living things. In the central courtyard, a waterfall hung suspended mid-cascade, each droplet frozen in its descent, creating a sculpture of motion arrested, of time itself held captive. The ice captured the light and threw it back in shades of blue and white and silver—no warmth, no color, nothing that spoke of life or growth or anything beyond winter's absolute dominion.

The halls were vast. Cathedrals of ice stretched in every direction, their ceilings lost in shadows and refracted light, their floors polished to mirror smoothness. Sound died in those spaces, swallowed by the oppressive silence that filled every corner.

Wind howled through the corridors. Snow fell in the courtyards. It was magnificent. It was perfect. It was utterly, devastatingly empty. Glacia moved through her palace like a ghost haunting its own mausoleum. Her footsteps made no sound on the ice floors. Her breath—if she still breathed in any way that mattered—left no fog in the frigid air.

She passed through chambers that could have held a thousand revelers and felt nothing at their emptiness. She climbed stairs that spiraled up into towers where she had not set foot in decades and felt no curiosity about what lay at their peaks.

The palace was hers. It had always been hers—her realm, her domain as Winter incarnate, ancient as the first frost. Once, in the days before the shattering, her sisters had walked these halls. Cora's laughter had echoed off crystalline walls, Talia had marveled at frozen waterfalls, even Alessia had visited to see winter's beauty in its purest form. Glacia had moved through these spaces with quiet pride, finding solace in the cold perfection she'd created.

Now the same halls felt like a crypt. The beauty meant nothing. The impossible architecture stirred nothing. She moved through her own realm like a ghost haunting familiar spaces, feeling no comfort, no peace, no connection to what had once been her sanctuary. She took no pleasure in it. She took no comfort from it. It was simply where she returned when the hunting was done, a place to store her collection and wait for the next shard to call.

On this particular day—though day and night meant little in the eternal twilight of her realm—she stood in the heart of the palace, in a chamber she had designated for a singular purpose. The room was circular, its walls rising up into a dome of ice so clear it revealed the stars beyond. In the center stood a pedestal of frozen crystal, and on that pedestal rested a silver box, its surface etched with patterns that shifted and writhed when viewed directly.

Inside the box were the shards. Hundreds of them. Tiny fragments of the Winter's Heart Mirror, each one pulsing with its own corrupt heartbeat, each one singing its poisonous song. She had gathered them one by one, kiss by kiss, death by death, and she kept them here, waiting for the day when she would have them all. Glacia stood before the pedestal, her hands folded at her waist, her posture perfect, her face expressionless. She wore a gown of ice-crystal that looked like armor—sharp edges, severe lines, a bodice that could have been carved from a glacier. Her white hair was pulled back in an elaborate braided crown, not a strand out of place, the style so precise it looked painful. Her skin was pale as fresh snow, her features sharp where they had once been soft, her lips colorless, her cheekbones high and cutting.

But it was her eyes that truly showed what she had become. They were pale blue, almost colorless, like looking into a frozen lake in the depths of winter. There was no warmth in them. No recognition. No humanity. They were beautiful like a freshly forged blade—perfect, cold, deadly.

She stared at the silver box, and something flickered across her face. A micro-expression, gone almost before it registered. Her left hand trembled—just once, just slightly—before she pressed it flat against her thigh, forcing it still. The shard in her chest pulsed, and the moment passed. She turned away from the pedestal with mechanical grace and moved toward the chamber's entrance.

She had felt it an hour ago—the pull of another shard, distant but distinct, calling to the piece embedded near her heart. The compulsion rose in her like a tide, irresistible, undeniable. She would go. She would find the victim. She would take the shard. She always did. ✽✽✽

The village was small, unremarkable, the kind of place that existed in the margins of maps and the edges of memory. Glacia walked through its snow-covered streets as the sun set, her presence causing frost to spread across windows and ice to form in water troughs. People saw her and fled indoors, slamming shutters, barring doors, gathering children close. They knew what she was. The stories had spread over the decades—the beautiful woman in white who came for those cursed by the great storm, whose kiss meant death, who could not be stopped or reasoned with or escaped. The Snow Queen.

Glacia felt their fear like a distant echo, something that registered but did not touch her. She followed the pull of the shard through the winding streets, past the village square, toward a small house at the edge of the settlement.

The door was open. Inside, a young woman sat by the fire, rocking a child who couldn't have been more than two years old. The woman was perhaps twenty-five, with dark hair and tired eyes, wearing a simple dress that had been mended many times. She was singing softly—a lullaby, something about stars and safety and morning coming soon.

She looked up as Glacia's shadow fell across the threshold, and her voice died. The shard was in her left eye. Glacia could see it glinting there, a tiny fragment of corruption that had turned the woman's iris from brown to a murky gray-green. The shard would have been working on her slowly, changing her perceptions, making her see flaws where there were none, turning love to suspicion, joy to bitterness.
"No," the woman whispered. She clutched the child tighter. "No, please. Not yet. Not—I have a daughter. Please."

Glacia stepped into the house. Ice spread from where her feet touched the floor, creeping across the wooden planks in crystalline patterns. The fire in the hearth guttered and dimmed, unable to withstand her presence.
"Please," the woman said again. Tears were streaming down her face now, freezing on her cheeks. "Please, I'll do anything. Just—just let me say goodbye. Let me—" "Put the child down," Glacia said.

Her voice was soft, empty, the sound of wind over a frozen lake. The woman's hands shook violently, but she obeyed. She set the little girl on the floor near the hearth, as far from Glacia as the small room allowed. The child began to cry, reaching for her mother, but the woman didn't look back. She kept her eyes on Glacia, her body positioned between the Snow Queen and her daughter.
"Will it hurt?" the woman asked. Her voice was steadier now, resigned.
Glacia tilted her head slightly, considering the question with the detached curiosity of someone examining an insect.
"Yes," she said finally. "But not for long." The woman closed her eyes. "Then do it quickly. Please. Before she's old enough to remember."

Glacia moved forward with the fluid grace of winter itself. She reached out and cupped the woman's face in her hands—hands that were cold as death, pale as bone, beautiful and terrible. The woman gasped at the touch, her skin already beginning to frost.
"I'm sorry," Glacia whispered, and somewhere deep beneath the ice, beneath the shard's corruption, beneath a hundred years of numbness, something screamed.

Then she leaned in and pressed her lips to the woman's mouth. The cold came instantly, violently, spreading from the point of contact like poison through veins. The woman's eyes flew open—both of them, the corrupted one and the clear one—wide with shock and agony. Her hands came up instinctively, grasping at Glacia's arms, trying to push her away, but she might as well have been trying to move a mountain.

Glacia held her there, lips locked, breathing winter into the woman's lungs. The cold spread down the woman's throat, into her chest, freezing her from the inside out. Her blood slowed, thickened, began to crystallize in her veins. Her heart stuttered, struggling to pump through the ice forming in her arteries. Her lungs seized, unable to draw breath around the frost coating their interior. But she couldn't die yet. Not until the shard was removed.

That was the cruelty of it—the victim had to remain conscious, had to feel every moment of the process, because the magic required awareness to complete the extraction. The woman's fingers dug into Glacia's arms hard enough to bruise—if Glacia could bruise, if she were still made of anything soft enough to damage. Her body convulsed, trying desperately to escape, to breathe, to live.
Behind them, the child was screaming, a high, piercing wail that should have shattered something in Glacia's chest. It didn't.

The cold reached the woman's eyes. Ice formed on her lashes, in the corners of her lids, spreading across the surface of her corneas. The shard in her left eye began to glow, responding to Glacia's magic, to the call of the larger piece in the Snow Queen's chest. Glacia pulled back slightly, just enough to see. The woman's lips were blue, her face white as snow, her eyes glazed with frost. But she was still alive—barely, impossibly, held at the edge of death by the magic that demanded the shard's release.

Glacia reached up with one hand, her movements precise, clinical. She placed her thumb and forefinger in the corner of the woman's left eye, and she pulled. The shard came free with a sound like breaking glass. It was small—no larger than a coin of the realm—but it pulsed with malevolent light, singing its corrupt song. Glacia held it up, examining it with the same detached interest she'd shown the woman's question, then closed her fist around it.

The magic released its hold. The woman's body went rigid for one final moment, every muscle locked in a rictus of agony. Then she collapsed, falling backward onto the floor with a sound like a sack of grain dropping. Her eyes stared up at nothing, frosted over completely, her mouth open in a silent scream.

Glacia stood over the body, the shard clutched in her hand, and felt nothing. No guilt. No remorse. No satisfaction. Just the faint, distant acknowledgment that she had completed her task, that she had one more piece of the mirror, that she was one step closer to gathering them all. Behind her, the child was still screaming. Glacia turned to look at the little girl—darkhaired like her mother, with the same tired eyes, now wide with terror and incomprehension.

The child was reaching toward the body on the floor, calling for her mama, not understanding why mama wouldn't get up, wouldn't answer, wouldn't hold her. For a moment—just a moment, a fraction of a second

—Glacia's hand trembled. Her fingers tightened around the shard until the edges cut into her palm, drawing golden blood that froze before it could fall. Something flickered in her colorless eyes, something that might have been horror or grief or the ghost of the goddess she had once been.

This is wrong, a voice whispered from somewhere deep inside her, from the place where Alessia's ember still burned, hidden and waiting. This is wrong, this is wrong, this is— The shard in her chest pulsed, and the thought shattered like ice under a hammer.

Glacia turned away from the screaming child and walked out of the house, leaving the door open behind her, leaving the body cooling on the floor, leaving the little girl who would grow up without a mother because the Snow Queen had needed one more piece of a broken mirror.

She walked through the village streets as people watched from behind shuttered windows. She walked out into the frozen wasteland beyond. She walked until the village was lost behind her, until there was nothing but snow and ice and the endless, empty sky. And she felt nothing.

The return to the palace was automatic, her feet following paths worn by a century of repetition. She passed through the gates—massive structures of ice carved with scenes of winter's beauty, now looking more like monuments to winter's cruelty—and into the vast, silent halls.

Her footsteps echoed in the emptiness, the only sound in a place built for thousands but inhabited by one. She made her way to the central chamber, to the pedestal with its silver box. She opened the lid with hands that did not shake, that showed no sign of the tremor from earlier, and she placed the new shard inside with all the others.
Four hundred and sixty-three.

She knew the count without thinking, the number etched into her consciousness by the shard's compulsion. Four hundred and sixty-three pieces recovered. Dozens if not more still scattered across the world, waiting to be found, waiting to be taken from the eyes of the corrupted, waiting to be gathered so the mirror could be whole again.
She didn't know why she needed to gather them. The compulsion didn't explain itself, didn't justify its demands. It simply was, as inevitable as winter itself, as undeniable as the cold.

Glacia closed the box and stood before the pedestal, her hands folded at her waist, her posture perfect, her face expressionless. The palace stretched around her in all directions—magnificent halls she never walked, soaring towers she never climbed, courtyards she never visited. It was beautiful. It was perfect. It was a monument built for a goddess who had died a century ago but whose body still walked, still hunted, still killed. She felt no pleasure in her collection. No satisfaction in her progress. No comfort in her palace's beauty. She felt nothing at all except the distant pull of the next shard, already calling to her from somewhere far away, demanding that she follow, that she hunt, that she take. This was her existence.
