This was what the mirror had made of her. This was the Snow Queen. I tell you this not to excuse what she did—there is no excuse for the deaths she caused, for the families she destroyed, for the children left orphaned by her quest.

I tell you this so you understand what I found when I finally reached her palace, when I stumbled through her gates as a wounded bear with no memory of who I was or why I had come. I tell you this so you understand the magnitude of what Alessia had preserved, hidden deep in Glacia's frozen heart—that last ember of warmth, that final spark of the goddess she had been. Because without it, there would have been no hope. No possibility of redemption. No chance that winter's gentle soul could ever be recovered from the blade she had become.

This was the Snow Queen I would find. This was what the mirror had made of winter's gentle soul. And this was the woman I would fall in love with, the woman I would die for, the woman who would teach me that even the coldest heart can thaw if given reason enough to feel again.
But I'm getting ahead of myself.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 6: The Wounded Beast
p: My memories of that time are... difficult.
Fragmented.

Like trying to recall a dream weeks after waking, where you remember the feeling more than the details, the shape of things rather than their substance. I was a bear for nearly a century—a hundred years of existing in a form that wasn't mine, with a mind that couldn't hold onto who I'd been. The curse saw to that. But I remember enough. Enough to tell you what happened. Enough to explain how a primordial force of winter ended up bleeding and broken at the feet of winter's goddess.
This is what I remember.

The world was cold. That was the first thing, the constant thing, the only thing that felt right in a existence that felt fundamentally wrong. The cold didn't bother me—couldn't bother me, even trapped as I was in flesh and fur and bone. I was still, in some deep and indefinable way, winter itself.

The frost that formed on my white fur each morning felt like a greeting. The wind that howled across the tundra felt like a song I'd once known. But I couldn't remember the words. I was massive, even for a polar bear. Easily twice the size of any natural creature, with paws that could crush bone and jaws that could snap a seal's spine with a single bite. My fur was pure white, untouched by the yellowing that marked older bears, and it seemed to shimmer in certain lights—a hint of the divine nature I couldn't access, couldn't remember. I was powerful. I was also utterly, devastatingly alone. The other bears avoided me. They sensed something wrong, something other, something that didn't belong in their world. I was too large, too strange, too much. So I wandered.

For years that blurred into decades that blurred into a century, I wandered the frozen wastes with no purpose, no direction, no memory of why the cold felt like home and the emptiness felt like loss. Sometimes—rarely, so rarely I might have imagined it—something would flicker in my mind. A flash of standing upright. A sense of hands instead of paws. A feeling of vast power that had nothing to do with muscle and teeth and claws. But then it would slip away, like trying to hold water in cupped paws, and I would be left with only the vague sense that I had lost something important. Something essential.
I didn't have the words for grief. Didn't have the capacity for mourning. But somewhere deep in my chest, in the place where the curse had buried my true self, something ached.

The wolves came on a day when the sky was the color of old ice. I'd been following the coast, searching for seals, when I caught their scent on the wind. Wolves weren't uncommon this far north, but they usually avoided me. I was too large, too dangerous, not worth the risk. But these wolves were desperate. I could smell it on them
—the sharp tang of starvation, the musk of fear-driven aggression.
The winter had been harsh even by northern standards, and prey was scarce. They'd been hunting in a pack, working together to bring down anything they could find. And they'd found me.

There were eight of them. Lean, rangy creatures with ribs showing through their fur and eyes that gleamed with hunger and calculation. They spread out as they approached, forming a loose circle, cutting off escape routes with the practiced efficiency of predators who'd hunted together for years.

The alpha—a scarred male with one torn ear—growled low in his throat. A warning. A challenge. I should have run. Even as large as I was, eight wolves working together could bring me down. Should have turned and fled toward the water, where my size would give me the advantage. But something in me—some buried instinct, some echo of what I'd been—refused to retreat. I rose up on my hind legs, towering over them, and roared. The sound echoed across the tundra, primal and terrible, carrying in it some fragment of the power I'd lost. For a moment, the wolves hesitated. For a moment, they remembered that I was other, that I was wrong, that I was something they should fear. Then hunger overrode caution, and they attacked. The alpha came first, darting in low to snap at my legs. I swiped at him with one massive paw, felt the impact as I connected with his shoulder, heard the yelp as he tumbled away. But the others were already moving, using his attack as a distraction. Teeth sank into my left haunch. I spun, roaring, trying to shake the wolf off, but another was already at my other side, tearing at my flank. I caught that one with my jaws, felt bones crunch, tasted blood. The wolf went limp and I flung it away, but the damage was done.

They were too fast. Too coordinated. Too desperate. I fought like the primordial force I'd been—all fury and power and winter's wrath compressed into flesh and bone. I killed three of them. Wounded two more badly enough that they fled, limping and bleeding. But the remaining three kept coming, kept tearing, kept bleeding me.

The alpha got his jaws around my throat. Not deep enough to kill, not with my thick fur and massive neck, but deep enough to hurt. Deep enough to weaken. I threw myself backward, crushing him beneath my weight, felt something in him break. He released me and scrambled away, but not before opening a gash that bled hot and red into my white fur.

The last two wolves circled, panting, weighing whether I was worth the cost. I stood my ground, swaying slightly, blood dripping into the snow. My left haunch was torn open. My flank was shredded. The wound on my throat pulsed with each heartbeat, and I could feel my strength draining away with each drop of blood. I roared again, but this time it came out weaker. A warning without teeth.

The remaining wolves looked at each other. Looked at their dead and dying packmates. Looked at me, still standing, still dangerous despite my wounds. They turned and fled. I watched them go, my vision starting to blur at the edges. Then my legs gave out and I collapsed into the snow, my blood spreading around me in a crimson pool that steamed in the frigid air. I should have died there. Would have died there, if not for something I couldn't see, couldn't sense, couldn't understand. A subtle warmth, urging me forward. I don't know how long I lay there. Time had lost meaning, compressed into the simple binary of pain and not-pain, consciousness and not-consciousness. The cold couldn't take me—blood loss and shock and the simple fact that even a divine bear can die if wounded badly enough might have.

But I didn't die. Something kept me breathing. Something kept my heart beating. Something whispered in a language I couldn't understand that I needed to move, needed to get up, needed to follow. So I did. I dragged myself to my feet, swaying, my vision swimming. The world tilted and spun, and I had to lock my legs to keep from falling again.

Blood still dripped from my wounds, leaving a trail in the snow behind me. I should have sought shelter. Should have found somewhere to den, to lick my wounds, to either heal or die in peace. Instead, I started walking. I didn't know why. Didn't question it. The thought simply existed in my mind, more feeling than words: This way. Go this way. So I went. The snow seemed less deep in certain directions. Not obviously—not in any way I could have articulated, even if I'd had the capacity for articulation. But when I turned left, the drifts came up to my chest. When I turned right, they only reached my shoulders. Straight ahead, they barely reached my haunches. I went straight ahead.

The wind bit less from certain angles. Again, nothing obvious. Nothing I could have explained. But when I faced north, the wind cut through my fur like knives. When I faced south, it merely stung. When I faced east, toward the rising sun, it felt almost... gentle. I went east. There were other signs, too subtle to name. A patch of ice that was slightly less slick. A drift that was slightly more packed. A route that was slightly less steep. None of it enough to notice consciously, but all of it adding up to a path, a direction, a pull. I followed it because I had no other choice. Because my body moved on instinct and my instinct said this way, this way, keep going this way. Hours passed. Maybe days. Time blurred into a haze of pain and cold and the simple mechanical act of putting one paw in front of the other. My wounds had stopped bleeding—the cold had seen to that, freezing the blood in my fur, sealing the worst of the tears. But I could feel my strength fading with each step, feel my body shutting down piece by piece. I should have stopped. Should have let the wounds take me. Should have laid down in the snow and let it all end. But something wouldn't let me stop. Something kept pulling me forward, kept whispering not yet, not yet, just a little further. So I kept walking.

I saw the palace through a haze of pain and exhaustion. At first, I thought it was a hallucination. A trick of my dying mind, conjuring impossible things from the white emptiness of the tundra. Because nothing that looked like that could be real. It rose from the frozen wasteland like a mountain made of light and ice, all soaring spires and impossible angles and crystalline beauty that hurt to look at. The architecture defied everything I understood about how things should be—towers that twisted in ways that just should not have been possible, bridges that spanned distances without suppor.
But even through the fog of my fading consciousness, even trapped in a mind that couldn't hold complex thoughts, I felt something when I looked at it. Recognition.

Not memory—I couldn't access memory, couldn't hold onto anything that specific. But a feeling. A sense of I know this place. I've been here before. This is... But the thought wouldn't complete. Couldn't complete. It slipped away like everything else, leaving only the vague impression of familiarity and the stronger impression of home.

I stumbled forward, my legs barely holding me. The palace grew larger as I approached, more impossible, more beautiful, more wrong. The gates were massive structures of ice carved with scenes I couldn't interpret
—figures and symbols and patterns that shifted when I looked at them directly. The gates were open. I don't know if they'd been open before or if they opened for me.

I don't know if it was chance or design or something else entirely. I only know that when I reached them, when I finally dragged my broken body to the threshold of that impossible palace, there was nothing barring my way. I stumbled through the gates and into a courtyard of ice and starlight.
The world tilted.

My legs gave out. I felt myself falling, felt the impact as my body hit the frozen ground, felt the last of my strength drain away into the ice beneath me. My vision was fading, darkness creeping in from the edges. I could feel my heart slowing, feel my breath coming in shallow gasps, feel the cold finally starting to seep into my bones.

This is it, I thought, in the last moment of clarity I had. This is where I die. And then, through the blur of my failing vision, I saw her. A figure, pale and cold and impossibly beautiful, moving through the courtyard with fluid grace. She seemed to glow in the starlight, her white hair and ice-crystal gown catching the light and throwing it back in shades of blue and silver. She moved like winter itself—elegant, deadly, perfect. She was the most beautiful thing I'd ever seen. She was terrifying. She was... Familiar. The thought came from somewhere deep, somewhere the curse couldn't quite reach. A place that remembered standing in halls of ice, remembered laughter echoing off crystalline walls, remembered a goddess with soft features and gentle eyes who'd struggled with seeing her own beauty. But that goddess was gone. The woman approaching me was something else—something hard and sharp and cold as the palace around her. Her eyes were pale blue, almost colorless. Her features were sharp where they should have been soft, her expression empty where it should have been warm. And she was walking toward me, her footsteps making no sound on the ice, her face expressionless as she looked down at the massive, bleeding bear that had collapsed just inside her gates. I tried to lift my head. Tried to make some sound, some gesture, some indication that I was more than I appeared. But my body wouldn't respond. The darkness was closing in, pulling me down, dragging me away from consciousness.

The last thing I saw before the world went black was her face, beautiful and terrible and cold as death, leaning down to look at me. The last thing I felt was the faintest flicker of something in my chest—not memory, not recognition, but something deeper. Something that whispered, even as consciousness fled: I know you. Then darkness took me, and I knew nothing at all.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 7: The First Signs of Thaw
ch.t: Chapter 7: The First Signs of Thaw
p: The Snow Queen stood over the fallen bear, and the silence of the courtyard was absolute. Even the perpetual wind that howled through her realm seemed to hold its breath. She felt nothing when she looked down at the bleeding mass of white fur. No pity for the animal's suffering, no fear of its massive power, no spark of the recognition that had briefly flickered in my fading consciousness.

The shard in her chest had long ago extinguished such inconvenient emotions. Glacia saw only an object. A magnificent object, to be sure. It was easily twice the size of any natural polar bear—a creature of impossible magnitude, far too large and far too pure white to be a simple mortal beast.

The blood pooling in the snow beneath it was an unsightly, vulgar red, ruining the perfection of the white courtyard. She knelt beside the animal, her movements precise and detached, like a scholar examining a specimen. She reached out a pale hand and pressed two fingers deep into the bear's thick, matted fur, finding the wound on its throat.

The sheer force required to inflict such a tear was astounding, and the wound itself was deep enough to be fatal, even for a creature of this size. As she pressed her fingers against the bear's flesh, her power—winter's cold, absolute domain—naturally flowed into the creature.

Her magic, usually focused on extraction and corruption, now sought to stabilize and assess. What she found surprised her. Beneath the physical structure of muscle, bone, and blood, there was a vast, ancient power coiled within the bear. It was a coldness that resonated with her own, a fundamental force that spoke of blizzards, glaciers, and gale force winds. This was not an animal. This was something primordial. Kael.

The name whispered through the deep, frozen caverns of her mind, unbidden and unwelcome. It came from nowhere, meant nothing, connected to nothing she could access. Just a word, floating up from some buried place the shard couldn't quite reach.
Glacia frowned, a barely perceptible tightening of her colorless lips. She pulled her hand back as if the bear had burned her.
'Why would I think that?'

The question disturbed her more than the dying creature at her feet. She didn't have thoughts like that anymore—random, unexplained, rising from some depth she'd thought long frozen. The shard in her chest pulsed, as if reminding her of its presence, of its control. She should leave. Should return to her collection, to her purpose, to the next shard calling from somewhere distant. This creature was nothing to her. An animal. A dying beast that had stumbled into her realm by accident.

She stood, turning away from the bear with mechanical grace. She made it three steps before she stopped. Her hands, folded at her waist, began to tremble. The shard in her chest pulsed again, harder this time, demanding she continue walking. Demanding she return to her purpose. Demanding she feel nothing, care about nothing, want nothing except the gathering of shards. But something else pulled at her. Something warm and insistent and utterly foreign. It whispered that she should turn around, that she should help, that this creature mattered in a way she couldn't explain and didn't understand.

Leave it, the shard commanded, cold and absolute. Save it, something else whispered, warm as the bright sun on a snowy day. Glacia's hands trembled harder. She pressed them flat against her thighs, trying to still them, trying to suppress whatever this was. Her breath came faster, shallower.

She didn't understand. She hadn't felt anything in over a century. Hadn't wanted anything except the shards. Hadn't cared about anything except the compulsion. So why did the thought of leaving this creature to die make something in her chest ache?

She turned back slowly, her movements uncertain for the first time in a hundred years. The bear lay where she'd left it, massive and broken and bleeding. Its breath came in shallow gasps that stirred the frost on the ground. It was dying. Would be dead within the hour if left alone. It's just an animal, she told herself. It means nothing.

But even as she thought it, she knew it was a lie. This was no simple animal. The power she'd sensed within it resonated with her own in a way that felt... familiar. Like an echo of something she'd once known. Once been part of. Winter creatures. She'd always had a fondness for winter creatures.

The thought surfaced from somewhere deep, surprising her with its clarity. She remembered—or almost remembered—walking through snow-covered forests with wolves at her heels. Remembered arctic foxes curling at her feet. Remembered the way winter's animals had once sought her presence, had once found comfort in her cold. When had that stopped? When had she become something they fled from instead of something they sought?

The shard pulsed again, trying to push the memories back down, trying to restore the numbness. But the ember—Alessia's hidden gift—burned brighter, and for once, the warmth was stronger than the cold. Glacia knelt beside the bear again, and this time, her hand didn't hesitate. Moving him was harder than she'd expected. Even with magic, even with power that could reshape glaciers and summon blizzards, the sheer mass of the creature made it difficult. She wrapped him in threads of ice and winter wind, lifting him as gently as she could manage, and carried him through the silent halls of her palace.

She'd never brought anything living here before. Not in a century. The palace was a mausoleum, a monument, a place for the dead and the dying. Life had no place in these halls. But she carried him anyway, through corridors of crystalline ice, past chambers that echoed with emptiness, deeper into the heart of her realm. The grand central hearth stood in a hall so vast its ceiling was lost in shadows and refracted starlight. The hearth itself was enormous—large enough to burn logs the size of full grown trees, built from ice that had never melted and never would. It had been cold and dark for over a century, as dead as everything else in this place. Glacia laid the bear down before it, his massive body dwarfing even that enormous space. Blood still seeped from his wounds, staining the perfect ice floor. His breathing was so shallow now that she had to watch carefully to see his chest rise and fall. She stood over him, her hands trembling again, and wondered what she was doing.
This is madness, the shard whispered. Leave him. Return to your purpose.

But the ember burned, and she stayed. She raised her hands, calling on magic she hadn't used in longer than she could remember. Not the cold that killed, not the frost that extracted shards, but the winter that healed. The winter that preserved. The winter that protected life during its dormancy so it could bloom again in spring.

The magic came reluctantly, as if it had forgotten how to answer her call. But it came. Blue-white flames erupted in the hearth. They burned with an impossible light, cold as the void but radiating a warmth that had nothing to do with heat. The flames danced and twisted, beautiful and contradictory, fire that was ice and ice that was fire. They cast strange shadows across the hall, making the crystalline walls shimmer with colors that didn't exist.

The bear's body responded immediately. His breathing deepened slightly, his massive chest rising and falling with more strength. The divine nature within him recognized the magic, reached for it, drew it in. Glacia knelt beside him again, her hands hovering over his wounds. She'd never done this before. Had not healed anything in over a century. Had only killed, only taken, only destroyed.

Her hands shook as she lowered them to his fur, as she let her magic flow into him with purpose and care instead of violence. The first touch sent a shock through her. His fur was soft beneath her fingers—softer than it should be, matted with blood and dirt as it was. And warm. Not with the warmth of fever or dying, but with the warmth of life, of power, of something vast and ancient that refused to surrender.

She felt his heart beating beneath her palm. Slow. Too slow. But steady. Live, she thought, and was surprised by the fierceness of it. Live. Her magic poured into him, guided by instinct she'd thought long dead. She found the wound on his throat first—the deepest, the most dangerous. Her power wrapped around it, cold and precise, knitting torn flesh back together. The blood crystallized and fell away, leaving clean tissue beneath. The wounds on his haunch and flank came next. Deeper examination showed broken ribs, internal bleeding, damage that would have killed a mortal creature ten times over. But he wasn't mortal. The divine nature within him fought alongside her magic, responding to her touch, healing faster than should be possible.

Hours passed. Or maybe days. Time lost meaning as she worked, her focus absolute, her hands steady despite the trembling that wanted to return. The cold fire burned in the hearth, its impossible warmth filling the hall, and slowly—so slowly—the bear's breathing steadied. His heart beat stronger. His wounds closed. The blood stopped flowing. By the time she finally pulled her hands back, exhausted in a way she hadn't felt in a long time, he was no longer dying. She sat back on her heels, staring at him. He was magnificent. Even wounded, even unconscious, there was a majesty to him that took her breath away. His fur gleamed white in the cold firelight, pristine now that the blood was gone. His massive paws were tipped with great silver claws that could rend stone. His face, even in sleep, held a nobility that spoke of ancient power and timeless strength.

What are you? she wondered, reaching out to touch his fur again. Her hand hovered over him, trembling. The shard in her chest pulsed, warning her, trying to pull her back. But the ember burned brighter, and her hand descended. His fur was so soft. She stroked it gently, marveling at the texture, at the way the firelight caught in each strand and threw it back in shades of silver and blue.

Her fingers traced the line of his massive shoulder, feeling the muscle and bone and power beneath. She'd forgotten what it felt like to touch something living. To feel warmth that wasn't her own. To want to touch something not because she had to, but because she wanted to.

The realization disturbed her. She pulled her hand back, pressing it against her chest where the shard pulsed with cold fury. The ember and the shard warred within her, and for a moment, the pain was so intense she gasped.
Why? she thought desperately. Why do I care? Why can't I leave?

The bear slept on, oblivious to her turmoil. His breathing was deep and even now, his heart beating with steady strength. He would live. She'd saved him. She should go. Should return to her collection, to her purpose, to the shards that called from across the world. She'd done what the strange compulsion had demanded. He was safe. He would heal. But she didn't move. Instead, she settled herself on the ice floor beside him, her back against the hearth, her eyes on his sleeping form.

The cold fire burned behind her, warming her in ways she didn't understand, and she watched the rise and fall of his chest with an intensity that should have frightened her. Hours passed. The fire burned on, never diminishing, never needing fuel. The bear's breathing grew stronger with each passing moment. Color—or whatever equivalent existed for a creature of winter—returned to him. The deathly pallor faded, replaced by vibrant life. And Glacia watched.

She didn't know why she couldn't leave. Didn't understand the pull that kept her there, sitting vigil over a creature she didn't know, shouldn't care about, had no reason to save. The shard pulsed with increasing fury, demanding she return to her purpose, but the ember burned steady and warm, and for the first time since the shattering, the warmth was winning. "What are you?" she whispered into the silence. The bear didn't answer. Didn't stir. Just kept breathing, kept healing. She reached out again, unable to stop herself, and laid her hand on his side. She could feel his heart beating beneath her palm, strong and steady. Could feel the vast power coiled within him, ancient and cold and somehow... familiar.
Kael.

The name whispered through her mind again, and this time, she didn't suppress it. She let it sit there, examining it, trying to understand why it felt important. Why it felt right. But there was nothing. No memory. No context. Just a name that meant nothing and everything at once.
"Who are you?" she asked, her voice barely audible. "Why did you come here? Why do I..."

The thought wouldn't complete. Couldn't complete. The shard pulsed, cutting it off, but not before she felt the shape of it. Not before she understood what she'd almost said. Why do I care? She pulled her hand back, pressing both palms against her face.
"I don't understand," she whispered. "I don't understand any of this."

The bear slept on, peaceful now, no longer fighting for each breath. His wounds were closed, his body healing, his divine nature responding to her magic in ways that suggested he would be fully recovered within days instead of weeks. She'd saved him. Against the shard's demands, against a century of conditioning, against every instinct the corruption had instilled in her, she'd saved him. And she still didn't know why.

Glacia lowered her hands and looked at him again. At his massive form, his white fur, his noble face. At the way the cold fire's light played across him, making him look like something out of legend. Like something important. Like something that mattered. Like something I've been waiting for, she thought, and the ember in her chest flared so bright it almost hurt. She reached out one more time, her hand trembling, and laid it gently on his fur. This time, she let it rest there, feeling his warmth, his life, his presence. "Stay," she whispered, though she didn't know if she was talking to him or to herself. "Please stay." The bear's breathing remained steady and deep. His heart beat strong beneath her palm. And for the first time in forever, Glacia felt something that might have been hope. She didn't move. Didn't leave. Just sat there beside him as the cold fire burned and the hours passed and something in her frozen heart began—slowly, impossibly—to thaw.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 8: Beauty and the Beast
p: I woke up to fire.

It was a cold fire—blue-white, dancing impossibly high in a hearth built of ice that should have melted centuries ago. The light of it filled the hall with shifting shadows and colors I hadn't seen since the shattering: a sliver of silver, a hint of sapphire, the brief, ghost-like appearance of gold. It was contradictory, beautiful, and utterly confusing to my bear mind.

My consciousness returned in pieces. First, the pain was gone. The agony that had defined my last days of wandering—the torn throat, the shattered ribs, the deep, draining wounds—was simply... absent. I felt whole. More than whole. I felt the ancient power of Winter coiled inside me, vibrant and strong, the curse pushed back to a faint, manageable ache.

I tried to stand, and my massive body responded instantly, effortlessly. I rose onto all fours, flexing paws that felt capable of rending mountains, my white fur shining pristine in the cold firelight. I was magnificent. I was a god-beast.

Then the next piece of consciousness hit, jarring and sickening: I was a bear, but I was also me. For a hundred years, the curse had dulled the edges of my human identity, reducing my existence to primal instinct: hunt, eat, sleep, survive. But now, in this place of powerful, contradictory magic, the walls of the curse had fractured.
Kael.

The name echoed in my mind. Not a roar, but a thought. This is not right. This is not my body. I looked at my forepaws, flexing my silver claws. I knew, intellectually, that these were weapons of pure, terrifying power. But my human mind saw hands—hands that remembered shaping ice, hands that remembered touching a woman's soft cheek.

I looked around the room. It was vast, dominated by the impossible hearth, its ceiling lost in the glittering ice architecture. It was majestic, chilling, and utterly familiar. I knew this space. I knew the high, singing note the ice made just at the edge of hearing. The Palace. The thought formed in words, sharp and clear. The Winter Palace. And then I saw her.

She was sitting beside me on the ice floor, her back propped against the base of the frozen hearth, as if she had fallen asleep waiting for something. She was wearing a intricate ice-crystal gown, her white hair a flawless braided crown, her posture perfect even in repose.
Glacia.

The name came with a flood of fragmented images—standing in halls of ice, laughter echoing off crystalline walls, a goddess with soft features and gentle eyes. But the images were incomplete, like trying to see through frosted glass. The curse still held most of my memories captive, but the fire—her fire—was working on them, slowly melting the ice of the curse that trapped who I'd been.

I stared at her sleeping form, and something in my chest ached. She looked peaceful. Vulnerable. She woke the moment I shifted my weight, her colorless eyes snapping open with instantaneous, chilling alertness. There was no grogginess, no soft transition from sleep to waking—only the immediate, flat awareness of a perfected hunter. Anything but vulnerable.
She looked at me, not with curiosity or warmth, but with the detached, analytical gaze of a collector observing a specimen.
"You are awake," Glacia said. Her voice was the sound of wind over frozen glass—soft, empty, perfectly pitched. "I suspected you would recover quickly."

I tried to respond, to say something, anything, but all that came out was a low rumble from deep in my chest. The frustration was immediate and overwhelming. I had words, I had thoughts, but my body wouldn't cooperate.

She stood with fluid grace, moving closer to examine me. Her hands—those pale, deadly hands—reached out to check my wounds. She ran her fingers through my fur where the worst injuries had been, her touch clinical, detached.

"The healing was successful," she said, more to herself than to me. "Your uncanny nature responded well to the magic. The wounds are completely closed. No scarring." I stood still under her examination, hyper-aware of every place her fingers touched. There was no warmth in her touch, no gentleness, but there was also no cruelty. Just... assessment. She stepped back, folding her hands at her waist, and studied me with those colorless eyes.
"You are no ordinary bear," she said. "I sensed it when I found you. There is something ancient in you. Something that speaks of winter."

I wanted to tell her yes, because I am Winter's Hand, because I've known you since before the world was young, because something terrible has happened to both of us. But all I could do was meet her gaze and hope she saw something in my eyes that told her I understood.
She tilted her head slightly, a barely perceptible movement.
"You understand me," she said. It wasn't a question. "Not the words, perhaps. But the meaning. The feeling." I tossed my head in a nod, a very un-bear-like gesture that made her eyes narrow slightly.
"Interesting." She circled me slowly, studying me from every angle. "You will stay."
It wasn't a question or an invitation. It was a statement of fact.

"You may be useful," she continued, her voice flat and cold. "I have a collection that requires guarding. And a purpose that demands my absence from this place. You will remain here and ensure nothing disturbs what I have gathered."

She moved toward the chamber's entrance, clearly expecting me to follow. I did, my massive paws silent on the ice floor, and she led me through corridors of crystalline beauty to a circular room I remembered from my dying vision. The silver box sat on its pedestal, etched with patterns that writhed in the cold light. "This," Glacia said, gesturing to the box, "contains fragments of something that was broken. I gather them. I retrieve them. And I keep them here, safe, until I have collected them all."

She turned to look at me, her expression empty. "You will guard this room. You will guard this box. You will allow nothing and no one to disturb it while I am gone." She paused, and something flickered across her face—too quick to identify, gone almost before it registered. "If you prove useless," she said softly, "I will likely kill you."

The words should have been terrifying. They were meant to be. But there was something in the way she said them—a formality, a distance—that reminded me of something. Someone playing a role they'd been given but didn't quite fit into anymore. I met her gaze and held it, and after a long moment, she turned away. "Come," she said. "I will show you the rest of the palace. You should know what you are guarding."

Over the next three days, a strange routine developed between us. She was cold. Formal. She spoke to me as if I were a useful tool she'd acquired, nothing more. But she also... cared for me, in her way. The first night, after she'd shown me through the palace's vast, empty halls, I returned to the hearth chamber.

The fire had died down to embers, and I curled up before it, exhausted despite my healed body. The mental strain of being more aware, of fighting against the curse's hold, had drained me. I woke hours later to find the fire burning high and bright again, filling the hall with its impossible warmth. Glacia stood across the room, her back to me, her hand still raised from whatever magic she'd used to rekindle it. She didn't acknowledge what she'd done. Didn't look at me. Just lowered her hand and walked away, her footsteps silent on the ice. But I'd seen her do it. Seen her notice I was uncomfortable and do something about it, even though she'd never admit it mattered.
The second day, she brought me food. A seal, freshly killed, its body still warm. She tossed it onto the ice floor in front of me with no ceremony, no warmth.
"Eat," she commanded. "You need to maintain your strength if you are to be useful."

But she stayed while I ate, watching with that analytical gaze, and when I'd finished, she asked, "Was it sufficient?" I nodded, and something that might have been satisfaction flickered in her eyes before the emptiness returned.

She talked to me constantly, though she claimed it was merely thinking aloud. She would move through the palace with me following—I'd started doing that instinctively, unable to bear the thought of her disappearing into those vast, empty halls—and she would speak.

"The architecture here defies natural law," she said once, gesturing to a bridge that spanned an impossible distance. "It exists because I will it to exist. Because winter itself bends to my command." A pause. "Or it did, once. Now I'm not certain which of us is in command." Another time, standing in a great tower: "I built this palace over centuries. Every spire, every hall, every impossible angle. It was meant to be beautiful. A monument to winter's perfection." Her voice was flat, empty. "I don't remember why that mattered." I listened to everything, storing away each word, each tiny crack in her frozen facade. And I followed her, this cold, terrible, magnificent creature who'd saved my life for reasons she didn't understand.

On the third day, she was reading in the hearth chamber—an ancient tome written in a language I couldn't identify, though something about the script felt familiar. I lay near the fire, watching her, and she glanced up once.

"You're always watching," she observed. "Why?" I couldn't answer. Couldn't explain that watching her felt important, that something in me needed to understand what had happened to her, needed to find the goddess I almost remembered beneath the Snow Queen's cold exterior. She returned to her reading, but I noticed she positioned herself so I could see the pages, as if she didn't mind my observation. As if, perhaps, she found some comfort in not being completely alone. The silence between us grew comfortable. Not warm
—nothing about her was warm—but... companionable. Like two creatures who'd found themselves in the same space and decided the other's presence was tolerable. ✽✽✽

It was on the evening of the third day that everything changed. I'd been lying by the fire, half-dozing, when an urge struck me. A need to try something, to communicate in a way I hadn't attempted before. The curse was weaker here, in her realm, with her fire healing my mind bit by bit. Maybe... I stood and moved to a clear section of the ice floor. Glacia was across the hall, studying something in the silver box, her back to me. I extended one massive paw and pressed my silver claws against the ice. The sound of scratching echoed through the chamber.
It was harder than I'd expected—my paws weren't made for precision, and the ice was harder than stone. But I persisted, dragging my claws in careful, deliberate lines. K.
The letter took forever. My paw slipped twice, and I had to start over. But eventually, it was there, crude but recognizable.
A.
Easier this time. I was getting the feel of it. E.
My paw was aching, the strain of such fine motor control in this body almost overwhelming. But I couldn't stop. This was important. This mattered. L.

I stepped back, panting from the effort, and stared down at what I'd created. KAEL. My name. Scratched into the ice floor of Glacia's palace. Proof that I was more than a beast, that I was— "What are you doing?" Her voice cut through my thoughts.

I turned to find her standing a few feet away, staring at the scratches in the ice. She must have heard the sound and come to investigate. She moved closer, her eyes fixed on the letters, and I saw her lips move silently, forming the word.
"Kael," she whispered.

The moment she spoke it, something happened. The ember in her chest flared—I could see it, a brief golden light beneath her icy gown. Her hand flew to her chest, pressing against the spot, her eyes going wide. And in that same instant, my mind opened. Memories flooded back—not all of them, not even most of them, but enough.

Enough to remember standing in these halls centuries ago. Enough to remember a goddess with gentle eyes who'd struggled to see her own beauty. Enough to remember that I'd known her, that we'd been... something. Friends? Almost friends? Glacia. Not the Snow Queen. Not a cold, terrible creature, but Glacia. Winter's soul. The eldest of the Horai.
"Kael," she said again, and this time her voice shook. "Why do I... why does that name..."
She looked at me, really looked at me, and for a moment
—just a moment—I saw recognition in her colorless eyes. Saw her seeing me, not just a useful beast but something more, something important, something that mattered.

Then the shard in her chest pulsed. I felt it like a physical blow—a wave of cold so intense it drove the air from my lungs. Glacia gasped, stumbling backward, both hands pressed to her chest now. Her face contorted with pain, and the recognition in her eyes shattered like thin glass.
My own mind fractured at the same moment.

The memories that had been so clear an instant ago scattered, fragmenting, slipping away like water through my paws. I shook my head, trying to hold onto them, but they were already fading. What was I...? Why did I...? I looked down at the name scratched in the ice. KAEL.

It meant something. It was important. But I couldn't quite grasp why. Glacia lowered her hands slowly, her breathing ragged. She stared at me with an expression I couldn't read—confusion, fear, something that might have been grief.
"I don't understand," she whispered. "I don't understand any of this."

She turned away abruptly, her movements sharp and agitated instead of her usual fluid grace. She walked to the far side of the chamber, putting distance between us, and stood with her back to me, her shoulders rigid. The silence stretched, broken only by the crackling of the cold fire. Finally, without turning around, she spoke.
"Return to the hearth. Rest. We will not speak of this again."

It was a command, but her voice shook slightly on the last word. I wanted to go to her. Wanted to somehow communicate that I understood, that something had happened to both of us, that we were connected in ways neither of us could fully remember. But my body was exhausted from the effort of scratching the name, and my mind was reeling from the fractured memories and their sudden loss.
I returned to the hearth and lay down, but I kept my eyes on her distant figure. She didn't move for a long time. Just stood there, one hand pressed to her chest, staring at nothing.

The next day, things returned to their cold routine. But something had shifted. She was more watchful of me now, her colorless eyes tracking my movements with an intensity that hadn't been there before. And I found myself staying closer to her, following her through the palace with even more determination, as if proximity might help me understand what had happened, might help me remember what I'd lost.

The fire burned brighter when I was near. I noticed it, and I think she did too, though neither of us acknowledged it. She brought me food without being asked. She spoke to me more frequently, though she still pretended she was merely thinking aloud. And once, when I was sleeping by the hearth, I woke to find her sitting nearby, watching me with an expression that might have been longing or confusion or something else entirely. When our eyes met, she looked away quickly and stood.
"I was merely ensuring you were still breathing," she said, her voice flat. "You are valuable. It would be inconvenient if you died."
But she'd been sitting there for a while. I could tell by the way the fire had burned down, by the way her posture had been relaxed instead of rigid. She'd been keeping vigil. Again.
On the fifth day after I'd woken, I was following her through the palace when she suddenly stopped in the middle of a corridor. Her hand flew to her chest, and her eyes went distant.

"There is another," she said, more to herself than to me. I moved closer, questioning, and she looked down at me. "A shard," she explained, her voice returning to its usual emptiness. "I can feel it calling. Distant, but distinct. I must retrieve it."

She turned and began walking toward the palace's entrance, her movements purposeful now, and I followed. We reached the central chamber where the silver box sat on its pedestal, and she stopped before it, staring at it with an expression I couldn't read. "I will leave tomorrow," she said. "The shard is far from here. It will take time to reach it, to extract it, to return." She turned to look at me, and her colorless eyes were hard, cold, empty. "You will remain here. You will guard the collection. You will guard the palace. Nothing and no one is to disturb what I have gathered. Do you understand?"
I nodded, and something flickered in her eyes—approval, perhaps, or satisfaction that I comprehended my duty.
"I will return when it is done," she continued. "However long that takes. You will wait."

It was a command, absolute and unquestionable. But there was something else beneath it, something I couldn't quite identify. A hesitation, maybe. An uncertainty. She looked at me for a long moment, and I wondered what she saw. A useful beast? A guard for her collection? Or something more, something that confused and disturbed her in ways she couldn't explain?
"Do not fail me, beast," she said finally, and turned away. ✽✽✽
She left at dawn the next day.

I followed her to the palace gates, massive and silent, and watched as she prepared to depart. She wore traveling clothes now—still ice and crystal, still beautiful and terrible, but more practical than her usual gown. Her white hair was pulled back in a severe braid, and she carried nothing except the cold that radiated from her like a physical force. She paused at the threshold and turned back to look at me.

"Guard well," she said. "I will know if you fail." But there was something in her eyes as she said it—not warmth, exactly, but something that might have been concern. Or uncertainty. Or the faintest hint of reluctance to leave. Then she turned and walked out into the frozen wasteland beyond, and I watched her figure grow smaller and smaller until she disappeared into the white emptiness.

The palace felt different without her. Emptier. The silence was more oppressive, the cold more absolute. I returned to the hearth chamber and curled up before the fire she'd made for me, and I realized with a start that I was lonely. I'd been alone for a century. Had wandered the frozen wastes with no companion, no purpose, no memory of anything beyond survival. But I hadn't been lonely then, because I hadn't been aware enough to understand what loneliness was. Now I was aware.

Now I remembered—in fragments, in pieces—that I'd once been something more than a beast. And now I was alone in a palace built for a goddess who'd saved my life for reasons she didn't understand, waiting for her to return from a hunt I didn't fully comprehend. I laid my head on my paws and stared into the cold fire, and I felt the curse's hold weakening further.

The fire was still working on my mind, still melting the ice that trapped my memories. Without Glacia here to distract me, without the constant pull of her presence, I could feel my human consciousness pushing harder against the curse's boundaries. Memories surfaced, clearer now. Standing in these halls centuries ago, discussing the nature of winter with a goddess who'd listened with quiet intensity. Flying through storms, shaping blizzards, bringing winter to the world with pride and purpose. The Horai—all four of them—laughing together in Alessia's garden, before whatever had happened to shatter their bond.
And Gerda.

I remembered Gerda now, remembered her fire and passion and the terrible thing she'd done when I'd tried to leave. Remembered the curse, the transformation, the century of wandering as a beast with no memory of who I'd been.

But I also remembered the piece of something that had lodged in my eye during that unnatural storm, that had changed how I saw Gerda, how I saw everything. That had made me cruel and cold and dismissive in ways I'd never been before. Something had happened. Something terrible. To me, and to Glacia, and possibly to the whole world. And somehow, impossibly, we'd found each other.

Two cursed creatures, two fragments of what we'd once been, drawn together by forces neither of us understood. I waited. And while I waited, the curse's hold weakened further, and I began—slowly, painfully
—to remember who I had been. And to wonder if the goddess who'd saved me was remembering too.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 9: Winter's Doubt
p: The palace was silent without her.

I'd grown accustomed to the sound of her footsteps on the ice, the whisper of her gown as she moved through the halls, the way the very air seemed to shift when she entered a room. Now there was only emptiness and the crackling of the cold fire she'd left burning for me.

Three days had passed since she'd left. Or was it four? Time moved strangely in this place, measured not by the sun—which barely rose this far north—but by the rhythm of my own thoughts, which grew clearer with each passing hour.

The fire helped. I could feel it working on my mind, melting the ice of Gerda's curse bit by bit, like spring thaw revealing what had been buried beneath winter's grip. Memories surfaced with increasing clarity: my true form, my purpose, the world as I'd known it before a century of animal existence.
I remembered Glacia as she'd been. Not the Snow Queen
—cold and terrible and empty—but the goddess who'd laughed with her sisters, while braiding flowers into their hair, in Alessia's garden before something had shattered their bond.
What had happened to her? What had turned winter's gentle soul into this creature of ice and death?

I paced the great hall, my massive paws silent on the frozen floor, and tried to piece together the fragments. The shard in her chest—I'd felt it pulse, felt its cold fury when she'd spoken my name. The silver box full of similar shards. The compulsion that drove her to hunt and kill.
Something had broken. Something terrible. And somehow, we were both caught in the aftermath.
I was contemplating this, lying before the hearth with my head on my paws, when I felt it.
The cold intensified.

Not the comfortable cold of the palace, the cold that felt like home. This was different—sharper, more aggressive, like the leading edge of a blizzard. The very air seemed to contract, and frost spread across the walls in patterns that hadn't been there moments before.
She was back.
I rose to my feet, every sense alert. Something was wrong. I could feel it in the way the cold pressed against my fur, in the way the palace itself seemed to brace for her arrival.
I moved toward the entrance hall, staying in the shadows near one of the great crystalline pillars. The massive gates swung open with a sound like breaking ice, and she swept through.

She looked the same—white hair in its severe braid, ice-crystal traveling clothes, pale skin that seemed to glow in the starlight. But there was something different in the way she moved. Not her usual fluid grace, but something harder, more mechanical. Like she was forcing herself forward through sheer will.
She didn't see me. Didn't look around. Just walked with rigid purpose toward the chamber where the silver box waited.
I followed at a distance, keeping to the shadows, my massive form surprisingly quiet despite my size. Something told me I needed to see this. Needed to understand.

The circular chamber was exactly as she'd left it—the silver box on its pedestal, the patterns etched into its surface writhing in the cold light. Glacia approached it with those same mechanical movements, her hands steady as she opened the lid.

The box was nearly full now. Hundreds of shards, glinting like malevolent stars, each one representing a life taken or destroyed. She reached into her gown and withdrew another shard—this one still seemed to pulse with a faint, sickly light.
Four hundred and sixty-four.
She placed it carefully among the others, her movements precise, controlled. Then she closed the lid with a soft click that echoed through the chamber.
And then she stopped.
Just stood there, her hands resting on the closed box, her head bowed. For a long moment, nothing happened. Then I saw it—her hands began to tremble.

It started small, barely perceptible, but it grew. Her fingers shook against the silver surface, and she pressed them down harder, trying to still them. But the trembling spread up her arms, into her shoulders.
She pulled her hands back and pressed them to her chest, right where I knew the shard was lodged. Her breathing came faster, shallower.
And then, so quietly I almost didn't hear it, she spoke.
"I'm sorry."

The words were barely a whisper, broken and raw. Her face—that perfect, cold, emotionless face—cracked. Just for a moment. Just long enough for me to see something underneath. Grief. Horror. A pain so deep it had no name.
"Why does it..." she started, then cut herself off, shaking her head violently.

The shard in her chest pulsed. I could see it—a flash of cold light beneath her gown, like lightning trapped in ice. Her whole body went rigid, and the emotion that had flickered across her face disappeared as if it had never been.
She lowered her hands slowly, her breathing steadying, her posture straightening. The Snow Queen was back, the moment of weakness erased.
Over the next week, something changed between us..

I followed her more closely now. Not just out of curiosity or the strange pull I felt toward her, but out of something that might have been protectiveness. She'd saved my life, had tended my wounds with magic she hadn't used in a century, had created fire to warm me when she could have left me to die.
And I'd seen her break, just for a moment. Had seen the goddess beneath the Snow Queen's frozen exterior.
She allowed my constant presence, though she pretended annoyance. "Must you follow me everywhere, beast?" she'd ask, but there was no real heat in it. And she never actually sent me away.

She talked more, her monologues about the palace's architecture or the nature of winter becoming almost conversational. And sometimes, when she thought I wasn't paying attention, I'd catch her watching me with an expression I couldn't quite read.

But there was tension too. She avoided eye contact more than before. When we were in the same room, she'd position herself so she didn't have to look directly at me. And several times, I caught her starting to say something, then stopping herself, her lips pressed into a thin line.
It was near the end of the week when things finally came to a head.

I'd been trying to communicate more, scratching simple shapes in the ice, making deliberate sounds that were almost words. The fire was still working on my mind, and I could feel my human consciousness pushing harder against the curse's boundaries. I had thoughts, complex and clear, but my body still wouldn't cooperate enough to express them.

She'd been avoiding the hearth chamber—the place where I'd scratched my name, where we'd both felt that flash of recognition before the shards had torn it away. But on the seventh day, she finally returned.

I was lying by the fire when she entered, carrying one of her ancient tomes. She paused when she saw me, and for a moment I thought she'd leave. But then she moved to her usual spot and sat down, opening the book with deliberate focus.
We sat in silence for a long time. The fire crackled. The ice sang its high, crystalline note. And the tension between us grew thicker with each passing moment.
Finally, I couldn't bear it anymore.
I stood and moved to the spot where she'd stood in the shard chamber—the exact position, facing the same direction. Then I mimicked her posture: head bowed, hands pressed to my chest.
I heard her sharp intake of breath.
"What are you doing?" Her voice was sharp, but there was something underneath it. Something that might have been fear.
I turned to look at her, holding her gaze. Trying to communicate what I couldn't say in words: *I saw you. I saw your pain. I understand.*
She stood abruptly, the book falling forgotten to the ice. "You were spying on me?"
I shook my head—that very un-bear-like gesture that always made her eyes narrow.
"You had no right—" She stopped, her hands clenching into fists at her sides. "You don't understand. You can't understand."
I moved closer, slowly, carefully. Not threatening, just... present.
"Stop," she commanded, but her voice cracked slightly. "Just stop."

I didn't stop. I came to stand directly in front of her, close enough that she had to look up to meet my eyes. And I held her gaze, refusing to let her look away, refusing to let her hide behind the Snow Queen's mask.
Her anger cracked like thin ice under pressure.

"You don't understand," she said again, but this time it came out almost pleading. "The extraction was... it was difficult. The victim was young. Younger than most. It took longer than it should have."
She turned away from me, wrapping her arms around herself in a gesture that looked almost human. Almost vulnerable.

"They never survive," she continued, her voice flat but with something trembling underneath. "Or almost never. The cold is too much. Their hearts stop, their blood freezes, and they die. Quickly, usually. Mercifully."
A pause. "This one... screamed for their mother."
The words hung in the air between us, terrible and raw.

"I used to feel nothing about it," she said. "The shard ensures I feel nothing. The compulsion drives me forward, and I hunt and I extract and I kill, and it's all just... necessary. Like breathing. Like existing."
She turned back to look at me, and her colorless eyes were wide with something that might have been confusion or fear or both.
"I don't know why it's becoming harder."
Then, so quietly I almost didn't hear it: "I don't know why you being here makes it harder."

She moved toward me—not away, toward—and sank down onto the ice floor beside me. It was unprecedented. She'd sat near me before, but never like this. Never with this kind of deliberate closeness, as if she needed the proximity.

"When I found you," she said, staring at the fire instead of at me, "I should have left you to die. The shard commanded it. Demanded I return to my purpose, to the hunt. But something else..." She pressed a hand to her chest. "Something else told me to save you."
Her hand trembled against her gown. "I don't understand it. The shard should prevent this. Should prevent me from caring about anything except gathering the other shards."
She looked at me then, really looked at me, and I saw the confusion and fear and desperate need to understand written across her face.
"But I think..." Her voice dropped to barely a whisper. "I think I'm starting to care anyway."
She reached out, her hand hovering over my fur, trembling. Then she touched me—just briefly, her fingers brushing against my shoulder before she pulled back as if burned.
"It doesn't matter," she said, but her voice shook. "I have a purpose. The shards must be gathered. All of them. That's all that matters. That's all that can matter."
But even as she said it, I could see the doubt in her eyes. Could see the war being waged inside her between the shard's compulsion and something else. Something warm.
We sat there in silence for a long time, the fire burning between us, and I felt something shift. Not break, not yet. But shift. Like ice beginning to crack under the first warmth of spring.
Three days later, I was with her in the shard chamber when it happened.

She'd been standing before the silver box, her hands resting on its lid, when she suddenly stiffened. Her hand flew to her chest, and her eyes went distant—that look I'd come to recognize. Another shard was calling.
"There's another," she said, more to herself than to me. "Far to the south."
She turned and walked from the chamber with purpose, and I followed. We moved through the palace to the great courtyard, and I watched as she approached something I'd never seen before.

The sleigh was magnificent and terrible in equal measure. It looked like it had been carved from a single massive piece of ice, all flowing curves and sharp angles. There were no reindeer, no visible means of propulsion—just the sleigh itself, gleaming in the starlight, radiating cold.
She ran her hand along its side, and I felt magic pulse through the air. The sleigh seemed to wake, frost spreading across its surface in intricate patterns.
She turned to look at me, and I saw resignation in her eyes.
"You're going to follow me regardless, aren't you?"
I nodded.
She studied me for a long moment, and I could see her weighing something. Then she sighed—a very human sound from a very inhuman creature.
"The sleigh can carry your weight," she said. "If you insist on coming."
It wasn't quite permission. Wasn't quite an invitation. But it was acceptance.
"You'll see what I do," she continued, her voice hardening. "What I must do. Don't interfere."
It was a command, but there was something else underneath it. Almost like a warning. Like she didn't want me to see but also didn't want to be alone.
I climbed into the sleigh, my massive weight making it sink slightly into the snow. She took her position at the front, her hands resting on rails that seemed to form themselves from the ice.
"Hold on," she said, and the sleigh launched into the air.
Flying in the sleigh was like being inside a blizzard and outside it at the same time.

We soared over the frozen wasteland, the palace shrinking behind us until it was just a glittering point on the horizon. The wind howled around us, but inside the sleigh it was calm, quiet, almost peaceful. The stars wheeled overhead, impossibly bright, and below us the world was nothing but white emptiness.
Glacia drove with magic, her hands steady on the rails, her eyes fixed forward. At first she said nothing, and I thought the journey would pass in silence.
But then she started talking.
"I can feel them," she said, her voice carrying easily despite the wind. "The shards. Each one calls to me, a pull I can't ignore. Like thirst. Like drowning and knowing air is just out of reach."
She glanced back at me briefly, then returned her gaze forward. It was easier to talk, I realized, when she didn't have to look at me.

"The compulsion is... overwhelming," she continued. "When I sense a shard, everything else fades. I must retrieve it. Must add it to the collection. The need consumes everything—thought, feeling, purpose. There's only the hunt."
We flew in silence for a moment, the sleigh cutting through the night air like a blade through silk.

"I've been hunting for over a century," she said. "Hundreds of shards. Hundreds of deaths. I used to not question it. The compulsion was absolute, and I was... empty. The shard in my chest had hollowed me out, left nothing but the need to gather."
Her hands tightened on the rails. "Now I... wonder. Why? What happens when I have them all? What purpose does this serve?"
She shook her head. "The compulsion doesn't explain. Doesn't offer reasons. It just drives me forward, shard after shard, death after death."
I made a low sound—not quite a growl, not quite a whine. Something that tried to convey understanding, sympathy.

She glanced back again, and something flickered in her eyes. "You're listening," she said, and there was wonder in her voice. "You actually understand, don't you? Not just the feelings, but the words. The meaning."
I nodded, and she turned back to face forward, but I could see her shoulders relax slightly.

We flew over a frozen lake, its surface smooth as glass. "I used to love winter," she said quietly. "Used to see the beauty in it—the way snow transformed the world, the peace of a frozen landscape, the promise of renewal that came with the cold. Winter wasn't death. It was rest. Dormancy. The world sleeping so it could wake again in spring."
Her voice dropped even lower. "I don't see that anymore. Now I only see the cold. The emptiness. The death."
I shifted closer to her, and she didn't move away. My warmth—the divine warmth that even the curse couldn't fully suppress—radiated against her back.
She shivered once. Just once. It was such a small thing, such a human thing, that it startled me. The Snow Queen, shivering.
I moved closer still, pressing my bulk against her back, sharing my heat. For a moment I thought she'd pull away, would command me to move back.
But she didn't. She leaned into my warmth, just slightly, and continued to drive the sleigh through the night.
"Thank you," she whispered, so quietly I almost didn't hear it.
We flew on in silence after that, but it was a different kind of silence. Companionable. Almost peaceful.
We reached the village as evening fell.

It was small—maybe fifty houses clustered together in a valley, smoke rising from chimneys, warm light glowing in windows. The kind of place where everyone knew everyone, where life moved at the pace of seasons and harvests.
The kind of place that would be devastated by what was about to happen.

Glacia brought the sleigh down outside the village, landing in a copse of trees where we wouldn't be immediately visible. She stepped out, her movements once again mechanical, purposeful. The Snow Queen, not the goddess who'd shared her doubts with me during the flight.
"Wait here with the sleigh," she commanded, not looking at me.
I climbed out after her.
She turned, her eyes flashing with anger. "I said wait—"
I met her gaze and held it. *No.*

She could have forced me. Could have used her magic to freeze me in place, to bind me to the sleigh. But she didn't. She just stared at me for a long moment, and I saw something in her eyes that might have been resignation or relief or both.
"Stay back, then," she said finally. "And don't interfere. No matter what you see."
She turned and walked toward the village, and I followed at a distance, keeping to the shadows.

The shard's pull led her to a house near the center of the village—modest but well-kept, with flower boxes in the windows and smoke curling from the chimney. Through the windows, I could see movement. A family gathered around a table. Warm. Safe. Alive.
Not for long.

Glacia approached the door, and I felt it—the shard. It was inside, lodged in someone's eye, its corruption already working. I could sense it now, could almost see it glinting in the lamplight through the window.
The door opened before she could knock. A man stood there—middle-aged, weathered, with the look of someone who worked with his hands. His eyes widened when he saw her.
"No," he breathed. "No, please, not here. Not my family."

Behind him, I could see others gathering. A woman—his wife, probably. Two younger children. And there, in the back, a young person. Late teens, maybe early twenties. Strong, healthy, with their whole life ahead of them.
And in their left eye, barely visible but unmistakable to those who knew what to look for: a glint of something that shouldn't be there.
"The shard must be removed," Glacia said, her voice flat and empty. "Stand aside."
"Please," the man begged. "They're just children. They haven't done anything wrong. Please."
"Stand aside," Glacia repeated, and there was no mercy in her voice. No warmth. Just cold, absolute purpose.
The family didn't move. The man spread his arms, blocking the doorway. "You'll have to go through me first."

Glacia raised her hand, and frost spread from her fingers. The man gasped as ice crept up his legs, freezing him in place. Not harming him—she wasn't cruel, just efficient—but immobilizing him completely.
The woman screamed and rushed forward, but Glacia froze her too. Then the children. One by one, she turned them into living statues, their eyes wide with terror, their mouths open in silent screams.
Only the victim remained unfrozen, standing at the back of the room, trembling.
"Please," he whispered. "I don't want to die. Please, I don't want to die."
Glacia stepped into the house, moving toward him with mechanical grace. "It will be over soon."
I couldn't bear it anymore. I moved forward from the shadows, a low, distressed roar building in my chest. The sound echoed through the village, primal and terrible.
Glacia stopped. Turned. Our eyes met across the distance.
For a moment—just a moment—I saw something in her face. Hesitation. Uncertainty. The ember fighting against the shard's compulsion.
Then the shard in her chest pulsed, visible now through her gown, and her face went blank again.
She turned back to the victim.
"No!" he screamed. "No, please, someone help me! Mother! Father!"
But his parents couldn't move, couldn't speak, could only watch in frozen horror as the Snow Queen approached their child.
Glacia reached out and cupped the victim's face with both hands. Her touch was gentle—almost tender—but there was nothing kind about what came next.
She leaned in and pressed her lips to his.

The cold spread instantly. I could see it—frost racing across the victim's skin, turning it pale, then blue, then white. The boy convulsed, his body trying to fight the invasion of winter's absolute cold, but there was no fighting it. No escaping it.
His screams turned to gasps, then to whimpers, then to nothing as the cold reached his lungs and froze the air in his chest.
But he didn't die.
Most victims died quickly—their hearts stopped, their blood froze, and it was over in moments. But this one was young, strong, his body fighting with everything it had to survive.
So the process took longer. Much longer.

I watched in horror as the victim's body convulsed again and again, as the cold worked its way deeper, as his eye—the one with the shard—began to frost over. He was conscious through most of it, aware and terrified and in agony.
"Mother," he gasped at one point, his voice barely audible. "Mother, it hurts. It hurts so much."
But his mother couldn't answer. Could only watch, frozen, as her child suffered.

Finally—finally—the shard began to emerge. It pushed its way out of the young man's eye like a splinter working free, trailing frost and blood and something darker. Glacia caught it in her hand, her fingers closing around it with practiced ease.
The boy collapsed, his body hitting the floor with a sickening thud. But his chest still rose and fell. Shallow breaths. Barely there. But alive.
Alive, but changed. I could see it already—the way the frost had spread across his skin, the way his left eye was now clouded and dead, the way he trembled with cold that would never fully leave him.
He would survive. But he would never be the same.
Glacia stood over him, the shard clutched in her hand, and for a long moment she just... stared. At the barelybreathing victim. At the frozen family. At the scene of devastation she'd created.
Something crossed her face. Something that might have been horror or grief or the first stirrings of conscience.
Then she turned and saw me standing in the doorway.
Our eyes met, and I saw it all in her face—the compulsion that had driven her here, the emptiness the shard enforced, and underneath it all, something warm and terrible and desperately confused.

I moved forward, stepping over the threshold, positioning myself between her and the family. Not threatening her—I could never threaten her—but... protecting her? From their hatred? From their fear? From herself?
I turned to look at the frozen family, and a low growl rumbled in my chest. A warning. *Stay back. Don't hurt her.*
Even though I understood their pain. Even though I sympathized with their loss. Even though what she'd done was monstrous.
I still moved to protect her.
She made a sound—something between a gasp and a sob. "Don't," she said, her voice sharp but shaking. "Don't... don't try to..."
She couldn't finish the sentence. Just stood there, the shard clutched in her trembling hand, staring at me with an expression I'd never seen before.
I turned back to her and moved closer, making a soft sound low in my throat. Comfort. Understanding. *I'm here.*
I reached out with my muzzle, gently touching her hand
—the one holding the shard.
She jerked away as if I'd burned her. "Don't," she said again, backing toward the door. "This is what I am. What I do. Don't... don't try to make it something it's not."
She turned and fled, moving with inhuman speed, disappearing into the night.

I looked back at the family one more time. The victim was still breathing, barely. The others were beginning to thaw—Glacia's magic fading now that she was gone. Soon they'd be free to tend to their child, to try to save what could be saved.
There was nothing I could do for them. Nothing that would help.
So I turned and followed her into the darkness.
I found her at the sleigh, standing with her back to me, her shoulders rigid. She didn't turn when I approached, didn't acknowledge my presence.
But I could see her hands trembling. Could see the way she pressed one hand to her chest, right where the shard was lodged.
"Get in," she said, her voice flat. "We're leaving."
I climbed into the sleigh, and she took her position at the front. The sleigh launched into the air, and we flew back toward the palace in silence.
But it was a different kind of silence than before. Heavy. Oppressive. Filled with things neither of us could say.

I could see her hands shaking on the rails. Could see the way she kept pressing her hand to her chest, as if trying to suppress something. The ember and the shard, warring inside her, and for the first time, the ember was strong enough to make the battle visible.
Several times during the flight, she opened her mouth as if to speak, then closed it again. Her breathing was uneven, her posture rigid with tension.

We landed in the palace courtyard as dawn was breaking—or what passed for dawn this far north, a slight lightening of the perpetual twilight. She climbed out of the sleigh and walked toward the palace without a word.
I followed.
She went straight to the shard chamber, moving with that mechanical purpose again. Opened the silver box. Deposited the new shard among the others.
Four hundred and sixty-five.
She closed the lid and stood there, her hands resting on the box, her head bowed.
I moved closer, my paws silent on the ice.
She must have heard me, but she didn't turn around. "Why?" she asked, her voice barely audible. "Why do you stay? Why do you... care?"

I couldn't answer in words. Couldn't explain that I saw the goddess beneath the Snow Queen's mask, that I understood she was as much a victim as those she hunted, that something in me recognized something in her.
So I did the only thing I could. I moved closer and leaned against her gently, offering my warmth, my presence, my silent support.
For a moment she stood rigid, resisting. Then, slowly, her hand came up to rest on my fur. Her fingers trembled as they touched me, as if she was afraid I might disappear.
"I don't understand any of this," she whispered.
We stood like that for a long time, the silence broken only by the distant sound of wind howling through the palace's impossible architecture.
Later, we sat by the hearth.

She'd positioned herself closer to me than ever before, close enough that I could feel the cold radiating from her, close enough that my warmth could reach her. The fire burned bright between us, casting dancing shadows across the crystalline walls.
She stared at the flames for a long time before speaking.
"I've done this hundreds of times," she said finally. "Felt nothing. Questioned nothing. The compulsion drives me forward, and I hunt and I extract and I kill, and it's all just... necessary."
She turned to look at me, and her colorless eyes were full of confusion and fear and something that might have been hope.
"Now I..." She paused, struggling with the words. "The compulsion is still there. Just as strong. The shard still demands I gather the others. But something else is there too."
Her hand moved to her chest, pressing against where the shard was lodged. "Since you came. Since I saved you. Since I..."
She trailed off, unable or unwilling to finish the thought.

"The shard in my chest should prevent this," she continued. "Should prevent me from caring about anything except the gathering. That's its purpose. That's what it does. It hollows you out, leaves nothing but the need."
She looked at me, and I saw the war being waged in her eyes—the shard's cold fury against something warm and desperate and alive.
"But I think..." Her voice dropped to barely a whisper. "I think I'm starting to care anyway."
Her hand trembled where it rested against her chest. She pulled it back, staring at it as if it belonged to someone else.
"I don't know if that's better or worse," she said. "The emptiness was... easier. Simpler. I didn't question. Didn't doubt. Didn't feel the weight of what I was doing."

She turned back to the fire. "Now I feel it. The horror of it. The wrongness. That child tonight—he'll live, but he'll never be whole again. Never be warm again. He'll carry winter in his bones for the rest of his life, and it's because of me."
A pause. "Because of what I am."
I moved closer, pressing my bulk against her side. She didn't pull away. Instead, she leaned into me, her hand coming up to rest on my fur.

"I don't know what's happening to me," she whispered. "I don't know why you make it harder and easier at the same time. I don't know why I can't bear the thought of you leaving, or why your presence makes this cursed existence less overwhelming."
She looked at me, and I saw tears forming in her eyes—the first tears I'd seen from her, the first sign that the ice around her heart was truly beginning to crack.
"I don't know if I can stop," she said. "The compulsion is still there. The shards still call. I'll have to hunt again. Have to extract again. Have to..."
She couldn't finish. Just pressed her face against my fur, her shoulders shaking with silent sobs.
I rested my head against her, offering what comfort I could. And we sat there as the fire burned and the palace sang its ghostly song and something fundamental shifted between us.
The doubt had taken root. And though neither of us knew it yet, that doubt would be the first crack in the mirror's hold over her frozen heart.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 10: What a Strange Garden
p: The weeks that followed were a study in contrasts—moments of quiet companionship at the palace hearth interrupted by the inevitable pull of the shards, the terrible necessity of the hunt.
We went out twice more in those weeks. Two more extractions. Two more lives irrevocably changed or ended. Two more shards added to the collection in that circular chamber.

I won't describe them in detail. You don't need to hear every horror, and I don't need to relive them. What matters is that each one was harder than the last. Each one left Glacia more shaken, more visibly at war with herself. The ember Alessia had planted was growing stronger, and with it came an awareness that made the killing almost unbearable.
Almost. But not quite. The compulsion still drove her forward, relentless as winter itself.
