By my count—and I was counting now, scratching marks into the ice when she wasn't looking—there were perhaps a dozen shards left to gather. Maybe fewer. The end of this terrible quest was approaching, though neither of us knew what waited at its conclusion.
It was after the second of those extractions, as we flew back to the palace in heavy silence, that the next shard made itself known.
"South," Glacia said, her voice flat with exhaustion. "Far south. Past the pine forests, past the foothills. I can feel it pulling."

I made a sound of acknowledgment, and she adjusted our course. The sleigh cut through the night air, and I watched the landscape pass beneath us—white giving way to dark green as we left the deepest winter behind, heading toward lands where spring was already beginning to take hold.

We flew for hours. The sun rose, pale and distant, and still we continued south. The pull was leading us farther than usual, into territories I didn't recognize even with my slowly returning memories.
"It's strange," Glacia said at one point, more to herself than to me. "The call feels... different. Muffled somehow. As if something is interfering with it."
I looked at her, questioning, but she just shook her head.
"We'll find it," she said. "We always do."

The landscape below us had changed dramatically. Snow gave way to muddy earth, then to the first hints of green. Patches of grass appeared, then wildflowers—small and hardy, the kind that bloomed early and feared no frost.
"There," Glacia said, pointing ahead.

I followed her gaze and saw a meadow spread out before us, vast and beautiful. It was covered in flowers—not the sparse early blooms we'd been passing over, but a riot of color that seemed impossible for the season. Yellows and purples and whites, swaying in a breeze that carried the scent of growing things.
Glacia brought the sleigh down at the meadow's edge. We landed softly, and I climbed out, my paws sinking slightly into earth that was soft and rich, nothing like the permafrost of the north.
"The shard is close," Glacia said, stepping down beside me. "Through there, I think."

She gestured across the meadow, and I saw what she meant—a kind of shimmer in the air, like heat rising from sun-warmed stone, except the day wasn't particularly warm. It was beautiful, that shimmer, catching the light and bending it into colors that shouldn't exist.

We started walking. The flowers brushed against my fur, and their scent was overwhelming after so long in the sterile cold of the palace. Sweet and green and alive in a way that made something in my chest ache with recognition.

Glacia walked beside me, her ice-crystal gown leaving frost on the flowers she passed. They wilted at her touch, their petals browning and curling, and I saw her notice it with a tightening around her eyes.
"I kill everything I touch," she murmured. "Even here."
I wanted to tell her that wasn't true, that she'd saved me, that her touch had brought me back from the edge of death. But I had no voice, so I just pressed closer to her side as we walked.
The shimmer grew stronger as we approached. It hung in the air like a curtain, and through it I could see more meadow, more flowers, more impossible beauty.
"What a strange garden," I said.
The words came out clear and perfect, and for a moment neither of us registered what had happened. Glacia nodded absently, still focused on the shimmer.
"It is strange. I've never seen flowers like these so early in the—"
She stopped. Turned to stare at me, her eyes wide.
I stared back, equally shocked. Had I just...?
"Glacia," I said, testing it, and her name came out in my voice—not a bear's rumble, but the voice I'd had before the curse, deep and resonant and unmistakably human.
"You're speaking," she whispered. "You're... how are you speaking?"

I looked around, suddenly aware that something had changed. The air felt different here, charged with a magic that wasn't the cold power of winter or the dark compulsion of the shards. This was something else. Something older and warmer and—
"We're not in the mortal realm anymore," Glacia said slowly, realization dawning on her face. "We crossed a boundary. This is... this is one of the seasonal realms."
As if in answer, the shimmer before us rippled and parted, and warmth rolled over us like a wave.

It hit Glacia first, and I saw her stagger. The sudden heat after so long in winter—it must have felt like walking into a wall. Her hand went to her chest, pressing against the place where the shard rested, and her face contorted with pain.
"Glacia?" I stepped toward her, and the warmth hit me too.

It was glorious. After a century as a beast in the cold, that warmth sank into my fur and bones and made me want to weep with relief. But I could see it was hurting her, see the way she struggled to breathe, the way frost formed on her skin as her body tried to protect itself.

"I'm fine," she gasped, but she wasn't. The shard in her chest was pulsing—I could see it through her gown, a dark spot that throbbed with each heartbeat. It was fighting the warmth, trying to pull her back, and the ember was fighting back, burning brighter in response.
She was caught between them, and the war was tearing her apart.
"We should go back," I said, my new voice urgent. "This is hurting you."
"No." She straightened with visible effort, her jaw set. "The shard is here. I can feel it. I have to—"
"Sister?"

The voice came from everywhere and nowhere, warm as summer honey and bright as morning sun. The flowers around us suddenly bloomed brighter, their colors intensifying, and the air filled with the scent of apple blossoms.

A woman appeared before us, stepping out of the shimmer as if she'd always been there. She was beautiful as spring—fresh and new and full of promise. Her hair was the color of new leaves, her dress seemed to be made of flower petals, and her eyes were the clear green of growing things.
"Glacia?" The woman's face lit up with joy, then immediately crumpled into distress. "Oh, sister, what happened to you?"
She rushed forward, arms outstretched, and pulled Glacia into an embrace. Glacia stood rigid in her arms, clearly uncomfortable, frost spreading from her body to coat her sister's petal dress.
"Talia," Glacia said, her voice strained. "I didn't mean to intrude. We were following a shard and—"

"A shard?" Talia pulled back, her brow furrowed in confusion. "What shard? Why would you be... oh, but you're here! It's been so long! I've been meaning to visit but I..." She trailed off, her expression going distant. "Why haven't I visited? I can't quite..."
Her gaze sharpened again, focusing on Glacia's face. "You look terrible. So cold. So... wrong. What happened?"
"The mirror," Glacia started, but Talia's attention had already shifted.

"And Old Man Winter!" She turned to me, her smile returning. "Though why are you...?" She tilted her head, studying my bear form with obvious confusion. "This isn't your usual shape. Did you and Glacia come together? How wonderful! But why a bear? Is this some new fashion?"
I opened my mouth to answer, still marveling at the ability to speak, but Talia was already moving on.

"You must stay!" she declared, clapping her hands together. "Both of you! It's been far too long since I've had visitors, and you both look exhausted. Come, come to the cottage. I'll make tea. Or is it lunch time? The sun is always at noon here, so it's hard to tell, but I'm sure you must be hungry."
She started walking, gesturing for us to follow, and after a moment's hesitation, we did. Glacia moved stiffly, still fighting against the warmth, and I stayed close to her side.
"I can speak," I said quietly, still amazed by it. "Glacia, I can actually speak to you."

She glanced at me, and something complicated crossed her face—wonder and pain and something that might have been joy. "The realm's magic," she said. "It must grant speech to animals. A gift of spring, perhaps."
I wanted to tell her it was more than that, that I was more than just an animal given temporary voice. But I didn't know how to explain what I barely understood myself, so I just nodded.

Talia led us through gardens that defied description. Every flower that had ever bloomed seemed to grow here, arranged in patterns that were both wild and perfectly ordered. Trees heavy with fruit lined paths of soft grass, and the air hummed with bees and butterflies and the songs of birds I'd never heard before.
And everywhere, there was warmth and life. Not the harsh heat of summer, but the gentle warmth of spring
—the kind that coaxed seeds from the earth and buds from branches. It soaked into my fur and made me feel more alive than I had in a century.

But Glacia suffered with each step. Frost formed on every flower she passed, and they wilted in her wake. She noticed, I could tell, and it made her pull into herself, trying to make herself smaller, less destructive.
"Here we are!" Talia announced, and a cottage appeared before us.
It was perfect! Thatched roof, climbing roses, windows that gleamed in the eternal noon sun. Smoke curled from the chimney, and the door stood open in welcome.
"Come in, come in," Talia urged, ushering us inside.

The interior was as warm and welcoming as the exterior promised. A fire burned in the hearth—real fire, not the cold flames of Glacia's palace—and the room was filled with comfortable furniture and the smell of baking bread.
"Sit, please," Talia said, gesturing to a large table already laden with food. "You must be starving."

I looked at the spread—fresh bread still steaming, butter and honey, bowls of berries, early vegetables, clear water in crystal pitchers—and my stomach clenched with sudden, desperate hunger. When had I last eaten anything but the raw meat Glacia brought me?
Glacia stood frozen in the doorway, staring at the table as if it were a foreign artifact.
"Sister?" Talia touched her arm gently. "When did you last eat?"
"I..." Glacia's voice was barely a whisper. "I don't remember. I haven't needed to. The shard..."
"Oh, nonsense," Talia said firmly, though her eyes were troubled. "Everyone needs to eat. Come, sit with me. Both of you."

She guided Glacia to a chair, and I settled on the floor beside them, my bulk too large for the furniture. Talia began filling plates, chattering about the gardens and the weather and a dozen other inconsequential things, and I realized she was doing it deliberately—filling the silence, making this feel normal, giving Glacia time to adjust.
Glacia picked up a piece of bread with trembling hands. She stared at it for a long moment, then slowly brought it to her lips.
I watched her take that first bite, saw the way her eyes widened slightly. She chewed slowly, as if relearning the motion, and swallowed with visible effort.
"Good?" Talia asked gently.
Glacia nodded, not trusting her voice, and took another bite.

Talia pushed a plate toward me, and I ate gratefully—bread and honey and berries that burst with sweetness on my tongue. It was the best meal I'd had in a century, made better by the simple fact of sharing it with others.
We ate in relative silence, Talia's chatter fading to a comfortable quiet. And for a little while, in that warm cottage with food and company, we were almost normal. Almost a family sharing a meal.
Almost.

Time moved strangely in Talia's realm. We stayed for what felt like days, though whether it was truly days or hours or weeks in the mortal world, I couldn't say. The sun never moved from its noon position, and sleep came when we were tired rather than when darkness fell.

Talia gave us a room—a guest chamber with a large bed for Glacia and soft rugs on the floor where I could rest. The first night (if it could be called night), Glacia sat on the edge of the bed, staring at nothing.
"I'd forgotten," she said quietly. "What it feels like to eat. To taste something. To sit at a table with others."
I lifted my head from the rug, watching her in the soft light from the window.
"A century," she continued. "A century of nothing but the hunt and the cold and the killing. I'd forgotten there was anything else."
"You're remembering now," I said, and the sound of my own voice still startled me. "That's what matters."

She looked at me, really looked at me, and I saw tears gathering in her eyes. "Is it? Does it matter if I remember what I've lost when I can't get it back? When I'm still compelled to hunt, still forced to kill?"
"Your heart is fighting," I said. "I can see it, Glacia. Every day it grows stronger. You're not lost. Not completely."
She turned away, but not before I saw one tear escape, freezing on her cheek before it could fall.
The next morning (or what passed for morning), we found Talia in her garden, tending to a bed of tulips. She looked up as we approached, her face brightening.
"There you are! I was just thinking about you. Or was I? Sometimes thoughts slip away like water." She frowned, then smiled again. "No matter. You're here now. Come, walk with me."
We walked through the gardens, and Talia talked—about the flowers, about the changing of seasons, about nothing and everything. But occasionally, her expression would shift, becoming troubled.
"Sister," she said at one point, stopping beside a fountain. "Something terrible happened. I felt it. A long time ago, but I can't... I can't quite remember what it was."
Glacia's hands clenched at her sides. "The mirror," she said. "A demon's mirror. It shattered, and the shards scattered across the world. One of them lodged in my chest."

Talia's face crumpled with distress. "Oh, Glacia. That's... that's terrible. We should help you. We should—" She paused, her expression going distant. "What were we talking about? Oh, look at these roses! Aren't they beautiful?"

It happened again and again over those strange days. Talia would ask what happened, would listen with growing horror as Glacia explained about the mirror, the shards, the compulsion to gather them. And then her attention would slip away, drawn to a butterfly or a bird or the way the light caught on a leaf.

"I should have helped you," she said during one of her clearer moments, gripping Glacia's hands. "Why didn't I help you? I felt the shattering. I knew something was wrong. But I can't remember... I can't hold onto it long enough to..."
"It's not your fault," Glacia said, her voice thick with emotion. "The shattering affected all of you. Made it hard to remember, hard to focus on the darkness."

"But you're my sister," Talia whispered, tears streaming down her face. "I should have found you. Should have..." She blinked, and the tears stopped as suddenly as they'd started. "Oh, but you're here now! That's what matters. Come, let me show you the apple orchard."
It was heartbreaking to watch—Talia's genuine distress and love constantly interrupted by her nature, her spring essence unable to dwell on darkness for long.
But it also meant we could talk. Really talk, in a way we never had before.
We were sitting by the fountain, the three of us, when I finally asked the question that had been burning in me since I'd regained the ability to speak.
"Who were you?" I asked Glacia. "Before the mirror. Before all of this. Who were you?"
She was quiet for a long time, staring into the water. When she finally spoke, her voice was soft, almost wondering.
"I was... gentler. I think. I struggled with my purpose—winter always seemed like death to me, while my sisters brought life. But I tried to find beauty in it anyway."

"You did more than try," Talia said, her voice unusually focused. "You created the most beautiful things, sister. Do you remember? The frost patterns on windows. You'd spend days on a single pane of glass, creating scenes of such delicate beauty that children would press their faces against the cold just to see them better."
Glacia's breath caught. "I... I'd forgotten."

"And the ice sculptures," Talia continued, her eyes distant with memory. "In the forests, where no one would see them but the animals. Deer made of ice that caught the moonlight. Wolves frozen mid-leap. Birds with wings spread wide. You said they were gifts. That winter could give gifts too, not just take them away."
A sob broke from Glacia's throat, raw and painful. "I don't do that anymore. I can't. All I do is kill and take and destroy."
"The shard," I said firmly. "The shard does that. Not you."

"Does it matter?" She turned to me, her face twisted with anguish. "The hands are still mine. The lips that kiss death into people are still mine. I feel them die, Kael. I feel their warmth leave them, feel their hearts stop beating. And I can't stop. I can't—"

"But you want to," I said. "That's what matters. The shard compels you, but you're fighting it. Every time it gets harder, that's you fighting. Every time you hesitate, every time you feel guilt or grief or doubt—that's the real you, breaking through."

"He's right," Talia said softly. "I can see it, sister. Even through my scattered thoughts, I can see you're still in there. The Glacia who loved winter creatures and created beauty from ice. She's not gone."

Glacia pressed her hands to her face, and her shoulders shook with her sobbing. Talia moved to embrace her, and this time Glacia didn't hold herself rigid. She leaned into her sister's warmth and wept—for the century lost, for the lives taken, for the self she'd forgotten.
I rested my head against her knee, offering what comfort I could, and we stayed like that until her tears finally stopped.
Later, when Glacia had gone to rest, Talia examined me more closely.
"Old Man Winter," she said, walking around me in a slow circle. "I remember you, you know. Proud and powerful and utterly sure of yourself. What happened?"
"A curse," I said. "From a sorceress named Gerda. I... I hurt her. Said terrible things. The shard in my eye made me cruel, and she cursed me for it."
Talia's expression grew troubled. "Gerda. Yes, I remember her. Powerful. Possessive. She loved you desperately, didn't she?"
"In her way," I said. "Though I'm not sure it was love so much as need. She wanted to own me, and I wanted to be free. The shard made me vicious about it."
Talia knelt before me, her hands hovering over my head. I felt her magic probe at the curse, testing its boundaries, and saw her face fall.
"It's strong," she said. "Bound with heartbreak and rage and very specific conditions. I can't break it. I'm sorry."
"Can you tell me anything about it?" I asked. "Anything that might help?"

She frowned, concentrating. "Curses born of heartbreak require heartbreak's opposite to break. Love, true and freely given. But there's something else..." She trailed off, her attention drifting to a nearby butterfly.
"Talia," I said urgently. "Please. What else?"

She blinked, focusing on me again. "Something about... frozen hearts? The wording is strange. You must be loved by someone whose heart you've frozen. But that's impossible, isn't it? How can someone whose heart you've frozen love you?"
My mind raced. Someone whose heart I'd frozen. But I'd never frozen anyone's heart. That was Glacia's curse, not mine. Unless...
"Thank you," I said. "That helps more than you know."
She smiled, but it was already fading into vagueness. "Does it? I'm glad. Now, where did I put my gardening shears?"

That evening, Glacia and I walked through the gardens alone. The eternal sun cast long shadows despite its noon position—another impossibility of this realm—and the air was sweet with the scent of jasmine.
"I can't stay much longer," Glacia said quietly. "The shard is calling again. And I'm afraid... I'm afraid I'm hurting this place just by being here."
I'd noticed it too. Wherever she walked, frost formed. Flowers wilted. The grass browned. Her very presence was antithetical to spring, and the realm was suffering for it.
"But I'm grateful," she continued. "For these days. For the chance to remember. For the chance to talk to you."
"I've wanted to talk to you for so long," I said. "There's so much I need to tell you. So much I've observed, so much I've felt."
She stopped walking, turning to face me. "Then tell me. While you still can."

So I did. I told her about watching her at the palace, seeing the war inside her. I told her about the moments when the ember broke through, when I saw glimpses of who she really was. I told her about my own slowly returning memories, the pieces of myself I was reclaiming.

"I was vain," I admitted. "Before the curse. Proud and powerful and utterly sure of my own importance. The shard made me cruel, but the capacity for cruelty was already there. I hurt Gerda badly, and I deserved what she did to me."
"No one deserves to lose themselves," Glacia said softly. "No one deserves to be stripped of their memories and their voice and their very form."
"Maybe not," I said. "But I'm learning things in this form that I never would have learned otherwise. Humility. Patience. The value of silence and observation." I paused. "The meaning of devotion."
She looked at me sharply. "Kael—"

"I'm devoted to you," I said simply. "Not because of a curse or compulsion, but because I choose to be. I see you, Glacia. Not the Snow Queen, not the corrupted goddess, but you. And I'm not leaving."
Tears gathered in her eyes again. "You should. You should run as far from me as you can. I'm a monster, Kael. I've killed hundreds. I'll kill more before this is done."
"You're not a monster," I said firmly. "You're a victim. And you're fighting. That's all anyone can ask."
She reached out and touched my face, her cold fingers gentle against my fur. "When we leave here, you'll lose your voice again. We won't be able to talk like this."
"I know."

"Then let me say this while I can." She took a shaky breath. "Thank you. For staying. For seeing me. For making this bearable. I don't know what I would have done without you these past weeks. Probably gone mad. Probably let the shard consume me completely."
"You're stronger than you think," I said.
"Only because you're there," she whispered.

We stood like that for a long moment, her hand on my face, my eyes locked with hers. And I felt something shift between us—something that had been building since the night she'd saved me, since the moment she'd created cold fire just to keep me warm.
It wasn't love. Not yet. But it was the seed of it, planted in frozen ground, waiting for the right moment to bloom.
On what we decided would be our last day in Talia's realm, we found her in the cottage, preparing a final meal.
"You're leaving," she said, not quite a question. "I can feel it. Winter is restless here."
"The shard is calling," Glacia confirmed. "And I'm damaging your realm. I can't stay."

Talia's face fell, but she nodded. "I understand. But promise me you'll finish this. Gather all the shards. Something important waits at the end—I can feel it, even if I can't quite grasp what it is."
"I promise," Glacia said.

"And visit the others," Talia added, her expression growing distant. "Alessia knows more than she says. She always does. She sees things clearly, our summer sister. And Cora... Cora remembers how to let things go. She understands transitions, thresholds. You'll need that wisdom."
She pressed something into Glacia's hand—a small flower, perfectly preserved. "My blessing," she said. "May you remember warmth even in the deepest cold."
Then she turned to me, her expression unusually focused. "Take care of my sister, Old Man Winter. Even in that form, you're still winter's hand. You belong together, you two. You always have."
"I will," I promised.
She embraced us both, and for a moment, I felt the full force of her power—the warmth of spring, the promise of renewal, the certainty that winter always, always ends.
"The last shard will be the hardest," she said as we prepared to leave. "Or was it the first? Time is strange, and I can't quite... but something about the last one. It will cost you. Both of you."
"What do you mean?" Glacia asked, but Talia's attention had already drifted.
"Look at the apple blossoms," she said dreamily. "Aren't they beautiful?"
We left her there, in her garden, surrounded by eternal spring. And as we walked back across the meadow toward the shimmering boundary, I felt the weight of what we were leaving behind.
"I don't want to go," Glacia admitted quietly. "I don't want to go back to the cold and the hunting and the killing."
"I know," I said. "But we have to finish this. Talia was right—something waits at the end. Something important."
We reached the boundary, and I could see the mortal realm beyond it—cold and gray and empty of the warmth we'd found here.

"Kael," Glacia said, stopping just before the shimmer. "Before we cross. Before you lose your voice again. I need you to know..." She struggled with the words. "These days have meant everything to me. Talking to you. Hearing your voice. Relearning who you are beneath the beast. I won't forget it."

"Neither will I," I said. "And Glacia? When this is over, when the shards are gathered and the compulsion is broken—I'll find a way to speak to you again. I'll find a way to tell you everything I'm thinking, everything I'm feeling. I promise."
She smiled, and it was the first real smile I'd seen from her—sad and small, but genuine. "I'll hold you to that."
Then she took a breath and stepped through the shimmer.

The change was immediate and brutal. The warmth vanished, replaced by the familiar bite of winter. The colors faded, the scents disappeared, and the magic that had sustained us drained away like water through a sieve.
I tried to speak, to say one last thing, but my voice was gone. The words died in my throat, coming out as nothing but a bear's rumble.

Glacia looked back at me, and I saw both relief and grief in her expression. Relief to be back in her element, where the shard's pull was clear and strong. Grief for what we'd lost, for the warmth and the voice and the brief glimpse of normalcy.
I moved to her side, and she rested her hand on my head for a moment.
"I know," she said softly, as if she could hear the words I couldn't speak. "I know."

The shard's call was clear now, pulling her south and east. She climbed into the sleigh, and I followed, settling into my usual place. As we lifted into the air, I looked back at the meadow, at the shimmer that marked the boundary to Talia's realm.
It was already fading, becoming harder to see. Soon it would be invisible, just another patch of ordinary meadow. But I would remember. We both would.
We flew in silence, but it was a different silence than before. We'd been changed by those strange days in spring—reminded of what we'd lost, yes, but also given hope that it might be found again.
The hunt continued. The compulsion drove us forward. But now we knew—both of us—that winter didn't have to last forever.
Even the longest, coldest, cruelest winter eventually yields to spring.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 11: The Bear Truth
p: I was falling.
Not through air or water or anything with substance
—just falling through nothing. Through void. Through darkness so complete it had weight, pressing against me from all sides like a living thing.

I tried to roar, to make some sound, but the void swallowed it. Swallowed everything. I was tumbling end over end through emptiness, and I couldn't tell if I was bear or man or something else entirely.
Then I saw it.
The mirror.
It hung suspended in the nothing, massive and terrible and beautiful. Its surface showed a thousand reflections

—all of me, all different. Man and beast and something in between. Each reflection showed a different moment: me with Gerda, me cruel and cold, me transformed, me dying in the snow, me at Glacia's palace.
All of me. Every version. Every choice. Every failure.
I reached for it—or tried to. My paws became hands became paws again. The mirror grew larger, or I was falling toward it, or it was falling toward me. The distance collapsed.
And then I hit it.

The impact was soundless but catastrophic. The mirror exploded outward in a storm of shards, each piece razor-sharp and glittering with malice. They flew at me from every direction, embedding themselves in my flesh, my fur, my face.
My eye.
Over and over, the shard pierced my eye. I felt it enter, felt the cold corruption spread, felt myself changing. And each time it happened, I heard laughter.
Gerda's laughter.

It echoed through the void, harsh and broken and full of rage and grief and something that might have been love twisted into something monstrous. The sound wrapped around me like chains, pulling me down, down, down into darkness.
"You wished to be only Winter's Hand," her voice whispered from everywhere and nowhere. "Now you shall be winter's beast."

The shards kept coming. Kept piercing. My eye burned with cold fire, and I could feel the corruption spreading through me like frost across glass. I was changing, losing myself, becoming something cruel and empty and—
I woke with a roar that shook the palace walls.

The pain in my eye was immediate and excruciating. Not the dull ache I'd grown accustomed to over the years, but a sharp, stabbing agony that felt like the shard was burrowing deeper, trying to reach my brain. I pressed my paw against my eye socket, trying to ease the pressure, but it only made it worse.

The cold fire in the hearth flickered and flared in response to my distress, casting wild shadows across the ice walls. I was in the great hall, in my usual spot by the fire, but for a moment I couldn't remember how I'd gotten there. The nightmare clung to me like cobwebs, fragments of it still playing behind my eyelids.
The mirror. The shards. Gerda's laughter.

My eye throbbed in time with my heartbeat, each pulse sending fresh waves of pain through my skull. I could feel it behind my eye,the shard. It had been there since the day of the shattering, nearly a century ago, but lately it felt like it was waking up. Growing stronger. Demanding attention.

I'd known about it for a long time. How could I not? Even through the fog of my curse, even when I was more beast than anything else, I'd felt it. A foreign presence lodged in my flesh, cold and patient and waiting.
But I'd been able to ignore it. To push it to the back of my awareness and focus on survival, on instinct, on the simple needs of an animal existence.
That was becoming impossible now.
The weeks after Talia's realm were a study in deterioration.

We continued the hunt, of course. The compulsion drove Glacia forward with relentless force, and I followed because I couldn't imagine doing anything else. The shard count climbed steadily: four hundred seventy, eighty, ninety. Each new shard added to the collection in that circular chamber, each one bringing us closer to some end we couldn't see.
But everything was harder now.

For Glacia, the war between the shard and the ember had intensified. The warmth of Talia's realm, the memories it had awakened, the conversations we'd shared—all of it had strengthened the ember Alessia had planted. Which meant the shard had to fight harder to maintain control.

I watched her struggle with every extraction. Her hands would shake as she approached her victims. She'd hesitate, sometimes for long minutes, standing frozen while the compulsion screamed at her to move forward. The actual extraction took longer too, as if some part of her was fighting the process even as she performed it.
And the victims suffered more for it.
I won't describe them all in detail. You don't need to hear every horror, and I don't need to relive them. But I'll tell you about a few, so you understand what we were living through.

There was an old man in a remote village, his cottage half-buried in snow. He was alone—his wife dead, his children grown and gone to the cities. When Glacia appeared at his door, he didn't run. Just looked at her with tired eyes and said, "I wondered when you'd come for me."

She stood in his doorway for nearly five minutes, her hands trembling at her sides. I could see the war raging inside her—the compulsion demanding she move forward, the ember begging her to stop. My own eye was throbbing, a dull ache that made it hard to focus, but I watched her struggle and wished desperately that I could speak, could tell her it was all right, could offer some comfort.
Finally, the compulsion won. It always did.

She performed the Winter's Kiss, and I watched the old man's eyes frost over, watched his body go rigid with cold. He survived—barely. When she pulled away, he was still breathing, but his skin had taken on a bluish tint that would never fully fade. He'd carry winter in his bones for whatever time he had left.

Glacia retrieved the shard from his eye with shaking hands. She didn't look at him as she left, didn't acknowledge his gasped "thank you" for letting him live. Just walked past me and climbed into the sleigh, her face a mask of ice.
But I saw her hands. They didn't stop trembling for hours.

During that flight back to the palace, my vision blurred badly. The pain in my eye spiked suddenly, and for a moment I saw double—two Glacias, two sleighs, two moons hanging in the sky. I shook my head, trying to clear it, and nearly lost my balance.
"Kael?" Her voice was sharp with concern. "Are you all right?"
I made a sound that I hoped was reassuring, but I could tell she didn't believe it. Her eyes lingered on me for a long moment before she turned back to guiding the sleigh.
She was noticing. Of course she was noticing. I was getting worse at hiding it.
The second extraction I'll tell you about was worse.
A young woman in a cottage at the edge of a forest. She had a shard in her eye, and she had a baby—maybe six months old, sleeping in a cradle by the fire.
When Glacia entered, the woman didn't beg for her own life. She begged for her child's.
"Please," she whispered, backing away with her hands raised. "Please, I'll do anything. Just don't hurt my baby. She's innocent. She doesn't have a shard. Please."

Glacia stood frozen in the doorway. I was behind her, and I could see her shoulders shaking. The compulsion was pulling at her, but the ember was fighting back with everything it had. A mother. A baby. The warmth of the cottage. The smell of milk and bread and life.
It was too much like the extraction that had broken her before.

My eye chose that moment to flare with pain so intense I nearly collapsed. The world tilted sideways, and I stumbled, my shoulder hitting the doorframe. The sound made both women look at me—Glacia with alarm, the young mother with terror.
"I'm sorry," Glacia whispered, and I couldn't tell if she was talking to the woman or to me or to herself.

The extraction was quick but brutal. The woman fought, which made it worse. She clawed at Glacia's arms, tried to pull away, screamed for her baby. But the Winter's Kiss is inescapable once it begins. The cold spread through her body, freezing her from the inside out.

She died. Not immediately—it took almost a minute, which is an eternity when you're watching someone's life drain away. Her eyes stayed open the whole time, fixed on the cradle where her baby was starting to wake and cry.

Glacia retrieved the shard with hands that shook so badly she nearly dropped it. Then she turned and walked out without looking back, without checking on the baby, without acknowledging what she'd just done.

I wanted to go to the child, to do something, but what could I do? I was a bear. I couldn't pick up a baby, couldn't feed it, couldn't comfort it. So I followed Glacia out into the snow, leaving the baby crying in a cottage with its dead mother.
That sound followed us for miles.

At the palace, Glacia went straight to the circular chamber and placed the shard in the box with all the others. Four hundred ninety-six. I watched from the doorway as she stood there, staring at the collection.
"Four hundred ninety-six," she said aloud, her voice hollow. "How many more? How many more lives? How many more children left alone?"
She pressed her hands against the pedestal, and I saw ice spread from her fingers, coating the silver box. Her whole body was shaking.

I moved toward her, wanting to offer comfort, but my eye suddenly exploded with pain so intense I couldn't see. The world went white, then dark, then fractured into a thousand pieces like a shattered mirror.
And in that moment of agony, something else took over.
I looked at Glacia and felt... nothing.
No compassion. No concern. No love.
She was weak. Pathetic. Crying over mortals who meant nothing, who were less than insects in the span of eternity. They died. So what? Everything died. That was the nature of existence.
She should be stronger. Colder. More like the true Snow Queen—the one who killed without hesitation, without remorse, without this ridiculous display of emotion.

The thought came with such clarity, such conviction, that for a moment I believed it completely. I took a step toward her, and a growl rumbled in my chest—not the concerned sound I usually made, but something darker. Threatening.
Glacia turned, and her eyes widened.
"Kael?"

Her voice was small, frightened, and some distant part of me recognized that I was scaring her. But the corrupted part—the part the shard controlled—didn't care. Thought she deserved to be scared. Thought fear might make her stronger.
I took another step, and the growl deepened.
Then, like a wave crashing over me, the real me surged back.

Horror flooded through me as I realized what I'd been thinking, what I'd been about to do. I stumbled backward, shaking my head violently, trying to dislodge the corruption. My paw came up to press against my eye, and the pain was so intense I nearly blacked out.
But I welcomed it. Anything was better than that cold, cruel clarity.

I collapsed, my legs giving out, and pressed my paw hard against my eye socket. The pain was excruciating, but it was mine. It was real. It meant I was still me, still fighting, still capable of feeling something other than that terrible emptiness.
"Kael!" Glacia was beside me in an instant, her hands hovering over me, uncertain. "What's wrong? What happened?"
I couldn't answer. Could only lie there trembling, fighting against the shard's influence, trying to push it back down into the depths where it had been sleeping.
It took several minutes before I could even lift my head. When I did, I found Glacia kneeling beside me, her face pale with worry.
"Let me see," she said softly.
I tried to pull away, ashamed of what she might find, terrified of what I'd almost done. But she persisted, her voice gentle but firm.
"Kael, please. Let me help you."
Slowly, reluctantly, I moved my paw away from my eye.
She leaned in close, studying my face, and I saw the exact moment she understood. Her breath caught, and her eyes widened with recognition and horror.

The area around my eye had changed. Frost patterns spread from the socket like cracks in ice, delicate and beautiful and wrong. The eye itself—I couldn't see it, but I could feel it. Cold. Dark. Different from my other eye.

Glacia reached out with trembling fingers and touched my face, just beside the eye. Her magic flowed through the touch—winter's power, cold and pure. It spread across my face like a numbing balm, easing the worst of the pain.
But we both knew it was just a temporary relief. It couldn't fix the root problem.
"I know what this is," she whispered.
I made a sound of despair, low and broken.
"You have a shard. Don't you?"
It wasn't really a question. She knew. Had probably known for a while but hadn't wanted to face it. I nodded, miserable, and saw tears gather in her eyes.
"How long have you known?"
I tried to communicate: a long time. Since before I found her palace. Since the day of the shattering, though I hadn't understood it then through the fog of my curse.
"And you didn't... you couldn't tell me." Understanding, not accusation. "Oh, Kael."
She wrapped her arms around my neck, pressing her face against my fur. I felt her tears—cold as ice, freezing before they could fall—and something in my chest cracked.
"We'll fix this," she said, her voice muffled against my fur. "I don't know how yet, but we will."
I could hear what she wasn't saying: *I can't extract it. I can't perform the Winter's Kiss on you. I can't.*
I nuzzled against her, trying to offer comfort despite my pain. Trying to tell her it was all right, that I understood, that I didn't blame her for any of this.

"You've stayed with me through all of this," she continued, pulling back to look at me. "Through every terrible thing I've done. Every life I've taken. You've been there, offering comfort, offering presence, offering... everything. I won't abandon you now."
She stood and moved to the hearth, adjusting the cold fire until it burned with a gentler light—soft and blue and soothing. Then she came back and sat beside me, one hand resting on my fur.
"Come," she said. "Rest by the fire. Let me help with the pain."

I followed her to the hearth and lay down, my head resting on my paws. She sat beside me, her hand moving in slow, soothing strokes through my fur. The cold fire cast gentle shadows across her face, and for the first time since we'd left Talia's realm, she looked almost peaceful.
"I should have seen it sooner," she said quietly. "Should have realized. You've been struggling for weeks. The stumbling, the way you flinch from light, the moments when you seem... different."
I made a soft sound, trying to tell her it wasn't her fault. She had her own burden to carry. Her own shard to fight against.
"The corruption," she continued. "That's what it was, wasn't it? Just now. The shard trying to control you, trying to make you cruel like it made me cruel."
I nodded, and she closed her eyes.
"I know what that's like," she whispered. "The thoughts that aren't yours. The coldness that feels so right in the moment and so horrifying after. Fighting against your own mind, your own heart."
Her hand stilled on my fur, and when she spoke again, her voice was thick with emotion.
"I don't know what I would do without you."

I pressed closer to her, trying to communicate everything I couldn't say. That I felt the same. That she'd become essential to me. That somewhere in the past weeks, loyalty had become something deeper, something that felt like love even though I couldn't name it.
We sat like that for a long time, her hand on my fur, my head resting against her leg. The cold fire burned steadily,and for a little while, the pain in my eye faded to something bearable.
"Talia said to visit the others," Glacia said eventually. "Alessia especially. She said Alessia knows more than she says, that she sees things clearly."
I made a sound of agreement.

"And there's a shard calling from that direction anyway. South and west. Toward summer." She paused, her hand resuming its gentle stroking. "We'll go to Alessia. She's powerful. If anyone can help you, it's her."

What she didn't say, what we both understood: if anyone could tell us what to do about a shard lodged in someone you cared about, it was Summer. The sister who saw through illusions. The sister who'd planted the ember in the first place.
The sister who might know how to save us both.
"Can you travel?" Glacia asked, studying my face with concern. "Is it too much?"
I shook my head firmly. I could do this. For her, I could do anything.
She touched my face gently, her cold fingers tracing the frost patterns around my eye. "Then we go at dawn."
That night, neither of us slept.

I lay by the cold fire, and Glacia sat beside me, her hand resting on my fur. We were closer than we'd ever been—not just physically, but in some deeper way. Two beings corrupted by the same evil, fighting the same battle, bound together by something that had grown beyond companionship into something neither of us could name.
"Kael," she said quietly, breaking the long silence. "Whatever happens. Whatever we find out. Thank you for staying."

I couldn't answer, but I leaned into her touch, trying to pour everything I felt into that simple gesture. She understood. I could see it in her eyes—the same fear, the same hope, the same confusing, growing love that neither of us knew how to express.

We sat like that until the first light of dawn began to filter through the ice walls, turning everything pale blue and silver. Glacia stood and moved to prepare the sleigh, and I followed, my eye throbbing but bearable.

At the palace gates, she paused and turned to me. Her hand came up to rest on my head, and we stood like that for a long moment—a goddess and a beast, a victim and a victim, two broken things trying to become whole.
"Let's go find some answers," she said.

I nodded, and together we climbed into the sleigh. As we lifted into the air, heading south and west toward summer, I looked back at the ice palace one last time. It stood against the pale sky like a monument to winter's beauty and winter's cruelty, and I wondered if we'd ever return to it.
If we'd survive long enough to return to it.

The shard in my eye pulsed with pain, and I felt the corruption stirring, waiting for another chance to take control. But Glacia's hand rested on my fur, warm despite her nature, and I held onto that warmth like a lifeline.
We flew toward summer, toward answers, toward whatever fate awaited us.
Together.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 12: The Summer Palace
p: We flew for hours.

The landscape beneath us transformed gradually, like watching the world wake from winter's sleep. The snow thinned, became patchy, then disappeared entirely. Bare earth gave way to grass—first brown and dormant, then green and alive. Trees appeared, their branches heavy with leaves that caught the wind and whispered secrets we couldn't hear from so high above.

My eye throbbed with each beat of my heart, a steady reminder of the corruption growing inside me. But I pushed the pain aside, focusing instead on the changing world below and the woman beside me who grew more tense with each passing mile.
"We're getting close," Glacia said, her voice tight. "I can feel it."
I looked at her questioningly, and she understood.

"The shard is pulling south and west. But there's something else." She paused, her hands tightening on the sleigh's reins. "Talia said we should visit the others. Alessia and Cora. I think... I think we need to find Alessia."
The name resonated through me—Summer, the second eldest, the one Talia had said saw things clearly. If anyone could help us understand what was happening, what we were becoming, it would be her.

The air grew warmer as we flew. Not gradually, but in waves, as if we were passing through invisible barriers of heat. Glacia began to shift uncomfortably beside me, and I saw frost forming on her skin—her body's instinctive defense against the rising temperature.
"There," she said finally, pointing ahead.
I followed, and the world changed.
Heat hit me like a physical blow—not truly painful, but intense, overwhelming after so long in winter's cold.
But Glacia—

She staggered, her hand flying to her chest where the shard rested. Frost spread across her skin in intricate patterns, her body desperately trying to protect itself from the warmth. The shard in her chest pulsed visibly through her gown, a dark spot that throbbed with each labored breath.

I moved to her side, pressing against her, trying to offer what support I could. But I could feel the war inside her intensifying—the shard fighting against the warmth, the ember responding to it, and Glacia caught between them like a leaf in a storm.
"I've been waiting for you."
The voice was warm and commanding, and we both turned.
Alessia.

She was summer embodied—radiant and powerful and fierce. Her skin was golden, as if she'd been dipped in sunlight, and her hair fell in waves of copper and gold that seemed to move with their own light. Her eyes were amber, warm but piercing, and they saw everything. She wore a dress that looked like it was made of light itself, shifting between gold and orange and deep red like a sunset caught in fabric.
She was beautiful. But more than that, she was formidable—more regal than Talia, more commanding, with a presence that made even the air around her feel charged with power.
Her gaze went immediately to Glacia, and her expression held no surprise—only deep sorrow and fierce determination.
"Sister." She moved forward with purpose, her hands already rising. "A century is far too long."
Glacia tried to speak, but she was struggling too hard to breathe, the heat and the shard and the ember all warring inside her. Alessia's expression softened with compassion.
"I know," she said quietly. "I know what you carry. What he did to you. Hold still."

Golden magic flowed from her palms, warm and bright and impossibly gentle. It wrapped around Glacia like a shield, and I watched as the temperature around her dropped, became bearable. The frost on her skin faded, and she gasped, drawing in a full breath for the first time since we'd crossed the threshold.

Alessia turned to me, and recognition flashed immediately in her eyes. "Old Man Winter," she said, and there was respect in her voice. "Ice King. Winter's Hand." She listed my titles as if she'd been expecting me as much as her sister. "You found each other. Good."
Her magic flowed over me as well—not cooling, but tempering, making the heat less overwhelming. And something else: the constant throb in my eye eased, just slightly, just enough to think clearly.
"There," Alessia said, lowering her hands. "You can breathe now. Both of you."
Glacia straightened slowly, her hand still pressed to her chest. "You knew we were coming."

"I've been watching for you since Talia told me you'd left her realm." Alessia's eyes moved to the place where the shard rested, and something that might have been satisfaction crossed her face. "And I can feel it—still there. Still burning. The ember has grown strong."
"The ember," Glacia whispered. "Talia said—she said something was interfering with the shard's hold. That was you?"
"We'll talk by the fire," Alessia said. "I'll explain everything." She turned her full attention to me, and I felt the weight of her gaze settle on my bear form.

She moved closer, and I held still as she examined me. Her hand came up toward my face, and I flinched instinctively as she neared my eye. She paused, then continued more gently, her magic probing at the shard lodged there.
Her expression grew troubled.
"You both carry his corruption," she said, and her voice was heavy with old anger. "This is worse than I feared it would be."
I opened my mouth, desperate to ask questions, to beg for help, and words came out.
"Can you help us?"
My voice. My actual voice, deep and resonant and unmistakably human. The relief that flooded through me was so intense I nearly collapsed.

Alessia looked at me with something that might have been sympathy. "I can ease your suffering. But the curse..." She raised her hand again, and I felt her magic sink deeper, probing not just at the shard but at the curse that bound me. Her frown deepened. "Gerda's work. Powerful. Bound with heartbreak and very specific conditions."
She tried something—I felt a tug, a pull, as if she were trying to unravel threads—but the curse held firm.
"I cannot break this," she said finally. "The conditions must be met. But I can ease the pain somewhat."
The throbbing in my eye lessened further, became almost bearable. I wanted to weep with gratitude.

"The shard and the curse are tangled together," Alessia continued, her voice troubled. "They're feeding each other, making both worse. Breaking one might affect the other, but I can't predict how." She stepped back, looking between us. "Come. You'll stay with me. Rest. Eat. And then I'll tell you what I know—and what I don't."
She turned and began walking, and we followed her through gardens that defied description.

Everything was in full bloom—not the tentative new growth of spring, but the abundant, ripe perfection of summer at its height. Fruit trees heavy with peaches and plums and apples lined paths of thick grass. Flowers I couldn't name grew in profusion, their colors so vivid they almost hurt to look at. The air was thick with the scent of ripe fruit and warm earth and sunshine itself.

Bees moved lazily from flower to flower, and cicadas sang in the trees, and somewhere in the distance I could hear the splash of fountains. The light was golden, rich, warm but not harsh—as if the sun here knew exactly how bright to shine.
And through it all, Alessia walked like a queen through her kingdom, and everything seemed to lean toward her, to bask in her presence.
The palace rose before us, and I stopped, awed despite everything.

It was made of golden stone that seemed to glow from within, all soaring columns and graceful arches open to the sky. Fountains played in courtyards, and gardens grew everywhere—climbing up walls, spilling over balconies, woven into the very architecture. There was shade everywhere, blessed shade, and the temperature beneath the colonnades was perfect.
It was a place of power and abundance, of life celebrated and cherished. Everything Glacia's ice palace was not.
I glanced at her and saw her staring at it with an expression I couldn't quite read—wonder and pain and something that might have been longing.
"This way," Alessia said, leading us through an archway into a cool, spacious room. "You'll stay here. Rest. I'll have food brought."

The room was large and comfortable, with soft furnishings in warm colors and windows that looked out over the gardens. There was a bed for Glacia and thick rugs on the floor where I could rest. Everything was open and airy and alive.
Glacia moved to the window and stood there, her hand reaching out to touch the stone as if she couldn't quite believe it was real.

"I'll leave you to settle in," Alessia said. "We'll eat at sunset. Well—" she smiled slightly, "what passes for sunset here. The sun never quite sets in summer, but it knows how to make a beautiful evening."
She left, and we were alone.
Glacia turned from the window, and I saw tears on her face.
"I'd forgotten," she whispered. "What it was like to be in a place like this. To be welcomed. To be..." She couldn't finish.
I moved to her side and pressed against her leg, and she sank down to sit on the floor beside me, her hand coming up to rest on my head.
"Thank you," she said quietly. "For being here. For staying."
"There's nowhere else I would rather be," I said, and the words felt like a gift I'd been waiting to give her. "I would follow you to the end of the world if you asked."
She looked at me, her eyes bright with tears. "You already have."
Her hand tightened in my fur, and we sat like that—close and quiet, speaking the truths we could only say when I had a voice—until Alessia returned to lead us to the feast.

The evening light was golden and soft, the sun hanging at that perfect angle that makes everything beautiful. We gathered in an outdoor pavilion, open to the gardens, with a table laden with food that made my mouth water.

Summer's abundance was on full display: ripe fruits cut open to show their jewel-like flesh, grilled meats fragrant with herbs, fresh vegetables in colors I'd almost forgotten existed. There was bread still warm from the oven, olive oil and honey, wine that caught the light like liquid gold.

Alessia gestured for us to sit, and we did—Glacia at the table, me on the floor beside her with a plate of my own. It was strange and wonderful to eat real food again, to taste something other than raw meat.
"Tell me about your journey," Alessia said as we ate. "How did you find each other?"

So Glacia told her—haltingly at first, then with more confidence. About finding me wounded at her gates, about the cold fire and the healing, about the weeks that followed. About the extractions and the growing doubt and the trip to Talia's realm.
Alessia listened intently, asking questions, her eyes moving between us with an expression I couldn't quite read.
"And Talia?" she asked. "How was she?"
"Scattered," Glacia said softly. "She remembered, but she couldn't hold onto it. Every time she tried to focus on what happened, on the darkness, her nature pulled her away."
Alessia nodded, unsurprised. "The shattering affected all of us. Made it hard to remember, hard to act. But you're here now. That's what matters."
She turned to me. "And you, Ice King? What do you remember of before?"
"More each day," I said, still marveling at the ability to speak. "The cold fire helped. Being in the magic realms helps. But there are still gaps. Still pieces missing."
"Gerda's curse was thorough," Alessia said. "She wanted you to forget everything—who you were, what you were, why you mattered. To be reduced to nothing but beast and instinct."
"She succeeded," I said quietly.

"Did she?" Alessia looked at me thoughtfully. "You're here. You stayed with Glacia when you could have run. You've been fighting the corruption in your eye, fighting to remember, fighting to help. That doesn't sound like a mindless beast to me."
I didn't know what to say to that.
The meal continued, and slowly the tension began to ease. Alessia had a way of making even dark topics feel bearable, of finding moments of lightness in the heavy conversation.
"Do you remember," she said to Glacia, "when you were young—well, younger—and you tried to make it snow in my realm?"
Glacia looked up, startled. "I... no. Did I?"

"Oh yes." Alessia's eyes sparkled with mischief. "You were so determined to prove that winter could exist anywhere. You stood in the middle of my gardens and concentrated so hard I thought you might burst. And do you know what happened?"
Glacia shook her head.

"It snowed. For exactly three seconds. Three perfect, beautiful seconds of snowflakes in summer." Alessia laughed, and the sound was warm and genuine. "Then they melted, of course. But you were so proud. You danced around like you'd conquered the world."
Something crossed Glacia's face—surprise, then wonder, then something that might have been joy. And then, impossibly, she laughed.
It was brief, rusty, as if she'd forgotten how. But it was real. Genuine. The first true laughter I'd heard from her in all our time together.
Everyone stopped. Even Glacia herself looked shocked, her hand flying to her mouth as if she could catch the sound and put it back.
Alessia smiled, and there was triumph in it. "There you are, sister. Still in there, I see."
Glacia's eyes filled with tears, but she was still smiling. "I didn't think I could anymore."
"You can," Alessia said firmly. "The corruption hasn't taken everything. Not yet."
I watched Glacia's face, saw the war of emotions there
—grief for what she'd lost, hope for what might still be saved, and something else. Something warm and alive and fighting.
The ember, I realized. This was the ember burning brighter.
Alessia's gaze moved to me, and I saw her notice how I was looking at Glacia. Something calculating crossed her expression, but she said nothing. Just smiled slightly and turned back to her wine.

After the meal, as the golden light deepened toward evening, Alessia led us to a fire pit in one of the gardens. The flames that burned there were golden, warm but not cold like Glacia's fire, and we settled around it—
Glacia and I close together on one side, Alessia across from us.
"Now," she said, her voice losing its lightness, becoming serious. "Let me tell you about the demon who destroyed my sister."
The fire crackled, and I felt Glacia tense beside me.

"His name is Malakar," Alessia began. "The Architect of Sorrow. The Lord of Reflection. He is a high-ranking demon whose domain is distortion, obsession, and perpetual doubt. He doesn't destroy through raw power
—he corrupts through psychological manipulation. He takes what exists and turns it into its inverse. Beauty into cruelty. Love into obsession. Creation into destruction."
"Why?" Glacia's voice was barely a whisper. "Why me?"

Alessia's expression was full of sorrow and anger. "Because you were vulnerable, sister. Because you struggled with your purpose, saw winter as death while the rest of us brought life. That self-doubt, that insecurity—it was the crack he needed."

She leaned forward, the firelight casting shadows across her face. "A corrupted Season goddess provides endless misery. Endless death. Endless fuel for his power. And you, Glacia, with your immense power and your deep insecurity—you were the perfect target."
"The mirror," I said. "Tell us about the mirror."

Alessia nodded. "The Speculum Aeterna. The Eternal Mirror. Or, more accurately, the Mirror of Unattainable Desires." She paused, letting the words sink in. "It doesn't show reality, Glacia. It shows what the viewer most desperately wants to see. What they want so badly they'll do anything to have it."
Glacia's breath caught. "The perfect winter. The peaceful world. It wasn't real?"

"It was a lie," Alessia said gently. "A beautiful, terrible lie designed specifically for you. It showed you what you wanted most—a world where winter was a gift, where you brought peace instead of death. And it told you that vision was real, was achievable, if only you would take the mirror and share it with the world."
"I thought..." Glacia's voice broke. "I thought I was finally seeing the truth. Finally understanding my purpose."
"I know," Alessia said. "That's what makes it so cruel. You were trying to do something good. Trying to bring beauty and peace. And that desire was weaponized against you."
I pressed closer to Glacia, feeling her trembling.

"When you took the mirror toward the divine realm," Alessia continued, "seeking to show it to the gods and spread that peace across the world—the collision between Malakar's corruption and the purity of the divine realm caused a catastrophic magical explosion. The mirror shattered, and each shard became a fragment of Malakar's essence, carrying his corruption."
"The shattering wasn't an accident," Glacia whispered. "It was the plan."
"Yes," Alessia confirmed. "The shards scattered across the mortal world, lodging in people's eyes, corrupting their perceptions. And the largest shard—the command center—lodged in your chest."
Glacia's hand went to the place where the shard rested, and I saw her face twist with horror and understanding.

"It compels you to gather the others," Alessia said. "You've been completing the ritual of your own enslavement. Every shard you collect, every person you kill to retrieve them—it all feeds Malakar's power. And when you place the last shard, when the mirror is complete again, his hold on you will be absolute. You'll be his forever, an engine of death and suffering that can never be stopped."
"A century," Glacia said, and her voice was hollow. "A century of killing. Hundreds of people. All planned. All part of his design."
She stood abruptly, frost spreading from her feet despite Alessia's shield. "I've murdered hundreds for his amusement!"
"For his power," Alessia corrected, standing as well. "Your suffering, their deaths, the chaos you've spread—it all feeds him. Makes him stronger."
Glacia was pacing now, her hands clenched into fists. "I can't—I can't bear this. Knowing that every death, every scream, every child left orphaned—it was all for nothing. All for a demon's game."
I rose and went to her, pressing my bulk against her back. She grabbed my fur with both hands, holding on as if I were the only solid thing in a world that had turned to quicksand.

Alessia's gaze moved to me, and her expression was grave. "And you, Ice King. Your shard carries the same essence. It corrupted your perception of Gerda, made you cruel when you already had the capacity for cruelty. It amplifies the worst in you, makes it impossible to resist."
"I know," I said, my voice rough. "I've felt it taking hold again. The corruption flashes, the cruel thoughts that aren't mine but also are. It's getting worse."
"The curse and the shard are feeding each other," Alessia said. "That's why your condition is deteriorating. They're tangled together, each making the other stronger."
Glacia looked down at me, her eyes wide with fear. "What do we do? If gathering the shards enslaves me completely, if his shard is killing him—what do we do?"
Alessia's face was troubled. "I don't know."
The admission hung in the air like a death sentence.
"The compulsion is absolute," Alessia continued. "You must gather the shards, Glacia. You physically cannot stop. Your body, your magic, your very essence is bound to complete the task."
"So I'm doomed," Glacia whispered. "I complete the mirror and become his forever."
"Maybe," Alessia said. "Or maybe there's something I haven't seen. Something that changes the equation."
Silence fell around the fire, heavy and oppressive. Then Alessia spoke again, and her voice was different—softer, more careful.
"There is one thing," she said. "Something Malakar doesn't know about."
We both looked at her.

"The moment the mirror shattered, I was there. Not physically, but in spirit. I felt the catastrophe across the realms, felt you falling, felt the corruption taking hold." She paused, and something fierce entered her expression. "I couldn't stop it. But I could do one thing."

She raised her hand, and golden light gathered in her palm. "I reached across dimensions, found your heart in the moment of corruption, and I planted something. A seed. An ember of pure summer warmth."
"It was so subtle," Alessia said. "A thread of my own essence, woven into your heart so deep that even Malakar couldn't detect it. He thought he had all of you, sister. But I kept a piece safe."
Tears were streaming down Glacia's face now. "You saved me. Even when I was lost, you saved me."

"I kept you alive," Alessia corrected. "You're saving yourself." She looked at me, and there was something knowing in her gaze. "The ember feeds on connection. On warmth. On love. Every moment of doubt, every time you've hesitated, every tear you've shed—that's the ember fighting back. And it's been growing stronger."
She gestured between us. "Every day you've spent together, every moment of care and companionship—it's made the ember burn brighter. You're waking up, Glacia. Coming back to yourself."
Glacia looked at me, and I saw understanding dawn in her eyes. "You. Being with you. That's why I can feel again. Why the doubt is growing."
"Love is the opposite of corruption," Alessia said simply. "Malakar thought he'd won. But he didn't count on you being loved."
The word hung in the air between us—love—and neither Glacia nor I could look away from each other.

But Alessia's expression remained troubled. "I don't know if it's enough. The compulsion is still there. You still have to complete the mirror. I don't know what happens at the end, whether the ember is strong enough to save you."
"Then we make it strong enough," I said, turning to look at Alessia. "We have time before the last shard. We use it."
Alessia studied me for a long moment, then nodded slowly. "Yes. Perhaps that's exactly what you need to do."

Later, after Alessia had left us to rest, Glacia and I walked through the gardens under a sky that glowed with a beautiful golden twilight. The air was warm and sweet, and for a little while, we could almost pretend we were just two people taking an evening stroll.
"I've been a weapon," Glacia said quietly. "A tool. For a century."
"You've been a victim," I said.
"Does it matter? The people are still dead."
"It matters. Intent matters. The you beneath the corruption wouldn't have done those things."
She stopped walking and turned to face me. "I want to believe that. I want to believe there's still something worth saving underneath all this ice and death."

"There is," I said firmly. "I've seen her. The woman who saved a wounded bear. Who created cold fire just to keep him warm. Who sits by the hearth and talks to him even though he can't answer. Who cries for the people she's forced to kill. That woman is worth saving."
"Alessia said the ember grows with love," she whispered.
The word hung between us, heavy with meaning.
"I think," I said carefully, "it's been growing since the night you saved me."

She looked up so we were at eye level, her hand coming up to rest on my face. "I don't know what I would have done without you, Kael. I think... I think I would have been lost completely. You gave me something to—someone to be human for."
Her eyes were bright with tears. "When this is over. If we survive this. I want—"
"Me too," I said quietly, understanding what she couldn't say.

She leaned forward and pressed her forehead against mine, and we stayed like that for a long moment—a goddess and a cursed force of nature, two broken things trying to become whole, love growing in the warmth of summer's garden.
In the morning—or what passed for morning in a realm of eternal golden light—Alessia found us in the gardens.
"You need to continue your journey," she said without preamble. "You need to see Cora."
"Autumn?" Glacia asked.

"She understands endings. Transitions. Thresholds. The space between what was and what will be." Alessia's expression was serious. "If anyone can see how this ends, it's her. What choice you'll face. What price will be required."

She moved closer, her voice dropping. "The shards are running out. Maybe just a few left. The compulsion will get stronger as you near completion. The ember will fight back harder. The war inside you will intensify beyond anything you've felt so far."
She turned to me. "Your shard will worsen too. The corruption will try to take you completely. Be prepared."
Then she looked between us, and her expression softened slightly. "When the time comes for the last shard, everything will depend on what you choose. Both of you."
She embraced Glacia, holding her sister close. "You're not alone. Remember that. No matter how dark it gets, no matter how strong the compulsion becomes—you're not alone."
She turned to me. "Protect her, Ice King. Not just from others, but from herself when the compulsion overwhelms. And let her protect you too. You'll need each other for what's coming."
She gave us supplies—food that wouldn't spoil, water that would never run dry, small magics to ease our journey. And then she led us back through the gardens to the hidden portal.
"Go to Cora," she said. "She'll know what comes next. What must be done."
Glacia looked back at the golden palace, at the gardens and the warmth and the brief respite we'd found there. "Thank you," she whispered. "For everything. For the ember. For not giving up on me."
"Never," Alessia said fiercely. "You're my sister. I will never give up on you."
We stepped through the portal, and the world changed again.

The heat vanished instantly, replaced by the cooler air of the mortal realm. Alessia's shields disappeared, and I felt the loss of my voice like a physical blow. The words I'd been able to speak, the thoughts I'd been able to express—gone again, locked behind the curse.

But something was different. The ember in Glacia's chest burned brighter than before, visible even through her gown as a warm glow that pulsed with each heartbeat. And when she looked at me, there was something in her eyes that hadn't been there before.
Hope. Understanding. And something that might have been love.
"West and north," she said, her hand coming to rest on my head. "To autumn's realm. To Cora. To learn how this ends."
We climbed into the sleigh, and I settled beside her. She rested her hand on my fur for a moment, and I felt the question in the gesture.
"Together?" she asked quietly.
I nodded, pressing closer to her side.
"Together," she affirmed.

The sleigh lifted into the air, and we flew toward autumn. Summer faded behind us, but the warmth remained—not in the air, but in the ember burning in Glacia's chest, in the understanding that had grown between us, in the love that neither of us had spoken but both of us felt.

We were burdened by knowledge now—Malakar's plan, the trap we were walking into, the uncertainty of whether we could survive what was coming. But we were also closer than ever, bound by something stronger than curses or corruption.
And as we flew toward whatever fate awaited us in autumn's realm, I held onto that warmth like a promise.
The ember was growing. Love was growing. And maybe
—just maybe—it would be enough.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 13: The Burden of Knowing
p: The moment we crossed back into the mortal realm, the weight of everything Alessia had told us settled over Glacia like a shroud.

I felt the loss of my voice like a door slamming shut. One moment I could speak, could tell her what I was thinking, what I was feeling—and the next, silence. The curse reasserted itself with brutal efficiency, and I was reduced once more to gestures and expressions and the mute devotion of a beast.
But it was Glacia who bore the heavier burden.

She stood at the edge of the portal for a long moment after we'd crossed through, staring back at the shimmer of golden light that marked the boundary to Alessia's realm. Her hand pressed against her chest where the shard rested, and I could see the ember's glow pulsing beneath her gown—brighter than before, but not bright enough to erase the darkness of what she now knew.
"A century," she whispered. "A century of being his puppet. His weapon. His tool."
I moved to her side and pressed against her shoulder. She didn't look up at me, but her hand came to rest on my back, her fingers curling into my fur.

"Every death. Every scream. Every child left orphaned." Her voice was hollow, empty of everything except grief. "All of it planned. All of it feeding him. Making him stronger while I thought I was—" She stopped, her breath catching. "I thought I was fulfilling some terrible purpose. Some cosmic necessity. But it was all just... entertainment. Fuel. A demon's game."

The sleigh waited nearby, patient and silent. Glacia finally turned away from the portal and climbed in, moving like someone much older now. I settled beside her, and she didn't take up the reins immediately. Just sat there, staring at nothing.
"How do I live with this?" she asked quietly. "How do I keep going, knowing what I've done? What I've been made to do?"
I had no answer. Could offer no words of comfort or wisdom. So I did the only thing I could—I pressed closer, letting her feel my warmth, my presence, my unwavering devotion.
She looked up at me, and something in her expression cracked. "You can't even answer me anymore. Can't tell me it will be alright. Can't tell me I'm not a monster."
I held her gaze, trying to communicate everything I couldn't say. *You're not a monster. You're a victim. You're fighting back. You're still in there, still fighting, still worth saving.*
Whether she understood or not, I couldn't tell. But after a long moment, she took up the reins, and the sleigh lifted into the air.

We flew west and north, following the pull of autumn's realm that only Glacia could sense. The landscape beneath us changed gradually—summer's abundance giving way to something cooler, more muted. But everywhere we looked, there were signs of winter's premature grip.
Frost on fields that should have been green. Ice forming on rivers that shouldn't freeze for months yet. Trees with leaves that had turned brown and brittle, falling too early, dying too fast.

"It's spreading," Glacia said on the second day, her voice tight with fresh guilt. "My corruption. My winter. It's bleeding into the world, making everything colder, harsher. Killing things that should still be alive."
I looked up at her, questioning, and she understood.

"The shard in my chest is so large, so powerful, that it's affecting the natural order. Winter is coming early because I exist. Because I'm still hunting. Still killing." She laughed, but there was no humor in it. "Even when I'm trying to fight it, I'm still destroying everything I touch."

The pain in my eye had been growing steadily worse since we'd left Alessia's realm. The brief respite her magic had provided was fading, and the shard was reasserting itself with a vengeance. By the third day, the throbbing was constant, and my vision in that eye had started to blur at the edges.
I tried to hide it. Tried not to let Glacia see how much it hurt, how the corruption was spreading again, how the cruel thoughts were becoming harder to push away.
But she noticed anyway.

We'd stopped to rest in a small clearing, and I was lying by the cold fire she'd created, trying to will the pain away through sheer stubbornness. She knelt beside me, her hand coming up to gently touch the side of my face near the corrupted eye.
"It's getting worse again," she said softly. "Isn't it?"
I couldn't lie to her. Couldn't pretend. So I nodded, just once.

Her expression crumpled. "This is my fault. If I hadn't been so weak and easy to corrupt, if I hadn't shattered the mirror, you wouldn't have a shard in your eye. You wouldn't be in pain. You wouldn't be—" She stopped, pressing her hand over her mouth.

I pushed myself up and pressed my forehead against hers, trying to tell her what I couldn't say. *This isn't your fault. You didn't choose this. Neither of us did. We're both victims of the same demon.*

"I can't lose you," she whispered against my fur. "I can't. You're the only thing keeping me sane. The only thing that makes this bearable. If the shard takes you, if you become like I was—cold and empty and cruel—I don't think I could survive it."

The ember in her chest pulsed brighter, responding to her emotion, to her fear, to the love she still couldn't quite name. I felt its warmth wash over both of us, a gentle reminder that we weren't alone in this. That Alessia had given us a weapon against the darkness, even if we didn't fully understand how to use it yet.

That night, as we rested under a sky heavy with premature snow clouds, Glacia talked to me. She'd been doing it more and more—speaking her thoughts aloud even though I couldn't respond, using me as a confessor, a witness, a anchor to her own humanity.
"I've been thinking about what Alessia said," she began, staring into the cold flames. "About the compulsion. About how I have to complete the mirror. How I physically can't stop."
She was quiet for a moment, her hand absently stroking my fur.

"Part of me wants to fight it. Wants to refuse. To say no, I won't be his puppet anymore, I won't kill another person for his amusement." Her voice hardened. "I'm so angry, Kael. So furious that he did this to me. That he took my insecurity, my self-doubt, my desire to be better—and he weaponized it. Turned it into a trap that's held me for a century."
The anger in her voice was new. Raw. Alive in a way the cold emptiness had never been.

"But the other part of me knows it doesn't matter what I want. The compulsion isn't something I can fight with willpower or determination. It's woven into my very essence. Refusing would be like trying to refuse to breathe." She laughed bitterly. "And maybe that's the cruelest part. He didn't just trap me—he made it so I'd trap myself. Every shard I collect brings me closer to complete enslavement, and I can't stop collecting them."
I pressed closer to her, and she wrapped her arm around me, holding on as if I were the only thing keeping her from flying apart.

"Sometimes I think about all the people I've killed," she continued, her voice dropping to barely a whisper. "I remember their faces. Their voices. The way they begged. The way they screamed. The children crying over their parents' frozen bodies." Her breath hitched. "I remember all of it, Kael. Every single death. And I have to live with that. Have to carry that weight forever, even if we somehow survive this."
Tears fell onto my fur.
