"How do I atone for that? How do I make amends for a century of murder? Even if it wasn't my choice, even if I was corrupted—they're still dead. Still gone. Still never coming back because of me."

I wished desperately that I could speak. Could tell her that carrying the weight of those deaths, feeling the guilt and grief of them, was itself a form of atonement. That the Snow Queen who'd killed without feeling wouldn't have cared about making amends. That her very anguish proved she was still herself underneath the corruption.
But I couldn't say any of that. So I just held still and let her cry, let her speak her grief and guilt and rage into the darkness, let her use me as the anchor she needed.

On the fourth day, we flew over a village that had been abandoned. The houses stood empty, doors hanging open, possessions scattered in the streets as if the inhabitants had fled in panic. Frost covered everything, and in the town square, there was a statue.
Not a statue. A person. Frozen solid, their face locked in an expression of terror.
Glacia brought the sleigh down without a word. She walked to the frozen figure and stood before it, her expression unreadable.

"I remember this one," she said quietly. "Three years ago. Maybe four. The shard was in his right eye. He ran when he saw me coming. Tried to hide in his home. Barricaded the door." She reached out and touched the frozen man's face with one finger. "It didn't matter. Nothing could keep me out. Nothing could stop me."
She turned away, and I saw her shoulders shaking.

"His name was Thomas. He had a wife. Two daughters. They watched me kill him. Watched me freeze him from the inside out. Watched me take the shard from his eye and leave his body standing there like a monument to my cruelty."

She walked back to the sleigh, her movements mechanical. "The village emptied within a week. Everyone fled, terrified the Snow Queen would return. And they were right to be afraid. I would have, if another shard had called me here."
She climbed into the sleigh but didn't take up the reins. Just sat there, staring at the frozen man.

"This is what I am," she said. "This is what I've done. And knowing it was a demon's plan doesn't change the fact that Thomas is dead. That his daughters grew up without a father. That this entire village was destroyed because of me."
I climbed up beside her and pressed my bulk against her side. She turned and buried her face in my fur, and I felt her whole body shaking with silent sobs.
"I don't know if I can do this," she whispered. "I don't know if I'm strong enough to keep going, knowing what I know. Knowing what's waiting at the end."

The ember pulsed in her chest, warm and insistent. I felt it through her gown, through her skin, a steady heartbeat of summer warmth in the endless winter. And I understood what Alessia had meant—the ember was fighting for her. Keeping her alive. Keeping her human.
But it needed fuel. It needed connection. It needed love.

I pulled back enough to look at her face, and she met my eyes. In that moment, I tried to pour everything I felt into my gaze. Every ounce of devotion, every fragment of the love I couldn't speak, every promise that I would stay with her no matter what came.

"You're the only good thing in my life," she said, her voice breaking. "The only thing that makes me feel like I'm still a person and not just a weapon. When I'm with you, the ember burns brighter. The compulsion is easier to bear. The guilt doesn't crush me quite as completely."
She cupped my face in both hands, her touch gentle against my fur.

"I don't know what we are to each other. I don't know if what I feel is love or just desperate gratitude that I'm not alone anymore. But I know that losing you would destroy me. That you matter more than anything else in this cursed existence."

I leaned into her touch, and she pressed her forehead against mine. We stayed like that for a long time, two broken things holding each other together, while the frozen man stood silent witness in the empty village square.
When we finally continued our journey, something had shifted. The grief was still there, the guilt still crushing. But underneath it, there was something else. Determination.

"Alessia said we need to see Cora," Glacia said as we flew. "That she understands endings. Transitions. What must be done." She paused, her hands tightening on the reins. "I think... I think she's going to tell us there's a price. That breaking free of Malakar's trap will require a payment be made."
I looked up at her, and she glanced down at me.

"I don't know what that price will be. But I know I'm willing to pay it." Her voice was steady now, stronger. "I've been a weapon for a century. I've killed hundreds. I've spread that demon's corruption across the world. If there's a way to end this—to stop Malakar, to break the compulsion, to save even one person from the fate I've inflicted on so many—then I'll pay whatever price is asked."
The ember flared brighter, as if responding to her resolve.
"Even if it costs me everything," she continued. "Even if it means my own destruction. I won't let him win. I won't let this century of death be for nothing."

By the fifth day, the landscape had changed again. The premature winter gave way to something else—a place where autumn still held sway. The trees here were dressed in gold and crimson and deep orange, their leaves falling in gentle spirals. The air smelled of earth and woodsmoke and the rich decay of the season's end.
"We're close," Glacia said, and I heard something in her voice I hadn't heard before. Not quite hope, but something adjacent to it. Purpose, maybe. Or acceptance.

My eye was worse than ever. The pain had become a constant companion, and the distorted flashes were coming more frequently. I'd catch myself looking at Glacia and thinking cruel thoughts—that she was weak, pathetic, unworthy of my time. Then the real me would surge back, horrified, and I'd have to fight to push the corruption down again.
It was exhausting. Terrifying. And getting harder every day.
But I didn't tell her. Didn't let her see how close I was to losing myself completely. She had enough to carry without adding my deterioration to her burden.

The forest grew denser as we traveled, the autumn colors deepening into something almost otherworldly. And then, as the sun began to set on the fifth day, Glacia brought the sleigh down in a clearing surrounded by ancient oaks.
"There," she said, pointing.

I looked where she indicated and saw nothing at first. Just trees and fallen leaves and the gathering dusk. But then I felt it—a pulse of magic, old and patient and inevitable. The kind of magic that understood endings.

Glacia climbed down from the sleigh and walked toward a particular copse of trees. As she approached, I began to see it—not with my eyes, but with something deeper. A cave mouth, hidden in the space between what was and what would be. A threshold that existed only for those who knew how to look.
"Cora's realm," Glacia said softly. "The space between summer and winter. The place where things end so other things can begin."
She stood before the hidden entrance, and I saw her hesitate. Just for a moment. Just long enough for me to see the fear in her eyes.
Then she straightened her shoulders and turned to look at me. The ember in her chest glowed warm and steady, and when she spoke, her voice was calm. Determined.
"Whatever she tells us, whatever price must be paid—we face it together. Yes?"
I moved to her side and pressed against her leg. She rested her hand on my head, and I felt the question in her touch, the same question she'd asked when we left summer's realm.
*Together?*
I nodded, and she smiled. It was small and fragile and tinged with sorrow, but it was real.
"Together," she said.
She took a breath, squared her shoulders, and stepped toward the threshold. I followed, staying close to her side, and together we crossed into autumn's realm.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 14: The Truth of Twilight
p: The world changed the moment we crossed the threshold.

Not violently, like the shock of summer's heat or the shimmer of spring's eternal garden. This was subtler. A shift in the quality of light, the weight of the air. We stepped from the cave's darkness into a world caught in perpetual golden hour—that perfect moment when day hasn't quite surrendered to night, when everything is painted in amber and bronze and deep, rich gold.

The air was cool but not cold, carrying the scent of woodsmoke and ripe apples and something spiced I couldn't quite name. Leaves drifted down around us in lazy spirals—crimson and gold and burnt orange
—falling from trees that seemed to exist in a state of eternal, beautiful decline. The light came from everywhere and nowhere, soft and warm, making everything look like it had been dipped in honey.
"It's beautiful," I said, and my voice—my voice, returned again—sounded hushed in the stillness.
Glacia looked at me, and I saw relief flash across her face at the sound of my words. "It always was," she said softly. "Cora's realm. I'd forgotten how much I loved it here."
Then we heard the music.
It was distant at first, barely audible over the whisper of falling leaves. But as we stood there, it grew stronger
—a heavy, pulsing bass line that resonated in my chest, punctuated by the teasing wail of a trumpet. Blues. Slow-burn, sultry, the kind of music that made you want to move closer, lean in, listen.
"This way," Glacia said, and there was something in her voice—recognition, maybe, or anticipation.

We followed the sound through a forest of oak and maple, their branches heavy with leaves that caught the golden light and turned it into something almost liquid. The music grew louder with each step, the bass line becoming a heartbeat, the trumpet a voice calling us forward.
And then the trees opened up, and we saw it.

The building rose before us like something out of a fever dream—all dark wood and stained glass, with warm light spilling from tall windows. It was intimate and grand at the same time, the kind of place that promised secrets and revelations in equal measure. A sign hung above the entrance, wrought iron formed into elegant script: The Threshold.
The music poured from inside, rich and full and alive.
"A cabaret?," I said, wonder coloring my voice.
"Burlesque," Glacia corrected, and there was affection in her tone. "Cora always did love a good show."
We pushed through the entrance, and the world inside was even more intoxicating than the music had promised.

The space was larger than it should have been, all velvet and gold and flickering candlelight. Round tables filled the floor, each one occupied by beings of every description—fae with wings like stained glass, humans with eyes that held too much knowledge, creatures I couldn't name but recognized as belonging to the spaces between things. The walls were draped in burgundy velvet, and mirrors hung everywhere, reflecting the candlelight until the whole space seemed to glow.
But all of that—the décor, the audience, the sheer theatrical beauty of it—faded into background the moment I saw the stage.
She commanded it absolutely.

Cora stood in a pool of rich, burgundy light that pulsed with the music, and she was magnificent. She wore a tailored suit in deep crimson, the jacket cut to emphasize broad shoulders and a narrow waist, the pants perfectly fitted. Gold thread traced leaf patterns along the lapels, catching the light with every movement. Her shirt was open at the collar, revealing a throat adorned with a choker of amber stones that glowed like captured sunlight. Rings glittered on her fingers—gold and copper and bronze—and a watch chain hung from her vest, swaying slightly as she moved.

Her hair was a shock of red—not the soft auburn of autumn leaves, but a vibrant, almost aggressive crimson cut short in a perfect pixie style that emphasized the sharp angles of her face. Her makeup was flawless, dramatic—dark liner that made her eyes look huge and knowing, lips painted a deep wine color, contour that could cut glass, and just a taste of glitter. She was androgynous and masculine and utterly, devastatingly beautiful.

But more than her appearance, it was her presence that held the room captive. She moved with a mix of theatrical grandeur and something more dangerous, more knowing—the kind of grace that suggested she saw too much, understood too well, and wasn't afraid to tell you truths you didn't want to hear.
"She's incredible," I breathed.
Glacia just nodded, her eyes fixed on her sister with an expression I couldn't quite read.

We found a table near the back, and a server appeared—a fae woman with autumn leaves for hair—and placed drinks before us without being asked. Spiced wine that smelled of cinnamon and cloves and something else I couldn't quite identify , something darker, richer.
On stage, Cora began to sing.

Her voice was deep and smoky, the kind of voice that wrapped around you like velvet and pulled you close. The bass line pulsed underneath, steady as a heartbeat, while the trumpet wove in and out, teasing and playful and just a little bit dangerous.
The velvet night is breathing in deep,
A secret the sun was too afraid to keep.

She moved across the stage with deliberate grace, every gesture calculated for maximum impact. Her hands traced patterns in the air, and I could have sworn I saw leaves falling in their wake—crimson and gold, there and gone in a blink.
The air is pure silk, running cool on your skin,
Tempting you, darling, to let the dark in.
"She's singing to us," Glacia whispered, and I heard the tremor in her voice.
"To everyone," I said. But even as I spoke, I felt it—the weight of Cora's attention, the sense that beneath the performance for the crowd, there was a message meant specifically for us.
Look close at the fruit, and you'll see the slow rot,
The truth that desire can never be bought.

The lights shifted, deepening to a burgundy so rich it was almost black. Cora's movements became more deliberate, more powerful. She shed the jacket with a flourish, revealing a vest embroidered with gold and silver thread that caught the light like fire.
Strip away the grief, that desperate, fast life,
I'm sharing the promise that sharpened the knife.
It's not just falling, it's a deliberate grace,
The most beautiful surrender you'll find in this place.
The music dropped suddenly, leaving only the bass line
—heavy, insistent, like a heartbeat or a countdown. The lights dimmed until there was only a single spotlight on Cora, and in that moment, everything changed.
Time slowed.

Not for the audience—I could see them still swaying, still caught in the music's spell. But for us, for Glacia and me, the world became thick and heavy, like moving through honey. Cora's eyes found us across the crowded room, and they burned—a bright fire, and something older, something that understood endings and thresholds and the prices that must be paid.
When she sang the next verse, I felt each word like a physical blow.
You brought your sweet heat, and you brought your bright core,
The ember. She was singing about the ember in Glacia's chest, the piece of summer warmth that Alessia had planted.
The ledger is marked, and it cries out for more.
The debt. The price. The sacrifice that was coming.
You must choose what to sacrifice for what lies before.
Glacia's hand found mine under the table, her fingers ice-cold and trembling. I squeezed back, trying to offer comfort even as my own heart hammered in my chest.
The brass crashed in—a single, devastating chord—and then silence.
Absolute. Complete. Suffocating.
Cora stood in the spotlight, her eyes still locked on ours, and spoke the final line with a weight that made the air itself feel heavy:
"Welcome... to the final door."
The silence held for three heartbeats. Four. Five.

Then the lights came up, the spell broke, and the audience erupted into applause. They cheered and whistled and stamped their feet, completely unaware of the message that had just been delivered, the warning that had been given.
But Glacia and I sat frozen, our hands still clasped, understanding settling over us like a shroud.
Cora took her bow with a flourish, blew a kiss to the crowd, and then—impossibly, in the space between one blink and the next—she was standing beside our table.

Her suit was different. Still crimson, still perfectly tailored, but the embroidery was now in copper leaves instead of gold, and the vest had been replaced by a waistcoat in deep burgundy, now sporting jewels of gold and obsidian. The change had happened so fast, so seamlessly, that I almost doubted I'd seen the first outfit at all.
"Darlings," she said, and her voice was warm and rich and full of affection. "You came."

Glacia stood, and for a moment she just stared at her sister. Then she moved forward and wrapped her arms around Cora, holding on like she was the only solid thing in a world that had turned to quicksand.
"Cora," she whispered. "I've missed you."
"I know, my dear. I know." Cora held her close, one hand coming up to stroke Glacia's white hair. "It's been far too long."

When they finally pulled apart, Cora turned her attention to me, and I felt the full weight of her gaze. Her eyes were amber—not the warm gold of Alessia's, but darker with flecks of red and brown that shifted in the candlelight.
"Old Man Winter," she said, and there was respect in her voice. "The Ice King himself. What an honor."
She didn't address me as a beast. Didn't acknowledge the curse at all, except in the way she looked at me—as if she could see through the fur and the form to the primordial force beneath.
"The honor is mine," I said, inclining my head. "Your performance was... extraordinary."

"Oh, you're sweet." She grinned, and it transformed her face from beautiful to devastating. "But we both know it was more than just a performance, don't we love? Come. Let's eat. We have much to discuss, and I do my best work over a good meal."
She led us through a door I hadn't noticed before—it simply appeared in the wall when she approached it—and into a private dining room that was somehow even more theatrical than the main space.

The walls were draped in velvet the color of autumn leaves at sunset—deep orange fading to burgundy fading to gold. Candles floated in the air, their flames steady despite having no visible means of support. A table dominated the center of the room, already laden with food that made my mouth water despite everything.

Roasted meats glistening with herbs and spices. Root vegetables caramelized to perfection. Fresh bread still steaming from the oven. Apples and pears arranged in artful displays. Wine the color of garnets in crystal decanters. Everything abundant, everything perfect, everything screaming of autumn's harvest.

"Sit, darlings, sit," Cora said, gesturing to chairs that were more like thrones—high-backed and carved with intricate patterns of falling leaves and bare branches. "Eat. You both look positively famished."
We sat, and Cora poured wine for all of us with a flourish. When she raised her glass, the candlelight caught the rings on her fingers, sending sparks of red and gold dancing across the walls.
"To reunions," she said. "To truth. And to the courage to face what must be faced."
We drank, and the wine was perfect—spiced and warm and just sweet enough to take the edge off the fear that had been building since the performance.

"So," Cora said, settling back in her chair with the easy confidence of someone completely at home in their own skin. "Tell me everything. How did you two find each other? What have my sisters told you? And more importantly—" her eyes sparkled with mischief, "—when did you fall in love?"
Glacia choked on her wine.
I felt heat rise in my face—an odd sensation for a creature of winter.

Cora just laughed, rich and warm and utterly delighted. "Oh, darlings. It's written all over both of you. The way you look at each other, the way you move together, the way that ember in your chest burns brighter whenever he's near." She pointed at Glacia with her wine glass. "You're not subtle, sweetheart. You never were."
"I—" Glacia started, then stopped. Looked at me. Looked back at Cora. "Is it that obvious?"
"Only to anyone with eyes," Cora said cheerfully. "But don't worry. It's beautiful. Tragic and doomed, but absolutely beautiful. My favorite kind of love story."
"Doomed?" I asked, and my voice came out rougher than I intended.

Cora's expression softened. "All love stories are doomed in one way or another, my sweet. That's what makes them worth telling. But we'll get to that. First, eat. Tell me about your journey. I want to hear everything."
So we did. Between bites of food that tasted like autumn itself—rich and earthy and just a little bit intoxicating
—we told her about finding each other, about the extractions and the growing doubt, about Talia's scattered memories and Alessia's revelations.

Cora listened with complete attention, asking questions, making observations, occasionally reaching out to touch Glacia's hand or my paw in gestures of comfort and connection. And somewhere during the meal, I noticed her outfit had changed again—the crimson suit was now a deep brown with gold embroidery, the waistcoat replaced by a vest in burnt orange. I hadn't seen it happen. One moment it was one thing, the next it was another, as natural as breathing.
"Alessia told you about Malakar," Cora said when we'd finished. It wasn't a question. "About the mirror, the corruption, the trap."
Glacia nodded, her hand tightening around her wine glass. "She told us everything. That I've been completing the ritual of my own enslavement. That when the mirror is whole, I'll be his forever."
"And the ember," I added. "She told us about the ember she planted. The piece of summer warmth that's been fighting the corruption."

Cora smiled, and there was fierce pride in it. "Alessia always was the clever one. Planting hope in the heart of winter itself. Very poetic. Very her." She leaned forward, her amber eyes intense. "But she couldn't tell you how it ends, could she? She can see clearly, our Alessia, but even she can't see the final door. That's my domain."
The room seemed to grow quieter, the candlelight dimmer. Even the food on the table seemed to lose some of its luster, as if acknowledging the weight of what was about to be discussed.

"Endings," Cora said softly. "Thresholds. The space between what was and what will be. That's what I understand. That's what I am." She stood, and her movements were liquid grace as she walked to a sideboard and poured herself more wine. When she turned back, her suit was different again—now a deep purple with silver embroidery, the vest replaced by a cravat in burgundy silk.
I was starting to understand. The constant changes weren't just theatrical flair. They were fundamental to who she was. Transition embodied. Change made manifest.

"Let me tell you about death," Cora said, settling back into her chair. "Not the corrupted kind, not the murder and the horror that Glacia has been forced to commit. Real death. Natural death. The kind that's necessary for anything to grow."

She looked at Glacia, and her expression was tender. "You've always struggled with winter, haven't you, sweetheart? Always seen it as the end, as death, as the season that takes away. But that's not what winter is. Not really."
"Then what is it?" Glacia asked, and her voice was small.

"It's the pause," Cora said. "The rest. The necessary ending that allows for new beginnings. You can't have spring without winter. You can't have growth without dormancy. You can't have transformation without death." She gestured around the room, at the autumn colors, the falling leaves visible through the windows. "Look at me. Look at my season. What am I?"
"The end of summer," I said slowly. "The beginning of winter."

"Exactly." Cora's smile was approving. "I'm the threshold. The in-between. I'm the death of what was and the promise of what will be. And I'm beautiful, aren't I? Tragic and melancholy and absolutely, drop dead gorgeous. Because endings can be beautiful. Death can be beautiful. When it's natural, when it's necessary, when it serves a purpose."

She turned back to Glacia. "Winter isn't death, darling. Winter is rest. It's the world taking a breath, gathering strength, preparing for rebirth. The seeds sleep in the frozen ground, but they're not dead. They're waiting. Transforming. Becoming what they need to be for spring."
Glacia's eyes were bright with tears. "But I've killed so many people. Hundreds. How is that beautiful? How is that necessary?"

"It's not," Cora said bluntly. "That's the corruption. That's Malakar twisting your nature into something it was never meant to be. He took your power—the power to bring rest, to allow transformation—and turned it into murder. That's not you, Glacia. That's him."

She reached across the table and took Glacia's hand. "But here's what you need to understand: transformation requires sacrifice. Always. You cannot become something new without letting the old self die. You cannot break free of corruption without paying a price. You cannot save what you love without giving up something you need."
The words hung in the air, heavy with meaning.
"What price?" I asked, though I thought I already knew.

Cora turned to me, and her eyes were ancient and knowing. "That's not for me to say, Ice King. The threshold shows you the door, but you have to choose whether to walk through it. You have to choose what you're willing to sacrifice."

She stood again, and this time when she moved, I saw the change happen—a flicker, a shimmer, and suddenly the purple suit was gone, replaced by one in deep forest green with gold buttons. It happened in the space between heartbeats, in the blink of an eye, in that liminal moment when you're not quite sure what you saw.

"Let me tell you about the burlesque," she said, and her voice took on a different quality—still warm, still rich, but with an edge of something deeper. "Do you know what it really is? What it represents?"
"Performance," Glacia said. "Transformation."

"Yes, but more than that." Cora gestured expansively. "It's about shedding. About revealing. About becoming. The performers come on stage as one thing, and through the act of performance, through the deliberate removal of layers, they become something else. They transform themselves. They choose who they want to be in that moment."

She moved closer to us, and I could smell autumn on her—woodsmoke and spices and the rich scent of decay that wasn't rot but transformation. "That's what you're both doing, whether you realize it or not. You're shedding your old selves. Glacia, you're shedding the corruption, the cold, the isolation. Kael, you're shedding the beast, the curse, the forgetting. You're both becoming something new."
"But transformation requires death," I said, understanding dawning. "The death of what we were."
"Yes." Cora's smile was sad and beautiful. "And sometimes, darling, that death is literal."
The room fell silent except for the soft crackle of candles and the distant sound of music from the main hall. Glacia's hand found mine again, and I felt her trembling.

"There are shards left to collect," Cora said quietly. "Not many. Maybe just a handful. And when they're all gathered, when the mirror is complete, the compulsion will end. But Malakar's hold will be absolute. Unless—"
"Unless what?" Glacia asked desperately.

Cora looked between us, and her expression was infinitely gentle. "Unless the ember is strong enough. Unless love is strong enough. Unless you're both willing to pay the price that transformation demands."

She moved to stand behind Glacia, her hands coming to rest on her sister's shoulders. "The ember feeds on love, sweetheart. On connection. On warmth. Every moment you've spent with him, every tear you've shed, every time you've chosen compassion over cruelty—it's made the ember stronger. It's been fighting the shard, keeping you alive, keeping you yourself."
"But it's not enough," Glacia whispered. "Is it?"
"Not yet," Cora admitted. "But it could be. If you feed it. If you let yourself love completely, without reservation, without fear. If you accept what that love might cost."

She turned to me, and I felt the weight of her attention like a physical thing. "And you, Ice King. Old Man Winter. Winter's Hand." She listed my titles with the same respect Alessia had shown. "You've been devoted to her since the moment you woke in her palace. You've stayed when you could have run. You've witnessed horrors and stayed anyway. You've loved her through the corruption, seen her at her worst, and loved her still."
"Yes," I said simply, because there was no point in denying it.

"That kind of devotion," Cora said softly, "is powerful magic. More powerful than any curse. More powerful than any demon's corruption. Love like that can break anything. Save anything. Transform anything." She paused. "But it requires sacrifice. True sacrifice. The kind where you give up everything."
"I would," I said, and I meant it with every fiber of my being. "For her, I would give up everything."

Cora's smile was heartbreaking in its beauty. "I know, my dear. That's why you're here. That's why you found each other. That's why the ember has grown so strong." She looked at Glacia. "And you, sweetheart? What would you sacrifice for him?"
Glacia looked at me, and I saw everything in her eyes
—love and fear and desperate hope. "Anything," she whispered. "Everything. I would rather die than lose him."

"Good," Cora said, and there was satisfaction in her voice. "Because that's what transformation requires. The willingness to die. The courage to let go of what you were so you can become what you need to be."
She moved away from us, pacing the room with that liquid grace, and I noticed her suit had changed again
—now a deep burgundy with copper embroidery, the cravat replaced by a simple collar. The changes were coming faster now, or maybe I was just noticing them more.

"Here's what I can tell you," Cora said. "The mirror must be completed. The compulsion cannot be stopped. Glacia will gather the remaining shards because she has no choice. And when the last shard is placed, one of two things will happen."
She held up one finger. "Either Malakar's hold becomes absolute, and Glacia is lost forever, enslaved to a demon's will, an engine of death and suffering for all eternity."

She held up a second finger. "Or the ember is strong enough to fight back. To break the hold. To transform the corruption into something else. But that will only happen if you both choose love over survival. If you both choose sacrifice over safety. If you both walk through the final door together, knowing you might not come back."
"How?" Glacia asked. "How do we make the ember strong enough?"

Cora's smile was gentle. "You already know, darling. You've been doing it all along. You love him. You let him love you. You choose connection over isolation, warmth over cold, hope over despair. And when the moment comes—when you're standing at the final door—you choose each other. No matter the cost."

She came back to the table and sat down, and I saw it again—a shimmer, a flicker, and the burgundy suit became one in deep orange with gold buttons. It was like watching autumn itself, the constant change, the beautiful decay, the transformation that never stopped.

"I can't tell you exactly what will happen," Cora said. "I can't see the other side of the door. That's not my gift. But I can tell you this: love is the most powerful magic in existence. It breaks curses. It transforms corruption. It turns death into rebirth. If you love each other enough, if you're willing to sacrifice everything for that love, then you have a chance."
"Just a chance?" I asked.
"That's all anyone ever gets, darling." Cora's smile was sad. "But it's a better chance than you had before. And it's a chance worth taking."

We sat in silence for a long moment, the weight of her words settling over us. The candles flickered, casting dancing shadows on the velvet walls. Somewhere in the distance, I could hear music—another performance, another transformation, another ending that promised a new beginning.
"I was closest to you," Cora said to Glacia, her voice soft. "Before the shattering. Do you remember why?"
Glacia shook her head, tears streaming down her face.

"Because we understood each other," Cora said. "We were the necessary darkness, the pause, the breath before the world began again. And we were beautiful, Glacia. So beautiful. We brought transformation. We brought change. We brought the death that allows for life."

She reached across the table and wiped the tears from Glacia's face with surprising gentleness. "You are not a monster, sweetheart. You never were. You're winter. You're rest. You're the pause that allows for growth. Malakar corrupted that, twisted it, turned it into something it was never meant to be. But underneath the corruption, you're still you. Still my sister. Still beautiful. Still necessary. Still loved."

Glacia broke down completely, sobbing into her hands, and Cora moved around the table to hold her. I pressed against Glacia's other side, offering what comfort I could, and for a long time we just sat there—three beings caught in the space between what was and what would be, holding onto each other in the face of an uncertain future.
When Glacia finally calmed, Cora pulled back and smiled. "Better?"
Glacia nodded, wiping her eyes. "Thank you. For everything. For the truth. For not giving up on me."

"Never," Cora said fiercely. "You're my sister. I will never give up on you." She looked at me. "And you, Ice King. Take care of her. Love her. And when the moment comes, be brave enough to do what must be done."
"I will," I promised.

Cora stood, and her suit was different again—back to crimson, but with silver embroidery this time, and a vest in deep purple. "It's late. You should rest. You have a long journey ahead of you, and you'll need your strength."

She led us through another door that appeared when she approached it, into a bedroom that was both intimate and cozy. A large bed dominated the space, piled high with blankets in autumn colors. Candles floated near the ceiling, their light soft and warm. Windows looked out over a forest caught in eternal twilight, leaves falling in slow, graceful spirals.
"Sleep," Cora said. "Dream. And in the morning, I'll send you on your way with my blessing."

She started to leave, then paused at the door. "One more thing," she said, looking back at us. "The final door—when you reach it, when you're standing at the threshold—remember this: transformation is always a choice. Death is always a choice. You can choose to walk through together, or you can choose to turn back. But if you turn back, nothing changes. The corruption remains. The curse remains. Everything stays exactly as it is."
"And if we walk through?" Glacia asked.

Cora's smile was mysterious and sad and somehow hopeful all at once. "Then you become something new. Both of you. Together." She paused. "Love is the most powerful magic, darlings. Never forget that. It can break anything. Save anything. Transform anything. Even death itself."
And then she was gone, the door closing softly behind her, leaving us alone in the candlelit room with the weight of her words and the knowledge of what was coming.
Glacia turned to me, and I saw everything in her eyes
—fear and love and desperate hope. "I'm scared," she whispered.
"So am I," I admitted. "But we're together. That has to count for something."
She sank down onto the floor beside me, her hand coming up to rest on my head. "When this is over—if we survive this—I want to tell you something. Something I should have said already."
"I know," I said softly. "I know, Glacia. And I feel the same way."
She leaned forward and pressed her forehead against mine, and we stayed like that for a long time, drawing strength from each other, preparing ourselves for whatever came next.

Eventually, exhaustion claimed us both. Glacia climbed into the bed, and I settled on the floor beside her, close enough that she could reach down and rest her hand in my fur. The ember in her chest glowed warm and steady, brighter than I'd ever seen it, pulsing in time with her heartbeat.
And as I drifted off to sleep, I thought about Cora's words. About transformation and sacrifice. About love and death and the courage to walk through the final door.
Whatever was coming, whatever price had to be paid, we would face it together.
That was enough. It had to be enough.

Morning came softly to autumn's realm—not a sunrise, exactly, but a gradual brightening of the golden light, a subtle shift in the quality of the air. I woke to find Glacia already up, standing at the window and watching the leaves fall in their eternal, graceful dance.
"Did you sleep?" I asked.

"A little." She turned to look at me, and I saw the determination in her eyes. "I've been thinking about what Cora said. About transformation. About sacrifice. About choosing love even when it costs everything."
"And?"

"And I'm ready." She moved away from the window and knelt beside me, her hand coming up to cup my face. "Whatever happens, whatever price has to be paid—I'm ready. Because I'd rather die trying to save you, trying to save myself, trying to save us, than live forever as Malakar's slave."

Before I could respond, there was a knock at the door, and Cora swept in. Her suit was different again—a deep emerald green with gold embroidery, perfectly tailored, absolutely stunning. She carried a tray with breakfast—fresh bread, honey, fruit, tea that smelled of spices and autumn.
"Good morning, darlings," she said cheerfully. "I hope you slept well. We have a few things to discuss before you go."

We ate together, and Cora talked about small things—the burlesque, her performers, the magic of autumn. But underneath the lightness, I could feel the weight of what was unsaid, the knowledge of what was coming.

When we'd finished, Cora stood and gestured for us to follow. She led us back through the building—which seemed to shift and change as we walked, rooms appearing and disappearing, hallways leading to places they shouldn't—and out into the forest.
The cave entrance was there, waiting, the threshold back to the mortal realm visible as a shimmer in the air.
Cora turned to face us, and her expression was serious. "This is where I leave you," she said. "Where you go next, I cannot follow. But I want you to remember something."

She took Glacia's hands in hers. "You are not alone, sweetheart. You have never been alone. Your sisters love you. The ember burns in your heart. And you have him." She glanced at me. "Love like that is rare. Precious. Worth fighting for. Worth dying for."

She turned to me, and her amber eyes were intense. "And you, Ice King. You've been devoted to winter all your life. You've served it, embodied it, been its hand in the world. But now you have a chance to be something more. To be not just winter's hand, but winter's heart. To love not just the season, but the goddess who embodies it."

She stepped back, and I saw tears in her eyes. "When you reach the final door, when you're standing at the threshold, remember: transformation requires death. But death is not the end. It's the beginning. The pause before the world begins again. The rest before the rebirth."
"Thank you," Glacia whispered. "For everything. For the truth. For the hope. For not giving up on me."

"Never," Cora said fiercely. She pulled Glacia into a tight embrace, holding her close. "I love you, sister. I always have. I always will. No matter what happens, no matter what you've done, no matter what you become—I love you."
When they pulled apart, Cora turned to me and, to my surprise, embraced me as well. "Take care of her," she whispered in my ear. "Love her. And when the moment comes, be brave enough to let go."

She stepped back, and her suit had changed one final time—back to the crimson from her performance, with gold embroidery that caught the light like fire. She looked every inch the queen of thresholds, the embodiment of transformation, the goddess of beautiful endings.
"Go," she said. "Face what must be faced. Choose what must be chosen. And remember—love is the most powerful magic. It can break anything. Save anything. Transform anything."
She raised her hand in farewell, and we turned toward the threshold.
"Glacia," Cora called, and we looked back. She was smiling, sad and beautiful and somehow hopeful. "Winter always ends. But it also always returns. Remember that."
And then we stepped through the shimmer, through the threshold, back into the mortal realm.

The change was immediate and jarring. The golden light of autumn vanished, replaced by the grey, overcast sky of the mortal world. The warmth disappeared, leaving only the bite of winter's cold. And my voice—my precious, temporary voice—vanished with it, locked away again behind the curse.

But something was different. The ember in Glacia's chest burned brighter than ever, visible even through her gown as a warm, steady glow. And when she looked at me, there was something in her eyes that hadn't been there before.
Understanding. Acceptance. And a fierce, determined love that made the ember flare even brighter.
"West and north," she said quietly, her hand coming to rest on my head. "Back to the palace. To face whatever comes next."

We climbed into the sleigh, and I settled beside her. She didn't speak as we lifted into the air, didn't try to fill the silence with one-sided conversation. She just rested her hand on my fur, and I felt the question in her touch, the same question she'd asked before.
Together?
I pressed closer to her side, and she understood.
Together.

The sleigh rose into the grey sky, and we flew toward the ice palace in silence. The landscape below was still caught in winter's premature grip—frost on fields that should have been green, ice on rivers that should have been flowing, snow on mountains that should have been bare.
Evidence of the corruption. Evidence of what Glacia had become.

But also evidence of what she was fighting. Because I could see it now—the places where the frost was lighter, where the ice was thinner, where winter's grip wasn't quite as strong. The ember was fighting back, pushing against the corruption, making space for warmth even in the heart of winter.
Glacia saw it too. I felt her tense beside me, felt her hand tighten in my fur.

"It's getting worse," she said quietly. "The compulsion. I can feel it pulling at me, demanding I find the remaining shards. There aren't many left. Maybe just a few. And when they're all gathered..." She trailed off, unable to finish the thought.
I pressed closer, offering what comfort I could.
"Cora was right," she continued, her voice barely audible over the wind. "Transformation requires sacrifice. Death requires courage. And love—" her voice broke, "—love requires everything."

The ember flared brighter, as if responding to her words, and I felt warmth spread through me despite the cold. It was working. The love between us, the connection we'd built, the devotion we'd shown—it was feeding the ember, making it stronger, giving us a chance.
Just a chance. But a chance worth taking.

The ice palace appeared on the horizon, its spires catching what little light filtered through the clouds. It looked cold and empty and lonely—a monument to isolation, to winter without warmth, to power without love.
But it wouldn't always be that way. Couldn't always be that way.
Because we had each other. We had love. We had hope.
And when the final door appeared, when we stood at the threshold between what was and what would be, we would walk through it together.
No matter the cost.

The sleigh descended toward the palace, and Glacia's hand never left my fur. The ember burned steady and bright in her chest, a beacon of warmth in the heart of winter, a promise that transformation was possible, that love could break anything, that even the darkest corruption could be overcome.
We landed in the courtyard, and Glacia sat for a long moment, staring at her palace, at the monument to her century of suffering.
"Soon," she whispered. "Soon this will all be over. One way or another."

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 15: The Eye of Winter
p: The pain started within hours of our return.

I'd felt it building during the flight back, a pressure behind my left eye that grew with each passing mile. But I'd pushed it aside, focused on Glacia, on getting home, on the warmth of her hand in my fur.
But once we were inside the palace, once the immediate urgency of travel faded, there was nothing left to distract me from it.

It felt like something was pressing against the inside of my skull. Not gradually increasing, but pulsing—sharp spikes of agony that made my vision blur and my breath catch. Each pulse sent darkness spreading across my sight, like ink dropped into water.
I tried to hide it. Tried to keep my movements steady, my breathing even. But Glacia knew me too well now.
"Kael?" She knelt beside me where I lay by the cold fire, her hand coming to rest on my head. "Your eye. It's worse, isn't it?"
I wanted to deny it. Wanted to tell her I was fine, that Alessia's magic was still holding, that we had time.
But I couldn't lie to her. Not anymore.
I nodded, and even that small movement sent pain lancing through my skull.
Her hand moved to my face, gentle, careful. She tilted my head toward the firelight, and I saw her expression change. Saw the fear flash across her features before she could hide it.
"The darkness," she whispered. "It's spreading. I can see it clouding over the eye."
Another pulse of pain, and I flinched despite myself.
"How bad is it?" she asked. "The pain?"
I couldn't answer, couldn't find a way to communicate the intensity of it. So I just pressed my head against her hand, and she understood.
"We'll figure this out," she said, but her voice shook. "We have to. I can't—" She stopped, swallowed hard. "I won't lose you to this."
The ember flared in her chest, warm and bright, and for just a moment the pain eased. Just a moment. But it was enough to let me breathe.
She stayed with me through the night, her hand on my fur, the ember's warmth a small comfort against the growing darkness in my eye.
The corruption came for me on the second day.
I'd been lying by the fire, trying to rest, trying to push the pain down to something manageable. Glacia had gone to check the mirror chamber, to count the shards, to try to sense how many remained.
The pain spiked suddenly, so intense I couldn't breathe. Couldn't think. Couldn't—
And then something else took over.
The world shifted. The pain was still there, but distant now, muffled. And in its place came clarity. Cold, sharp, perfect clarity.
I heard footsteps and turned to see Glacia returning. She looked tired. Worn. Fragile.
Pathetic.
The thought came unbidden, but it felt right. True. She was weak. Had always been weak. A goddess who cried over mortals, who hesitated, who let guilt and doubt corrupt her purpose.
"Kael?" She moved toward me, concern in her eyes. "Are you—"
A growl ripped from my throat, low and threatening. I rose to my feet, and the movement was predatory. Aggressive.
She stopped, confusion crossing her face. "What's wrong?"
Everything. You're what's wrong. Weak. Broken. Pathetic creature crying over every kill.
I stalked toward her, my lips pulling back from my teeth. Another growl, deeper this time, resonating through my chest.
"Kael, that's not you. That's the shard—"
The shard shows the truth. You're nothing. A broken goddess playing at redemption.
I moved closer, and she held her ground, but I could see the fear in her eyes. Could smell it. Good. She should fear me. Should recognize what I was.
You think love will save you? You think this bear, this cursed beast, means anything?
My muscles coiled, ready to spring. Ready to—

"I'm going to complete the mirror," she said quietly, not backing down. "I'm going to become his slave. And maybe I deserve it for what I've done. But you don't deserve this, Kael. You don't deserve what the shard is doing to you."
Weak. Always been weak. Always been—
Pain.
Sudden, sharp, overwhelming pain that had nothing to do with the shard and everything to do with what I was thinking. What I was about to do.
No.
No, this wasn't me. This wasn't—

I fought. Clawed my way back through the darkness, through the corruption, through the cold clarity that wanted to consume me. It was like swimming through ice, every movement agony, every thought a battle.
But I had something the shard didn't account for.
I had her.
I focused on Glacia. On her face. On the fear there, yes, but also the steadiness. The determination. The love that burned in her chest as bright as the ember itself.
I focused on her hand reaching toward me despite my aggression. On her voice saying my name. On the warmth she'd brought to my frozen existence.
And slowly, agonizingly, I pushed the corruption back.
When I finally returned to myself, I was shaking. My legs barely held me. And the look on Glacia's face—
I whimpered, a broken sound, and dropped to the floor. Pressed my head against the ice in submission, in apology, in horror at what I'd almost done.
But she understood. She always understood.
She dropped to her knees and wrapped her arms around my neck, and I felt her trembling. Felt the tears on my fur.
"It's getting worse," she whispered. "Kael, it's getting so much worse."
I pressed against her, trying to communicate everything I couldn't say. That I was sorry. That I was fighting. That I would keep fighting as long as I could.
That I loved her.
When she finally pulled back, she touched my face gently, examining my eye. The darkness had spread, clouding more of my vision. I could barely see out of it now, just shapes and shadows.
"We're running out of time," she said quietly. "Both of us."
Three days later I woke to find Glacia standing at the window, her hand pressed to her chest, her face tight with pain.
"Another shard," she said when she saw me watching. "Close. Maybe a day's flight south."
She looked at me, at my clouded eye, at the way I moved carefully to avoid jarring the constant pain in my skull.
"You should stay here," she said. "Rest. You don't need to
I was already moving toward the door.
"Kael, please. You're in so much pain. I can do this alone."
I stopped and turned to look at her, and she saw the answer in my eyes.

She closed her eyes, and I saw the war on her face—the compulsion demanding she go, the guilt over what she'd have to do, the fear of what was happening to me, the love that made her want to protect me even as I insisted on protecting her.
"Together, then," she whispered. "Always together."
The flight south was agony.
Every movement of the sleigh sent pain lancing through my skull. The wind felt like knives against my face. My vision kept blurring, the darkness spreading and receding in waves.
But I stayed conscious. Stayed present. Because Glacia needed me.

She drove in silence, her hands white-knuckled on the reins, her face a mask of concentration. But I could see the ember fighting in her chest, pulsing brighter and dimmer as the compulsion and her own will warred for control.

"It's getting harder," she said at one point, her voice barely audible over the wind. "Every time, it's harder to do this. The ember fights back. Makes me feel everything. Makes me remember that these are people, not just—not just vessels for shards."
She looked at me, and her eyes were full of tears that froze on her cheeks.
"I don't know how much longer I can bear this."
I pressed against her side, and she leaned into me, drawing what comfort she could from my presence.
"Just a few more," she whispered. "It has to be just a few more. And then—"
She didn't finish. Didn't say what came after. Because neither of us knew.
The village appeared below us as the sun began to set. Small. Remote. The kind of place where people lived simple lives, far from the concerns of gods and demons and corrupted mirrors.
The kind of place that didn't deserve what was about to happen.
Glacia brought the sleigh down at the edge of the village, and we sat there for a long moment, neither of us moving.

"I can feel it," she said. "In the workshop at the edge of the village. An old man. A woodcarver." Her voice broke. "He's alone. Working on something. I can sense—" She pressed her hand to her chest. "He's creating something beautiful."
Her hands were shaking.
"I have to do this," she said, and it sounded like she was trying to convince herself. "I have to. The compulsion—
I can't stop it. I can't—"
The ember flared, and she gasped, pressing her hand to her chest.
"But I don't want to," she whispered. "Gods, I don't want to."
I moved closer, pressed my head against her shoulder. Tried to give her what strength I had, even though I was barely holding myself together.
She took a shuddering breath, then climbed out of the sleigh.
"Stay here," she said. "Please. You don't need to see this."

But I followed anyway. Because I'd promised. Because she shouldn't have to face this alone. Because even if I couldn't stop it, I could bear witness. Could remind her that she was more than the monster the shard tried to make her.

The workshop was warm, lamplight spilling from the windows. Through them, I could see an elderly man bent over a workbench, his weathered hands moving with practiced precision. Wood shavings curled away from his tools. Around him, the walls were lined with his work—carved animals, intricate boxes, toys for children, walking sticks with handles shaped like birds.
A lifetime of creation. Of beauty made from simple wood.
Glacia stopped at the door, and I saw her whole body trembling.
"I can't," she whispered. "I can't do this. He's just—he's just making things. Creating beauty. Like I used to. Before—"
The compulsion pulsed, and she cried out, doubling over. The shard in her chest flared dark, demanding obedience.
"No," she gasped. "No, I won't—"
But her hand was already reaching for the door. Already pushing it open. The compulsion was absolute. Undeniable.
The old man looked up as she entered. His eyes were kind, crinkled at the corners from years of smiling. He didn't look afraid. Just... sad. As if he'd been expecting this.
"Ah," he said softly, setting down his carving tools. "The Snow Queen. I wondered if you'd come for me eventually."
"I'm sorry," Glacia said, and her voice was breaking. "I'm so sorry. I don't want to do this. I don't—"
"I know," he said gently. He stood slowly, his joints stiff with age, and gestured to the carving on his workbench. "Would you like to see what I was making? Before—well. Before."
Glacia's breath hitched, but she moved closer, drawn despite herself.
It was a carousel horse. Delicate, beautiful, mid-leap with its mane flowing back. Every detail was perfect—the curve of the neck, the flare of the nostrils, the joy captured in wood.
"For my great-granddaughter," he said. "She's turning six next month. She loves horses." He smiled, though his eyes were wet. "I suppose I won't finish it now."
"I'm sorry," Glacia whispered again. "I'm so sorry."
"I know you are." He reached out and patted her hand, and she flinched at the contact. "I can see it in your eyes. You're not doing this because you want to. Something's making you. Something dark."
Tears were streaming down Glacia's face now. "I can't stop it. I've tried. I can't—"
"Then don't fight it," he said gently. "It's all right. I've lived a good life. Made beautiful things. Loved my family. That's more than many get." He glanced at the carousel horse. "I just wish—"
His voice broke, and he looked away.
"What?" Glacia asked. "What do you wish?"
"That someone would finish it for her. That she'd have something to remember me by. Something beautiful, not—" He gestured vaguely. "Not just the memory of how I died."
I moved forward then, pushing past Glacia to stand beside the workbench. I looked at the carousel horse, then at the old man, then back at Glacia.
She understood.
"You want—" Her voice was barely audible. "You want time to tell me how to finish it?"
"If you would," he said. "If there's time. If you—"
"There's time," she said, and her voice was fierce despite the tears. "Tell me. Show me. I'll finish it. I promise."

So he did. For twenty minutes, while the compulsion burned in Glacia's chest and made her shake with the effort of resisting, the old man taught her how to finish the carousel horse. Where to carve the final details. How to sand it smooth. What oil to use to bring out the grain.
Glacia listened to every word, memorizing it all, her hands trembling as she held the half-finished carving.
"There," he said finally. "That's everything. You'll do it justice. I can tell. You have the hands of a creator, not a destroyer. Whatever's making you do this—it hasn't taken that from you."
"Thank you," she whispered. "For trusting me with this."
"Thank you," he replied, "for giving me time to make sure she'll have something beautiful."
He took a breath, squared his shoulders, and turned to face her fully.
"I'm ready now."
Glacia's whole body was shaking. The compulsion was screaming at her, the shard burning in her chest. She'd held it off as long as she could.
"I'm sorry," she said one more time.
"I know," he said gently. "It's all right. I forgive you."
And then she reached out and touched his face, and the cold began to spread.

It was worse than any extraction I'd witnessed before. The ember was fighting back with everything it had, making the process slower, more painful. The old man's breath came in gasps as frost spread across his skin, as ice formed in his veins, as the cold reached deeper and deeper.
But he didn't scream. Didn't beg. Just kept his eyes on Glacia's face, and in them was nothing but compassion.
"It's all right," he whispered as the cold reached his heart. "You're not a monster. You're just—trapped. Like I am now. But you—you can still—"
The shard released from his eye, and he went still.
Glacia caught the shard with shaking hands, then collapsed to her knees, sobbing. The carousel horse fell from her other hand, rolling across the floor.
I moved to her and pressed against her, and she grabbed my fur with both hands, holding on as if I were the only thing keeping her from falling apart completely.

"He forgave me," she whispered. "He forgave me, and I killed him anyway. I killed a man who spent his life making beautiful things, who just wanted his greatgranddaughter to have something to remember him by, and I—"
She couldn't continue. Just sobbed into my fur while the lamplight flickered over the old man's frozen body and the walls lined with a lifetime of creation.
We stayed like that for a long time. Too long. Until finally, the compulsion released its hold enough for her to move.
She stood slowly, the shard clutched in one hand, and picked up the carousel horse with the other.
"I'll finish it," she said to the old man's body. "I promise. She'll have something beautiful. Something that shows how much you loved her."
But the words felt hollow. Because no carved horse, no matter how beautiful, could replace a greatgrandfather's love.
The flight back to the palace was silent except for Glacia's quiet weeping.

My eye was worse. The pain had intensified during the extraction, as if the proximity to another shard had fed the corruption in my own. The darkness had spread further, until I could barely see anything out of that eye at all.
But the physical pain was nothing compared to what I felt watching Glacia break apart.

When we reached the palace, she went straight to the mirror chamber and placed the shard with all the others. Four hundred and ninety-seven pieces of a demon's trap, each one bought with blood and suffering.
"How many more?" she whispered, staring at the nearlycomplete mirror. "How many more people have to die?"
She turned to look at me, and I saw the desperation in her eyes.
"It has to be close to done. It has to be. I can't—I can't keep doing this."
That night, we sat by the cold fire, and she examined my eye.
Her touch was gentle, careful, but I still flinched. The pain was constant now, a throbbing ache that never fully faded.
"It's almost completely dark," she said quietly. "I can barely see your eye anymore. Just—just shadow and corruption."
She pressed her forehead against mine, and I felt her tears on my fur.
"I'm losing you," she whispered. "Piece by piece, I'm losing you to this thing. And I don't know how to stop it."
I wished I could tell her that I was still here. Still fighting. That as long as I had her, I could keep the corruption at bay.
But the words wouldn't come. So I just pressed closer, and hoped she understood.

"There can't be many shards left," she said after a long silence. "I've collected four hundred and ninety-seven. The compulsion—it feels different now. Stronger. More urgent. Like I'm close to the end."
She pulled back to look at me, and I saw hope and fear warring in her expression.

"But I can't sense where the remaining ones are," she said, her voice tight with confusion. "The compulsion is so strong, pulling me forward, telling me I'm almost done. But there's nothing. No direction. No pull toward the next shard." She wrapped her arms around herself. "What happens when I complete it? When the mirror is whole and Malakar—" Her voice broke. "I don't know what comes next. I don't know what he'll make me become."
She looked at me, and I saw the terror in her eyes.
"But whatever it is," she whispered, "we'll face it together."
The ember pulsed in her chest, warm and bright, and for just a moment, the pain in my eye eased.

She started to say something else—something about the compulsion, about the fear—but different words came out instead. Words she hadn't planned. Words that felt like they'd been pulled from somewhere deep inside her, from that warm place where the ember burned.
"I love you."
The words hung in the air between us, and she stared at me with wide eyes, as if she'd surprised herself. As if she was hearing the truth of it for the first time.
"I—" She pressed her hand to her chest, to the place where the ember pulsed. "I love you, Kael."
Her voice broke on my name, and tears spilled down her cheeks. But they weren't tears of grief or fear. They were something else entirely.
Wonder. Recognition. Understanding.
"How did I not see it before?" she whispered. "All this time, I thought—I thought it was just the ember fighting the shard. Just warmth against cold. But it's not. It's you. It's been you all along."
She cupped my face in both hands, her touch gentle despite the cold that radiated from her skin.
"I love you," she said again, and this time it came easier, more certain. "And I'm going to fight for you. For us. No matter what it costs."
I wanted to tell her I loved her too. Wanted to say all the things I'd been holding inside. But all I could do was press my head against her hand and hope she felt it.
We sat like that for hours, drawing comfort from each other's presence, holding onto the warmth between us as the darkness continued to spread.
The next episode came six days later.
It was worse than the first. So much worse.
I'd been resting—or trying to—when the pain spiked so suddenly and so intensely that I roared. The sound echoed through the palace, and I heard Glacia running toward me.
But by the time she reached me, I was already gone.
The corruption was deeper this time. Stronger. It didn't just change my thoughts—it changed everything. My perception. My understanding. My very sense of self.
I saw Glacia enter the room, and I didn't see the woman I loved. I saw an enemy. A threat. Something that needed to be eliminated.
She was weak. Corrupted. Tainted by sentiment and guilt. She was the reason winter had become soft, had become something to be endured rather than feared.
She needed to be removed.
I moved toward her with predatory intent, and she backed away, her hands coming up defensively.
"Kael, stop. This isn't you. You're stronger than this."
I am exactly what I should be, I thought, the corruption singing through my veins. Winter's true hand. Not this pathetic creature who follows a broken goddess and pretends it's devotion.
I lunged, and she threw up a wall of ice between us. I shattered it with one blow, the impact sending shards flying.

You're nothing, the cruel thoughts continued as I stalked toward her. A failure. A goddess who couldn't even accept her own nature. Who let a demon corrupt her because she was too weak to see the truth.
"Fight it," she said, and her voice was steady despite the fear in her eyes. "I know you're in there. I know you can hear me. Fight it, Kael."
There's nothing to fight. This is clarity. This is truth. You're weak, and you're going to fail, and you're going to drag everyone down with you.
I was close enough to strike now. Close enough to hurt her. My body tensed, ready to lunge, ready to—
Her hand came up and pressed against my face, right over my corrupted eye.
The ember's warmth flooded through me, and the pain was excruciating. But it was also real. It cut through the corruption's cold clarity and reminded me of something the shard wanted me to forget.
Love.
I loved her.
The thought was small at first, barely a whisper against the corruption's roar. But it grew. Spread. Became something the shard couldn't suppress.
I loved her. I loved her. I loved her.
The mantra became my anchor, and I used it to claw my way back. Used it to fight through the darkness and the cold and the corruption that wanted to consume me.
It took longer this time. So much longer. And when I finally returned to myself, I collapsed, shaking and weak and terrified of what I'd almost done.
Glacia was there immediately, her arms around me, her tears on my fur.
"You came back," she whispered. "You came back to me."
But we both knew it had been close. Too close.
And when I finally had the strength to look at her, I saw the truth reflected in her eyes.
My left eye was almost completely dark now. Just a thin ring of color around the edge, the rest consumed by shadow.
I was running out of time.
The compulsion came again four days later.
Glacia tried to resist it. Tried to push back against the pull. But the shard in her chest was relentless, and the pain of resistance was too much.
"I have to go," she said, her voice tight with agony. "East. Not far. Maybe half a day."
She looked at me, at my nearly-blind eye, at the way I moved carefully to avoid triggering the worst of the pain.
"You should stay," she said. "Please, Kael. You can barely stand. You don't need to—"
But I was already moving toward the sleigh.
She didn't argue. Just helped me climb in, then took the reins with shaking hands.
This extraction was faster than the last. The victim was an old man, alone in the woods, no family to mourn him. The shard came free quickly, and he died without much suffering.
But it didn't matter. Fast or slow, alone or surrounded by family—it was still death. Still murder. Still another piece of Malakar's trap falling into place.
Four hundred and ninety-eight shards.
Back at the palace, Glacia went to the mirror chamber while I rested by the cold fire.
I heard her counting. Heard the soft clink of shards as she examined them. Heard her voice, quiet and confused.
"Four hundred and ninety-eight," she said when she returned. "I've collected four hundred and ninety-eight shards."
She sat down beside me, her brow furrowed.
"We estimated around five hundred total when this started. Maybe a few more, maybe a few less. But if I've collected four hundred and ninety-eight, that means there should only be one or two left."
She paused, and I saw confusion cross her face.
"But I can't sense them. I can't feel any shards calling. The compulsion is quiet. It's like—it's like there's nothing left to find."
She looked at me, and I saw the first hint of terrible understanding beginning to dawn.
"Where are they?" she whispered. "Where are the last shards?"
I didn't know. Couldn't answer. But something cold settled in my chest, something that had nothing to do with winter and everything to do with fear.
She reached out and touched my face, her fingers gentle near my corrupted eye.
"The shard in your eye," she said slowly. "It's been there since the shattering. Since the very beginning. It's part of the count. Part of the five hundred."
Her hand moved to her own chest, to the place where the largest shard rested.
"And mine. The piece that compels me to gather all the others."
She looked at me, and I saw the horror in her eyes as the truth crystallized.
"There are no more shards to find," she whispered. "Just yours. And mine."
The ember flared in her chest, bright and desperate, as if trying to deny what we both now understood.
The mirror was nearly complete. Four hundred and ninety-eight pieces gathered and placed.
Only two remained.
The one in my eye.
And the one in her heart.

ch.src: S. Nightwell, Winter's Heart: A Snow Queen Tale (2025), Chapter 16: The Final Shard
p: Two days passed like a slow death.
We didn't speak of it—couldn't speak of it, with my voice locked away by the curse and the corruption. But it hung between us like a blade suspended by a thread, waiting to fall.
I tried to tell her. Tried to make her understand what needed to happen.

I would position myself before her, point at my ruined eye—completely blind now, dark as a void, the shard visible as a shadow beneath the surface. I would nod, firm and resolute. I would press my head against her hand, trying to communicate: Do it. Take it. Free yourself.
And every time, she would turn away.
"No," she said the first time, her voice breaking. "Don't ask me to do this."
The second time, she didn't even speak. Just shook her head and walked away, her hands clenched into fists.
By the third day, we were in the shard chamber, standing before the pedestal where all four hundred and ninety-eight pieces rested in a crystalline container that pulsed with dark magic.

The shards called to each other constantly now—a resonance I could feel in my bones, in my corrupted eye, in the very air around us. They wanted to be whole. Wanted to complete what had been shattered. But they couldn't. Not yet. Not until all the pieces were gathered.
Two more. Just two more, and Malakar's trap would spring shut forever.
The argument had become physical.
I planted myself between her and the door. Pointed at my eye. Pointed at the mirror. Nodded with every ounce of determination I possessed.
This is the only way. You know it is.
"I won't," she said, and her voice was steel wrapped in anguish. "I won't do it, Kael. I can't. Don't ask me to kill you."
I moved closer, pressing my forehead against her chest, right where the ember burned. Trying to make her feel what I felt—the certainty, the willingness, the love that made this choice inevitable.
She pushed me back, not hard, but firm. "No. There has to be another way. There has to be—"
I shook my head. Pointed at the mirror again. At my eye. At her.
There is no other way. You know there isn't.

"Then I'll stay cursed!" Her voice rose, echoing off the ice walls. "I'll stay the Snow Queen forever. I'll keep hunting shards that don't exist. I'll—" She stopped, pressing her hands to her face. "I won't kill you. I won't."

The ember flared in her chest, so bright I could see it through her gown, pulsing in time with her heartbeat. The warmth of it filled the chamber, fighting against the cold, fighting against the shard's hold.
Fighting for her.

I wanted to tell her that her refusal was exactly why I loved her. That her willingness to sacrifice herself rather than hurt me was the most beautiful thing I'd ever witnessed. That if I could speak, I would spend hours trying to convince her, to make her understand that my life for her freedom was a trade I would make a thousand times over.
But I couldn't speak. Could only stand there, a mute beast, trying to communicate the impossible with gestures and desperate eyes.
She sank down to sit on the floor, her back against the pedestal that held the chest. I moved to her side and laid my head in her lap, and she buried her fingers in my fur.

"I finally found you," she whispered. "After a century of being alone, of being lost, I finally found someone who sees me. Who stays. Who loves me despite everything I've done. And now you want me to—"
She couldn't finish. Just held onto me like I was the only solid thing in a world that had turned to quicksand.
We sat like that for a long time, the mirror shards looming above us, four hundred and ninety-eight shards glittering in their infernal chest like stars in a corrupted sky.
Two more to go. Two final pieces to complete the demon's masterwork.
And we both knew where they were.
The air shimmered like heat rising from summer pavement, but the warmth that flooded the chamber was autumn—rich and complex and alive with change.

Color exploded across the ice. Golds and crimsons and deep burgundies bled into the frozen walls like watercolor on wet paper. The harsh, cold light softened to something golden, something that felt like late afternoon sun filtering through leaves.
And then she was there.

Cora stepped through the shimmer wearing a threepiece suit in burnt orange, the vest embroidered with falling leaves in copper thread. Her hair was short and swept back, a deep auburn that caught the light like fire. Jewels glittered at her throat, her wrists, her fingers
—topaz and citrine and amber that seemed to hold autumn sunlight captive.
She looked at us with eyes that shifted between gold and brown and green, and smiled—warm and sad and knowing all at once.
"Well," she said, her voice rich and theatrical, "isn't this a pretty little tragedy we've stumbled into?"
Glacia stood quickly, and I rose with her. Cora's gaze moved between us, taking in my blind eye, Glacia's tearstained face, the chest of shards behind us.
"Cora," Glacia whispered. "How did you—"

"Darling, I'm autumn. I know when something's ending." She moved closer, and I noticed her suit had changed—the burnt orange now a deep wine red, the embroidery now done in gold. "I've been watching the paths, you see. All the little doors opening and closing. All the thresholds you might cross." She paused, her expression growing heavier beneath the theatrical delivery. "And I'm afraid, my loves, that they all lead to the same place."

The moment she spoke, something shifted. The corruption that had held my voice captive suddenly loosened, pushed back by autumn's power cutting through winter's tainted magic. I felt it like chains falling away.
"Glacia," I said, and my voice—my actual voice—filled the chamber.
She turned to me, her eyes going wide. "Kael—"
"I can speak," I said, and the wonder of it nearly brought me to my knees. "Gods, I can speak."
I moved to her, and she met me halfway, her hands coming up to touch my face as if she couldn't quite believe it. "Your voice. I can hear your voice."

"My gift to you both," Cora said, and when I looked at her, her hair had grown longer, falling in waves past her shoulders, the color shifting from auburn to a deep mahogany. "A little breathing room in the corruption. The curse remains, sweet bear, but while I'm here, you can speak freely." She gestured dramatically, and suddenly there were chairs that hadn't been there before—carved wood that still held autumn's colors, upholstered in velvet the color of falling leaves. "You'll need that voice. For what comes next."
Glacia's hands tightened on my fur. "What comes next? You mean—"

"I mean we need to have a conversation about endings, darling." Cora moved to one of the chairs and sat with fluid grace, crossing her legs. Her suit had become a dress now—or had it always been a dress? Something flowing and layered in shades of rust and gold. "About thresholds and transformations and the prices we pay to become something new."

A table appeared, laden with wine and bread and autumn fruits. Cora poured wine into two glasses and a large wooden bowl with a flourish, as if we were gathering for a celebration instead of a funeral.
"Sit," she said, and there was command beneath the warmth. "Please. Death deserves more ceremony than standing in the cold."
We sat, though I could feel Glacia trembling beside me. Cora raised her glass in a toast, her rings catching the light—had she been wearing that many before?
"To endings," she said softly. "And to what comes after."
We drank, and the wine tasted of harvest and smoke and the bittersweet beauty of things passing away.

"You've realized the truth," Cora said, setting down her glass. Her hair was short again, slicked back, and she wore a tailored jacket in deep plum. "The final two shards. One in your chest, sister mine, compelling you to gather all the others. And one in his eye, fused there since the shattering."
"Yes," Glacia whispered.

Cora turned to me, and her expression—beneath all the performance, all the shifting beauty—was full of genuine sorrow. "Kael. Ice King. Winter's Hand. Old Man Winter himself." She leaned forward, elbows on her knees, and suddenly she looked more masculine, more angular, her features sharp and knowing. "You understand what you are, don't you? What you've always been?"
"Primordial," I said quietly. "Winter's essence given form."

"Exactly." She snapped her fingers, and sparkles of light danced in the air. "Not mortal. Not even truly immortal like my sisters and me. You're the season itself, darling. Winter walking around in a very handsome package." Her smile faded. "And that's why this is going to hurt so much worse than it should."

She stood and began to pace, and with each step her appearance shifted—masculine, feminine, something in between. Suit to dress to something flowing and undefined. Short hair to long to something swept up with jeweled pins.

"When a shard lodges in a human," she said, gesturing dramatically, "it's like a splinter. Painful, yes. Corrupting, absolutely. But ultimately separate from who they are. You can pull it out—violently, agonizingly

—and they might survive. Many don't, but some do." She stopped pacing and looked at me, and her eyes were ancient and sad. "But you, my dear winter king, are not human. You're not flesh and blood in any conventional sense. You're magic given consciousness. You're winter itself, walking and talking and—" she glanced at Glacia, "—apparently falling in love."
"What are you saying?" Glacia asked, though I could hear in her voice that she already knew.

Cora turned to her, and suddenly she was wearing a suit again—black this time, with a shirt the color of dying leaves. "I'm saying, darling, that the shard isn't just in him. It's part of him now. A century of fusion, of interweaving, of becoming inseparable from his essential nature." She moved closer to Glacia, her voice dropping to something gentler. "Removing it means removing the essence that makes him Kael. It means unraveling winter itself."
"It will kill him," I said quietly.

"Completely," Cora confirmed. "Absolutely. Finally." She looked between us, and I saw tears glittering in her eyes, making her mascara run heavily, despite the theatrical delivery. "There is no other way. I've looked at every door, every threshold, every possible path forward. And they all require the same price."
"No," Glacia said. "No, there has to be—"

"There isn't." Cora's voice was firm but kind.
